prompt: Write a cranky blog post about trying a bunch of new web calendar apps and finding that none of them do what you need. Include a theory about why so many of them exist.
response:
I tried four new web calendar apps over the weekend, and I am now more irritated than I have been since the last time a software company asked me to “sync my workflow.”

My needs are not complicated. I want a month view. I want a week view. I want to put an event on a Tuesday. I want that Tuesday event to repeat every Tuesday, except for two Tuesdays when it does not. I want to drag things around without triggering a modal. I want time zones to work when I am in a different time zone. I want keyboard shortcuts that do not require a certificate. I want to export my data when I leave, because I will leave. I do not want an onboarding tour. I do not want a coach. I do not want the app to notice that I have been “stressed” because I double-booked a dentist appointment and a budget review.

The first one was beautiful. It had a soft gray palette, a floating toolbar, and a command bar that opened when you pressed a key I did not know I was pressing. The landing page promised “time, finally in focus.” I clicked through, created an account, and was immediately asked to connect my email, calendar, chat, notes, and “favorite productivity surfaces.” I did not know what my favorite productivity surfaces were. I have a job and a life. I put in one event: “Dentist, 3 p.m.” It asked if I wanted to “build a routine around it.” No. I want to brush my teeth and avoid pain.

The second one was more serious. It looked like it had been designed by people who actually schedule things. It had proper keyboard navigation, which made me hopeful. Then I tried to create a recurring event with exceptions. It wanted me to create a “series.” Fine. Then it wanted me to edit the series, not the individual occurrence, unless I first “detached” it from the series. I have a standing team meeting every Tuesday at 10 a.m., except next Tuesday and the Tuesday after that because we are in a time zone that does not care about my team. This is not a philosophical problem. It is a Tuesday.

The third one was minimal, which is what I liked at first. The interface was almost empty. No clutter. No badges. No little animated dots suggesting that the calendar was “alive.” But it was so minimal that it had also removed the parts of a calendar that make it useful. No drag-and-drop. No easy way to change an event’s time. No real recurring-event handling. No reliable time zone display. It was a list of text blocks arranged in a grid, and the grid had the emotional depth of a parking garage. I could put my life in it, but only if my life consisted of standing very still.

The fourth one was the worst, because it was trying to be everything. It was a calendar, a task manager, a project board, a chat client, a notes app, and a “personal operating system.” It had templates for freelancers, managers, students, founders, and “intentional humans.” I selected a template and it generated a week for me. It gave me a “morning alignment block,” a “deep work sprint,” and a “reflect on your energy” slot. I had not asked for alignment. I had asked for a place to put “parent-teacher conference” and “pick up dry cleaning.” The app was not helping me organize my time. It was organizing me.

Why are there so many of these?

My theory is that calendars are not the product. Calendars are the trapdoor.

A calendar is the one place where your actual life becomes visible in a structured way. It has dates. It has durations. It has obligations. It has the hard edges of work, family, health, and deadlines. If a company can get you to put your events in its system, it can sit next to your time. It can remind you, suggest, track, measure, optimize, and eventually sell you something adjacent. A notes app wants a calendar so it can say, “Review this note on Friday.” A task app wants a calendar so it can say, “You are behind.” A chat app wants a calendar so it can say, “Are you free now?” A health app wants a calendar so it can say, “You broke your streak.” A project tool wants a calendar so it can say, “Your team is misaligned.”

A calendar is the front door to attention. Everyone wants to own the front door.

The strongest objection to this complaint is that I am the problem. Maybe I am a difficult user. Maybe I am clinging to an old model of software because I do not like change. Maybe these apps are trying to solve real problems I have stopped noticing because I am stuck in my little web-calendar cave, typing “Dentist, 3 p.m.” like a man yelling at the sky.

That is partly true. I am cranky. I do not like being onboarded. I do not like being told my week needs “balance.” I do not like software that treats a simple appointment as a behavior-modification opportunity. But the fact that I could not put a recurring meeting with two exceptions into four separate interfaces in under ten minutes each is not just my failure. A calendar should be able to hold ordinary human nonsense: double bookings, canceled plans, time zone confusion, a child’s school event that moves without notice, a doctor’s office that changes its hours, a boss who says “let’s push that” at 4:58 p.m.

I went back to the old clunky web calendar I have used for years. It looks like it was designed in 2009 by someone who had given up on typography. It has a blue button that says “Save.” It does not know my energy level. It does not have a command bar. It does not ask me to define my “time philosophy.” I can click a day, type an event, move it, delete it, and close the tab.

It is not delightful. It is not a platform. It is not a life OS.

It is a calendar. And for now, that is enough.

prompt: Write a personal essay about the meaning of life, framed around a workshop or dinner conversation. I'm tired of tidy answers and want something thoughtful.
response:
I went to a workshop on the meaning of life because my father had died and I was looking for a sentence that would make the loss sit still. The workshop was in a basement room at a community center, the kind of room with a window that showed only a strip of concrete. The email had called it “A Conversation About What Matters,” which made it sound like a support group for people who had accidentally become alive. There were nineteen chairs. Twelve were filled. The coffee was burnt, and the heating vent made a low clicking sound, as if the building itself were trying to decide whether to stay open.

The facilitator asked us to write on an index card the first answer that came to mind: What is life for? I wrote: To keep going. It was honest and useless. Around the table, people read theirs. “To love.” “To leave things better than you found them.” “To experience as much as possible.” A man in a work jacket said, “To pay for the next meal.” Nobody laughed, because the joke was true.

The room wanted a tidy answer. I could feel it. We had come, maybe, to be told that the mess of being alive had a name, a purpose, a bottom line. If someone had stood up and said, “Life means X,” we would have been disappointed, because X would have been too small. If no one said anything, we would have been disappointed, because we would have left with the same weight. The question is not like a math problem. It does not yield to a clean derivation.

A woman named Elena spoke. She was in her fifties, wearing a coat with a broken button. She said her son had been diagnosed with schizophrenia at nineteen, and for a while she had searched for a reason in the way people search for a cause: if I can find the reason, I can fix it. “I used to think meaning was something you were supposed to know,” she said. “Now I think it’s something you do at 2 a.m. when he’s scared and doesn’t know why.” She did not say it like a lesson. She said it the way someone describes a chore that has become part of the house.

That stayed with me. Not because it was pretty, but because it moved the question from a thing to be found to a way of being present. Meaning was not a hidden object under the rug. It was the shape of a night: the water glass, the low voice, the decision not to argue with a hallucination, the slow waiting for morning. It was also exhaustion, resentment, the way love can feel like a job no one trained you for. A tidy answer would have stripped all that out.

During the break, I talked to a man named David. He was an actuary, or had been, and he told me he had spent thirty years calculating the likelihood of death. “I used to think if you could put a number on it, you could manage it,” he said. His wife had early Alzheimer’s. “Now I sit with a person who is leaving me a little every day, and I can’t adjust to it the way I used to adjust to risk.” He paused. “I don’t know if it means anything. I know it’s happening. That’s different.”

That distinction mattered. Meaning is not the same as significance. A life can be significant without feeling meaningful. A parent can be doing something that matters enormously and feel only drained, absurd, trapped. A person can feel a surge of meaning while doing something shallow. The two do not line up neatly. The world does not issue certificates. Sometimes the most important things are the ones that feel least like answers.

After the workshop, five of us went to a diner. The kind with red vinyl booths and a coffee urn that never seems to empty. We ordered plates we didn’t finish. A young man named Marcus, maybe thirty, said he had come because his mother made him. “She thinks if I don’t find my purpose, I’ll end up dead or bitter,” he said. “I have a job. I lift weights. I watch videos. I try not to be a jerk. Is that supposed to be enough?” The question landed hard. It was the question under the other questions.

If the meaning of life is high—transcendence, legacy, vocation—then most days are failures. If it is low—comfort, pleasure, not hurting anyone—then it can be swallowed by triviality. A life of data entry and gym sessions may be morally decent and existentially thin. A life of grand passion may be destructive. The problem is that the question asks for a scale, but lives are not one-dimensional. They are bundles of attention, obligation, boredom, desire, accident.

I thought of my father in the hospital. The room had a clock that ticked too loudly. He had dementia, not the dramatic kind from movies, but the quiet kind that erases the last ten years first. One morning he looked at me and said, “You’re the wrong person.” I knew he meant my mother. My body answered before I could choose a feeling. But later, when I held his hand, he relaxed. He didn’t know who I was, not really, but he knew the weight of the hand. Was that meaning? It was not an answer. It was a fact: a body recognizing another body in a world where recognition is failing.

That is where the tidy answers fail. They want to say, “Love is the meaning,” or “Service is the meaning,” or “Happiness is the meaning.” But love can be confusing and painful. Service can be exploited. Happiness can be bought or chemically induced. None of them, by itself, does the work. The meaning of a life is not one of its parts. It is more like the pattern that appears when you look at the whole: what a person paid attention to, what they refused, what they could bear, what they changed in others, what they failed to see.

The hardest objection is the one the universe makes by being silent. We are brief. The earth will continue. Our names will be forgotten. The cells in our bodies will be replaced, and then the body will stop. If that is true, then any meaning we claim is a local fiction, a story told by animals who are afraid of the dark. I don’t know how to argue that away. I don’t want to. The silence is part of the question. A meaningful life is not one that escapes the silence; it is one that lives inside it without pretending it isn’t there.

But silence does not make all responses equal. If meaning is only what we make, then a tyrant’s meaning and a nurse’s meaning are on the same level, and that is false. We can judge meanings by how well they account for the world and for other beings. A meaning that requires blindness is not deep; it is a defense. A meaning that survives contact with suffering and boredom, without requiring cruelty or self-deception, has more claim on us. The fact that we die does not make cruelty and kindness the same. It makes them urgent. A hand held in a hospital room is not cosmic. It will not last. It will not be recorded in the stars. But it is a real event: one finite creature answering another. The ground for meaning is not a cosmic purpose. It is our shared exposure to pain, confusion, desire, and death. That ground is thin. It can be misleading. It can be broken by power and self-deception. But it is not nothing. For some, that will not be enough. They will want a guarantee, a voice from outside the system. I don’t have one.

Marcus at the diner asked if not being cruel was enough. I wanted to say yes, because it was a generous standard and a hard one. I also wanted to say no, because a life can be non-cruel and still asleep. You can avoid harm and never really wake up. You can be safe and small. The question is not only what you avoid, but what you answer. What do you turn toward? What do you spend your irrecoverable hours on? What are you willing to be changed by?

Elena said something then that I almost missed. She said, “I don’t think my life has a meaning. I think it has a direction. It keeps pointing toward him.” That was better. Direction is not a destination. It can shift. It can be wrong. It can be imposed by love or obligation or fear. But it is something you can test against the world. If your direction only serves your comfort, it may be thin. If it opens you to what is outside you, if it makes you more capable of seeing and bearing, it has weight.

David said he was trying to learn what his wife liked before she forgot. He had started writing down small things: the way she took her tea, the song that made her hum, the name of her first dog. “It’s like building a map of a country that’s disappearing,” he said. I thought that was a meaning, but I didn’t say it, because the phrase would have made it smaller. It was not a meaning. It was an act of fidelity in the face of loss. It was also grief, and fear, and the stubborn human need to say, You were here. You mattered. I was paying attention.

When we left the diner, the night was cold and the streetlights made the wet pavement look like oil. Nobody said, “So that’s the answer.” We didn’t have one. Maybe that was the point. The meaning of life is not a sentence you can carry home. It is the quality of your attention in the middle of things: whether you are meeting the world as it is, whether you are answering what is asked of you, whether you are willing to be finite. It is made in small, unglamorous acts, and it is always at risk of being lost.

I walked to the bus stop with the question still in me. It did not feel solved. It felt less sharp, maybe, the way a wound is less sharp when you stop trying to ignore it. I didn’t know what my life meant. I knew what was in front of me: the bus, the cold, the people I would see tomorrow, the things I had failed to say, the work of staying awake. That was not a tidy answer. It was the next step.

prompt: I'm a psychiatrist and patients keep asking me to certify their pets as emotional support animals. Write a candid, funny essay from the clinician's side about how that system really works and what's wrong with it, even if the outcome is mostly harmless.
response:
## The Letter for the Cat

The request usually comes near the end of the session, after we have discussed trauma, medications, and whether the patient can get out of bed, in a tone that suggests we have finally arrived at the practical matter. “Can you write a letter for my cat?” The cat has been mentioned twice before: once as a source of comfort, once as the reason the patient is late. Now the cat is about to become a legal actor.

The word patients use is “certify,” and that word does a lot of work. There is no certification. There is no national registry, no exam, no badge, no continuing education for the animal. In the American version of this system, the useful document is usually a letter from a mental health professional saying that the patient has a disability and needs an animal for emotional support. In housing law, the term tends to be “assistance animal,” but in the waiting room it is “my cat” or “my dog” or, in one memorable case, “my very small horse, which is technically a goat.” That is all there is. And yet the letter has the social force of a passport.

In a perfect world, the letter is narrow: I diagnose a condition, the animal is part of the treatment plan, and the need is specific enough to survive contact with reality. In the world I actually inhabit, the letter often starts life as a template found online, with blanks for diagnosis, animal, and signature. The patient prints it, brings it in, and asks me to make it real. Sometimes I rewrite it. Sometimes I refuse. Sometimes I write a different letter that says less than the patient wants and more than I can defend.

The examples are almost silly. A woman with depression wants her beagle certified because the dog “keeps her from spiraling.” A man with anxiety wants his cat because the cat “doesn’t ask questions.” A young person wants a letter for a 120-pound dog because the lease says no pets and the dog is the only family member who doesn’t charge rent. A couple wants their parrot declared necessary so they can keep it in a studio where the walls are paper and the neighbor is asthmatic. A patient with a history of hospitalizations asks for a letter for a cat that has never left the apartment, including the bathroom, and is now being presented as a stabilizing factor in community living.

None of these people is necessarily a villain. That is what makes the whole thing so irritating. Most of them are not trying to defraud anyone. They are trying to keep a source of comfort, avoid a pet fee, stop feeling like a burden, or preserve the one relationship in their life that does not require them to explain themselves. The system is bad because it turns a vulnerable person’s attachment to an animal into a legal argument, and then hands the pen to a clinician who has forty-five minutes and a stack of prior authorizations.

The line between a service animal and an emotional support animal is not always clean, but it is real. A service dog is trained to do things: retrieve medication, interrupt a panic attack, detect a seizure, pull a cart, block a doorway, alert to a drop in blood sugar. The value is task. The animal has a job. An emotional support animal’s value is presence. That is not worthless. A calm dog can make a room feel safer. A cat can make a person feel less alone. But presence is a different claim, and the system has almost no way to verify it except the patient’s word and the clinician’s signature. There is no demonstration. There is no test. The cat sits on the exam table and stares at me with the moral authority of a creature that has never once been asked to justify its own existence.

The honest summary is that most of the time nobody gets hurt. The cat is well fed. The dog does not bite. The landlord is annoyed but not ruined. The parrot screams, but only at the mailman. If the outcome is mostly harmless, why fuss? Because the problem is not the individual cat. The problem is that a clinical judgment has become a consumer good.

A diagnosis is supposed to be a description of a person’s functioning. When it becomes a key to a no-pet building, a waiver of a pet deposit, or a way to keep a dog in a hotel room, the diagnostic language starts to drift. “I have anxiety” becomes “I need a dog.” “The dog helps” becomes “the dog is required.” The patient is not lying, exactly. The patient is translating a real need into the only administrative language available. But the translation is lossy. It flattens a complicated human situation into a sentence on letterhead: *I treat this patient, who has this condition, and this animal is necessary.* That sentence can sound authoritative even when the clinical basis is thin.

Housing is where this bites. A landlord may be required to make a reasonable accommodation for an assistance animal, but the building still contains other humans: people with allergies, people afraid of dogs, people who pay for a quiet unit and get a barking one, people who do not want a stranger’s pet licking their hands in the elevator. The ESA letter does not negotiate that. It simply says, “This animal is part of someone’s treatment,” and leaves everyone else to adjust. That is not malice. It is externalities. The patient gets comfort; the neighbor gets dander; the landlord gets a complaint; the building manager gets a headache. The animal gets a warmer lap and a wider range of movement than it would otherwise have.

There is also the animal. An emotional support animal is not a job. It is a pet asked to stand in for a support system. If the patient is sleeping sixteen hours, the animal may be left in a dark apartment with no exercise. If the patient is having a panic attack, the animal may be held too tightly, scolded, or expected to perform a kind of therapy it was never trained to do. The letter can make the animal indispensable and therefore riskier: the patient cannot give it up, cannot leave it, cannot accept a shelter visit, cannot move, cannot get help, because the help is now also the legal basis for keeping the animal. The cat becomes less a pet and more a fixture, like the refrigerator or the Wi-Fi.

For the clinician, the worst part is that the request makes me a gatekeeper in a domain I did not choose. I am not a housing officer. I am not a landlord. I am not an animal control officer. I am supposed to be treating a person, and suddenly I am deciding whether a cat gets to live in a second-floor apartment. When I say no, I sound like I am taking the dog away. When I say yes, I feel like I have signed a pet ownership permit with medical letterhead. The patient is not asking me to prescribe a medication. The patient is asking me to vouch for a relationship between a human and an animal that I may know almost nothing about. I do not know if the dog is housebroken. I do not know if the cat scratches. I do not know if the “very small horse” has been introduced to other people. I know the patient’s diagnosis, their reported symptoms, and the fact that they brought a photo of the animal with a little bandana on.

You could argue that if the outcome is harmless, the clinician should just sign the paper. Medicine is full of low-stakes paperwork. A note for work, a letter for insurance, a form for a gym. Why be precious about a cat? The answer is that the note is not low-stakes if it is being used to override a rule that protects other people. A work note says, “This person cannot lift heavy boxes for two weeks.” It does not say, “This person is entitled to bring a goat to the office.” The difference is that the first describes a limitation; the second grants a right in a shared space. Once the letter starts doing that kind of work, it is no longer just a note. It is a claim on other people’s tolerance, their property, their noses, their nerves.

There is also the trust problem. If landlords learn that ESA letters are easy to obtain, they may deny legitimate requests. If patients learn that a letter can be obtained without a real treatment connection, they may stop engaging in harder treatment. If clinicians become known for signing anything, the profession’s credibility suffers. I have seen what happens when a medical document becomes a magic word. People stop asking whether the claim is true and start asking whether the form is filled out correctly. The question changes from “Does this patient need this animal?” to “Does this letter look official enough?” That is not medicine. That is bureaucracy with a stethoscope.

What I look for now is not dramatic. I ask what the animal does for the patient that no other thing can do. How often is the animal present? What happens when the animal is not available? Is the animal safe, manageable, and under the patient’s control? Is the need tied to a diagnosis, not just a preference? Does the patient have any other supports, or is the animal the entire support structure? If the answer is that the animal is genuinely part of the treatment, I may write a letter. But I write it as a clinical opinion, not a certification. I name the animal, the diagnosis, the functional need, and the limits. I do not say “the animal is required” unless I truly mean that. I do not turn the diagnosis into a talisman. And I do not pretend that I have evaluated the animal, because I have not. I have evaluated the patient’s claim about the animal, which is a different and much weaker thing.

The system is wrong because it asks a clinician to certify something that is not certifiable. It takes a real human need, attaches it to a pet, and then demands a piece of paper that can be used against third parties who were never part of the treatment. It mistakes comfort for necessity, presence for function, and a signature for proof. Most of the time the damage is small: a cat in a no-pet building, a dog that barks at the mail, a landlord who has to reread the Fair Housing Act at 10 p.m. But the smallness of the harm is not the point. The point is that the system has made a clinical relationship into a loophole, and then blamed the clinician for not operating it well enough.

The cat, of course, remains indifferent. It has never read the housing code. It does not care whether I use the phrase “disability-related need.” It will sit on the letter while I sign it, as if to say, “I am the real clinician here.”

prompt: I just found out some online forum members pool money to synthesize experimental drugs and try them on themselves. It's obviously reckless, yet I feel weirdly pleased it exists. Write a short blog post making sense of that mixed reaction.
response:
**The Strange Comfort of Recklessness**

When I found out that a group of online forum members pool money to synthesize experimental drugs and test them on themselves, my first thought was: this is insane. Of course it is. Unknown substances, unknown doses, unknown interactions, no medical backup, no safety net. One bad batch can end a life or leave someone with damage that never fully fades.

And yet, I felt a small, uncomfortable pleasure. Not because I want to do it. Not because I think it’s wise. But because it feels like a raw, almost old-fashioned form of curiosity: people deciding, against the grain of modern caution, that they would rather find out than wait for permission.

That’s the part that pulls at me. We live in a culture that has made risk so official, so managed, so full of disclaimers that it can sometimes feel like the unknown has been papered over. “Consult a professional.” “Follow the guidelines.” “Wait for the study.” All reasonable, mostly. But there’s something in human nature that resists being kept perfectly safe. We want to press on the edge, even when the edge is thin.

What I’m pleased by, I think, is not the recklessness itself but the energy behind it. These are people taking responsibility in a very direct, very dangerous way. They’re not waiting for an institution to tell them what can be known. They’re forming a community around a question, putting money where their curiosity is, and accepting the consequences. There’s a kind of seriousness in that, even when the method is terrible.

The mixed feeling comes from recognizing both sides at once: the impulse is understandable, maybe even admirable in spirit, but the practice is brutal. Curiosity does not become wisdom just because it’s brave. A body is not a laboratory. And the people who disappear from these stories don’t get to post updates.

So the pleasure I feel is probably less approval and more recognition. It’s the part of me that still wants to know what happens, even when knowing might cost too much. The healthiest version of that impulse isn’t to imitate them. It’s to take the question seriously without turning myself into the experiment.

prompt: People on Twitter are sharing their salaries publicly this week. You've had an unusual tech career: a Japanese salaryman job, a consulting practice, a few small software businesses. Write a candid post that makes the case for talking openly about pay and puts your own numbers on the table, with whatever lessons you think younger engineers should take from them.
response:
I’m putting my numbers up this week, rounded and approximate, because salary secrecy is mostly a company advantage. When only the employer knows what you make, the employer can decide what you’re worth. When a few dozen engineers exchange rough numbers, the market shows up. I’m not saying every exact W-2 should be public. I’m saying if you can share total cash safely, do it: base, bonus, signing, location, currency, and whether the number is pre-tax or post-tax.

My career has been unusual enough that maybe my numbers are less likely to be copied and more likely to be useful.

1. **2009–2012: Japanese “salaryman” software engineer at a systems integrator in Osaka.**  
   First-year base: 3.2M yen, about $22k. Bonuses: two, totaling around 1.5 months, so maybe $25k all-in before overtime. Overtime was expected; some was paid, some wasn’t. I thought it was normal because every new grad around me got a similar number.  
   Lesson: a low salary can feel like the price of entry until you learn it is often just the price of not negotiating. My actual leverage was boring: I could do Japanese client work in English, and I was willing to sit in rooms with older engineers and ask questions. That later became worth a lot. Don’t mistake a local norm for your value.

2. **2013–2018: independent consulting.**  
   I started by fixing broken integrations for mid-size companies. First year revenue: $85k. I took home maybe $42k after tax, health, and the mess of being my own accountant. Peak year: $470k revenue. I took about $210k. That sounds good next to Japan, but it was a trap: I was selling hours. No product, no equity, no team that could earn without me. If I got sick for a month, income dropped.  
   Lesson: consulting is a great way to learn what customers pay for, but it is not a career unless you convert it into something that compounds—software, equity, a firm, or a product.

3. **2018–2020: first micro-SaaS.**  
   I built a small tool for construction companies. Revenue: $16k year one, $58k year two. Net profit: negative. I took $0 from it for most of that period. I kept going because I thought the product had a chance, and because I had savings from consulting. It died.  
   Lesson: small business income is not salary. If someone says “I make $100k from my SaaS,” ask whether that is revenue, profit, or founder salary after burn. The difference is everything.

prompt: Everyone says reusing other people's code is good and reinventing the wheel is bad. Is that actually true? Write a blog post on when a software company should build things itself versus buy or outsource.
response:
# Build, buy, or outsource? The wheel question is the wrong question

The advice to reuse code is aimed at a real failure: companies waste time building generic plumbing because it is interesting or because they want to own every layer. A startup that spends four months building its own identity provider before its product works is not being strategic; it is being cute.

But the same advice can become a bad habit. “Reuse” sounds free. It is not. It transfers work from your codebase to your integration layer, your vendor risk, your data model, and your future flexibility. The right question is not “Has someone else written this code?” It is “What is this capability doing for our business?”

A wheel is a bad thing to reinvent if you are building a carriage. It becomes a different question if you are building a car.

## The default should be buy, but only for real wheels

For most software companies, many systems are wheels: authentication, payments, email, search, logging, monitoring, data warehouses, tax calculation, fraud screening, basic CRM. If you are not selling identity, do not build an identity provider. If you are not a payments company, do not build card processing. If you are not an observability company, do not build your own application performance monitoring from scratch.

The time saved is real. A small team can spend months on token rotation, recovery flows, MFA, audit logs, and compliance before it has something a mature provider already has. A company that needs to send transactional email is usually better off using a provider than writing SMTP handling, bounce processing, and deliverability monitoring itself.

“Buy” also includes open source. Using Postgres instead of writing a database is usually right. Using a PDF library instead of inventing one is usually right. The key is that the component is replaceable and not where customers form their opinion of you.

## But reuse has a price

Every external dependency is a decision about who controls your future. A SaaS tool may be cheap at first and then become expensive as you scale. If you process $100M in card transactions a year, a common card fee of 3% is $3M. If your product is high-volume payments, that number is not a detail; it is your business. A company that can negotiate direct banking relationships or optimize payment routing may save enough to justify an in-house team. Most companies cannot, and should not try.

Vendor APIs also shape your product. If a CRM lacks the fields your sales process needs, you end up building workarounds on top of it. If a search service cannot rank the way your marketplace needs, you may spend years gluing together filters and heuristics. The cost of reuse is not just the invoice. It is the integration code, the data exports, the security review, the support tickets, the fear of price changes, and the exit plan you hope you never need.

Open source has a different cost: you inherit maintenance. A library can be abandoned, can have a vulnerability, can change its license, can require a database version you do not want. Reusing code is not outsourcing risk away; sometimes it is accepting risk into your own on-call rotation.

A small example: suppose a 12-person startup needs customer support. A helpdesk SaaS costs $1,000 a month and takes a week to configure. Building an internal ticketing system might take two engineers for three months. At a rough $10,000 per engineer-month, that is $60,000 before maintenance. Unless the support workflow is unique and central, the SaaS wins. Now suppose the company is selling a support automation product. The same ticketing system is the product. Then the $60,000 is not overhead; it is the thing customers are paying for.

## Build when the thing is the product

A logistics company should build routing because routing quality is the product. A job board should invest in search and matching because candidates and employers choose it based on relevance. A developer-tools company should build the CLI, API, or agent that makes developers feel the difference. If the capability is the reason customers pick you, buying it usually means buying someone else’s average.

Netflix is a useful example. It built Open Connect, a network of caches placed with internet service providers, to reduce bandwidth costs and improve streaming performance. It also invested heavily in recommendation and personalization because the streaming experience itself was the product. For a company selling a different thing, those same systems would be plumbing.

The same logic applies to data. If your product improves by learning from usage, the data pipeline and model serving may be core. If you are just storing logs for debugging, a managed warehouse is probably fine.

## Build when the external option constrains your core

Sometimes the right move is not “build everything” but “build the piece that the vendor makes slow, expensive, or impossible.” If your core workflow requires a data model that no SaaS supports, you may need to own that data model. If your customers are in regulated industries and you cannot send data to a third-party processor, you may need to host the function yourself. If your product’s speed depends on a query pattern that a managed service cannot optimize, you may need to tune, fork, or replace it.

The test is whether the external dependency is a ceiling. If it limits the thing you are trying to become, it stops being a wheel and starts being a constraint.

This is also where “buy” can be a trap. If you depend on a small vendor, you are buying a bet that the company survives, stays profitable, and remains aligned with your roadmap. If your product’s main feature is a thin wrapper around that vendor’s API, your moat is thin and your margin depends on the vendor’s choices.

## The strongest objection: companies are bad at building

The strongest objection to this view is that companies are bad at building. They start infrastructure projects that never end, hire platform engineers to solve problems that a SaaS would have solved in a week, and lose focus. That is true often enough that the buy-first advice is well earned.

The mistake is not that building is risky. The mistake is building without a business reason. A company should not build authentication because it wants to understand authentication. It should build authentication because identity is its product, or because no acceptable external identity system exists for its customers. It should not build a data warehouse because it dislikes vendor pricing; it should build one because analytics is its core product or because the external options prevent the analyses it needs.

Internal ownership is a cost center unless it protects or creates something important. If the answer to “what are we protecting?” is “our engineers like it,” that is not a business case.

## Outsource when it is a project, not a capability

Outsourcing is most defensible for bounded work: a marketing site, a one-time data migration, a mobile app that will not be the core product, a legacy system rewrite with a known end. The deliverable is finite, the requirements are stable, and the company will not need to evolve it every week.

It is less defensible when you outsource a living platform and then expect the vendor to understand your strategy. If the system must change as fast as your business, you need internal ownership of the design, even if some implementation is contracted. Outsourcing can save time; it can also leave you with a system you cannot change without the original team, a vendor who no longer answers emails, or a codebase that encodes assumptions nobody remembers.

## A practical test

Before choosing, ask:

1. If we bought this, would we be buying a commodity or a core differentiator?
2. How much of our revenue, growth, or brand depends on doing this better than the vendor’s default?
3. What is the total cost of ownership, including integration, operations, security, and switching?
4. Can we leave? If we stored all our data in a proprietary format, is that acceptable?
5. What happens in three years if this becomes central? If the answer is “we will be stuck,” buy carefully or build.
6. What happens if we build it badly? If the failure is a tax on the company, buy.

When in doubt, buy the commodity, but keep the data in a format you can leave, and reserve internal engineering for the parts where your customers can tell the difference. The real failure is not building a wheel; it is choosing a dependency without understanding what it will constrain later.

# Build, buy, or outsource? The wheel question is the wrong question

The advice to reuse code is aimed at a real failure: companies waste time building generic plumbing because it is interesting or because they want to own every layer. A startup that spends four months building its own identity provider before its product works is not being strategic; it is being cute.

But the same advice can become a bad habit. "Reuse" sounds free. It is not. It transfers work from your codebase to your integration layer, your vendor risk, your data model, and your future flexibility. The right question is not "Has someone else written this code?" It is "What is this capability doing for our business?"

## The default should be buy, but only for real wheels

For most software companies, many systems are wheels: authentication, payments, email, search, logging, monitoring, data warehouses, tax calculation, fraud screening, basic CRM. If you are not selling identity, do not build an identity provider. If you are not a payments company, do not build card processing. If you are not an observability company, do not build your own APM from scratch.

The time saved is real. A small team can spend months on token rotation, recovery flows, MFA, audit logs, and compliance before it has something a mature provider already has. A company that needs to send transactional email is usually better off using a provider than writing SMTP handling, bounce processing, and deliverability monitoring itself.

"Buy" also includes open source. Using Postgres instead of writing a database is usually right. Using a PDF library instead of inventing one is usually right. The key is that the component is replaceable and not where customers form their opinion of you.

## But reuse has a price

Every external dependency is a decision about who controls your future. A SaaS tool may be cheap at first and then become expensive as you scale. If you process $100M in card transactions a year, a 3% fee is $3M. If your product is high-volume payments, that number is not a detail; it is your business. A company that can negotiate direct banking relationships or optimize payment routing may save enough to justify an in-house team. Most companies cannot, and should not try.

Vendor APIs also shape your product. If a CRM lacks the fields your sales process needs, you end up building workarounds on top of it. If a search service cannot rank the way your marketplace needs, you may spend years gluing together filters and heuristics. The cost of reuse is not just the invoice. It is the integration code, the data exports, the security review, the support tickets, the fear of price changes, and the exit plan you hope you never need.

Open source has a different cost: you inherit maintenance. A library can be abandoned, can have a vulnerability, can change its license, can require a database version you do not want. Reusing code is not outsourcing risk away; sometimes it is accepting risk into your own on-call rotation.

A small example: suppose a 12-person startup needs customer support. A helpdesk SaaS costs $1,000 a month and takes a week to configure. Building an internal ticketing system might take two engineers for three months. At a rough $15,000 per engineer-month, that is $90,000 before maintenance. Unless the support workflow is unique and central, the SaaS wins. Now suppose the company is selling a support automation product. The same ticketing system is the product. Then the $90,000 is not overhead; it is the thing customers are paying for.

## Build when the thing is the product

A logistics company should build routing because routing quality is the product. A job board should invest in search and matching because candidates and employers choose it based on relevance. A developer-tools company should build the CLI, API, or agent that makes developers feel the difference. If the capability is the reason customers pick you, buying it usually means buying someone else's average.

Netflix is a useful example. It invested heavily in streaming infrastructure, encoding, delivery, and recommendation systems because the streaming experience itself was the product. The cost and performance of delivery mattered to both users and the business. For a company selling a different thing, those same systems would be plumbing.

The same logic applies to data. If your product improves by learning from usage, the data pipeline and model serving may be core. If you are just storing logs for debugging, a managed warehouse is probably fine.

## Build when the external option constrains your core

Sometimes the right move is not "build everything" but "build the piece that the vendor makes slow, expensive, or impossible." If your core workflow requires a data model that no SaaS supports, you may need to own that data model. If your customers are in regulated industries and you cannot send data to a third-party processor, you may need to host the function yourself. If your product's speed depends on a query pattern that a managed service cannot optimize, you may need to tune, fork, or replace it.

The test is whether the external dependency is a ceiling. If it limits the thing you are trying to become, it stops being a wheel and starts being a cage.

This is also where "buy" can be a trap. If you depend on a small vendor, you are buying a bet that the company survives, stays profitable, and remains aligned with your roadmap. If your product's main feature is a thin wrapper around that vendor's API, you have not built a company; you have built a reseller with extra steps.

## The strongest objection: companies are bad at building

The strongest objection to this view is that companies are bad at building. They start infrastructure projects that never end, hire platform engineers to solve problems that a SaaS would have solved in a week, and lose focus. That is true often enough that the buy-first advice is well earned.

The mistake is not that building is risky. The mistake is building without a business reason. A company should not build authentication because it wants to understand authentication. It should build authentication because identity is its product, or because no acceptable external identity system exists for its customers. It should not build a data warehouse because it dislikes vendor pricing; it should build one because analytics is its core product or because the external options prevent the analyses it needs.

In other words, internal ownership is a cost center unless it protects or creates something important. If the answer to "what are we protecting?" is "our engineers like it," that is not a business case.

## Outsource when it is a project, not a capability

Outsourcing is most defensible for bounded work: a marketing site, a one-time data migration, a mobile app that will not be the core product, a legacy system rewrite with a known end. The deliverable is finite, the requirements are stable, and the company will not need to evolve it every week.

It is less defensible when you outsource a living platform and then expect the vendor to understand your strategy. If the system must change as fast as your business, you need internal ownership of the design, even if some implementation is contracted. Outsourcing can save time; it can also leave you with a system you cannot change without the original team, a vendor who no longer answers emails, or a codebase that encodes assumptions nobody remembers.

## A practical test

Before choosing, I would ask:

1. If we bought this, would we be buying a commodity or a core differentiator?
2. How much of our revenue, growth, or brand depends on doing this better than the vendor's default?
3. What is the total cost of ownership, including integration, operations, security, and switching?
4. Can we leave? If we stored all our data in a proprietary format, is that acceptable?
5. What happens in three years if this becomes central? If the answer is "we will be stuck," buy carefully or build.
6. What happens if we build it badly? If the failure is a tax on the company, buy.

When in doubt, buy the commodity, but keep the data in a format you can leave, and reserve internal engineering for the parts where your customers can tell the difference. The real failure is not building a wheel. It is building a cage and calling it strategy.

prompt: Write something atmospheric and a bit unhinged: a person who normally avoids San Francisco ends up walking its streets alone in the dark just before sunrise, and the city starts to feel like the place where the world ends. Feel free to bring in poetry.
response:
I have always avoided San Francisco the way a dog avoids a door it once walked through and came back different. I do not say this with certainty. I only know that when I see a postcard of the bridge, my stomach turns over like a coin. So when I opened my eyes in a room above a laundromat on Steiner Street, the heater ticking like a trapped insect, and the streetlight outside made the curtain the color of a bruise, I did not ask how I had come to be there. I knew better than to ask.

It was 4:07 a.m. The city was empty in the way a throat is empty before it swallows. I pulled on my coat, took the key from the lock, and went down the stairs. The fog was not coming in; it was already inside, standing in the middle of intersections, draped over the hydrants, leaning against the parked cars with the patience of something that had been waiting for me. Eucalyptus smelled of medicine and burnt sugar. The hills rose around me, each street a steep tongue tasting the dark, and every time I reached what I thought was the top, the city tilted again and showed me another drop into black.

No one walked. No one slept, either. I passed a laundromat, a bodega, a church with its windows painted the blue of a drowned vein. A cat sat on a mailbox and did not blink. Its eyes were not eyes but two small holes punched in the night, and through them I could see the fog moving in a direction that had no name. I kept walking because stopping seemed to invite the city to notice me.

At the corner of Fillmore and Mason, a cable car appeared out of the murk. It had no driver. The bells rang once, a thin metallic cry, and the car swung down the hill, its red body catching the streetlights like a wound that had learned to glow. I followed it. It did not stop. I did not stop. The streets climbed and climbed, and the names changed in my head: not streets anymore but arteries, capillaries, the small white bones of a body learning to die. Leavenworth. Laguna. Post. Each sign a word from a liturgy I had once heard in a dream.

Then I saw the poem. It was not written on a wall or scratched into a bench. It was simply in the air, or in me, or on the back of my eyelids, in letters made of fog:

> Here the city kneels  
> in the salt of its own ending,  
> fog on its knees,  
> streetlamps like prayers  
> that have forgotten the god.  
> Walk west, walker,  
> the map is a mouth  
> and the Pacific is the tooth.

I wanted to laugh. The laugh came out as a cough, wet and small, and the fog swallowed it. Around me the buildings began to thin. The fog rolled over the tops of the houses like a tide, and I understood that I was no longer in a city but on the edge of a thing. San Francisco is a peninsula, I remembered, a finger of land pressed into the water, a place where the continent narrows and forgets itself. In daylight it is tourists and coffee and hills full of houses with names like Paradise or Corona. At this hour it was a threshold. The Transamerica Pyramid flickered in the distance, a needle trying to stitch the sky shut. The Golden Gate was not a bridge but a gate, and beyond it the dark moved with the slow certainty of a sea that had no bottom.

I reached the seawall. The fog pressed against my face, cold and wet, tasting of iron and old salt. The streetlights made haloes in the mist, and each halo contained a shape that was almost a person. I looked for a door, a bus stop, a taxi, a window with light in it. There was only the wall and the dark water beyond it, the water making small sounds like fingers tapping on glass. The city climbed behind me, all its empty streets tilted upward, all its lamps burning with the pale exhaustion of the just before. I thought: this is where it ends. Not with fire, not with trumpets, but with a hill after hill after hill, a street that never levels, a fog that does not lift because there is nothing above it to lift into.

The sky began to change. Not brighten—change. A gray light opened in the east, thin as a cut, and for a moment the whole city looked like a model made of bone and wire. The fog thinned enough for me to see the water, black and endless, and the water was not moving away from the shore; it was moving toward it, inch by inch, patient as a thought. I took a step back. Then another. My feet knew the streets before I did. I walked uphill, and the city accepted me, or refused to release me, or simply continued. Behind me, the first light touched the bay and the bay did not answer. Ahead, the hills rose, and the streets went on, and the poem was still there, only now it had one more line:

> And the walker who came from nowhere  
> became the city’s last name.

I have always avoided San Francisco the way a dog avoids a door it once walked through and came back different. I do not say this with certainty. I only know that when I see a postcard of the bridge, my stomach turns over like a coin. So when I opened my eyes in a room above a laundromat on Steiner Street, the heater ticking like a trapped insect, and the streetlight outside made the curtain the color of a bruise, I did not ask how I had come to be there. I knew better than to ask.

It was 4:07 a.m. The city was empty in the way a throat is empty before it swallows. I pulled on my coat, took the key from the lock, and went down the stairs. The fog was not coming in; it was already inside, standing in the middle of intersections, draped over the hydrants, leaning against the parked cars with the patience of something that had been waiting for me. Eucalyptus smelled of medicine and burnt sugar. The hills rose around me, each street a steep tongue tasting the dark, and every time I reached what I thought was the top, the city tilted again and showed me another drop into black.

No one walked. No one slept, either. I passed a laundromat, a bodega, a church with its windows painted the blue of a drowned vein. A cat sat on a mailbox and did not blink. Its eyes were not eyes but two small holes punched in the night, and through them I could see the fog moving in a direction that had no name. I kept walking because stopping seemed to invite the city to notice me.

At the corner of Fillmore and Mason, a cable car appeared out of the murk. It had no driver. The bells rang once, a thin metallic cry, and the car swung down the hill, its red body catching the streetlights like a wound that had learned to glow. I followed it. It did not stop. I did not stop. The streets climbed and climbed, and the names changed in my head: not streets anymore but arteries, capillaries, the small white bones of a body learning to die. Leavenworth. Laguna. Post. Each sign a word from a liturgy I had once heard in a dream.

Then I saw the poem. It was not written on a wall or scratched into a bench. It was simply in the air, or in me, or on the back of my eyelids, in letters made of fog:

Here the city kneels
in the salt of its own ending,
fog on its knees,
streetlamps like prayers
that have forgotten the god.
Walk west, walker,
the map is a mouth
and the Pacific is the tooth.

I wanted to laugh. The laugh came out as a cough, wet and small, and the fog swallowed it. Around me the buildings began to thin. The fog rolled over the tops of the houses like a tide, and I understood that I was no longer in a city but on the edge of a thing. San Francisco is a peninsula, I remembered, a finger of land pressed into the water, a place where the continent narrows and forgets itself. In daylight it is tourists and coffee and hills full of houses with names like Paradise or Corona. At this hour it was a threshold. The Transamerica Pyramid flickered in the distance, a needle trying to stitch the sky shut. The Golden Gate was not a bridge but a gate, and beyond it the dark moved with the slow certainty of a sea that had no bottom.

I reached the seawall. The fog pressed against my face, cold and wet, tasting of iron and old salt. The streetlights made haloes in the mist, and each halo contained a shape that was almost a person. I looked for a door, a bus stop, a taxi, a window with light in it. There was only the wall and the dark water beyond it, the water making small sounds like fingers tapping on glass. The city climbed behind me, all its empty streets tilted upward, all its lamps burning with the pale exhaustion of the just before. I thought: this is where it ends. Not with fire, not with trumpets, but with a hill after hill after hill, a street that never levels, a fog that does not lift because there is nothing above it to lift into.

The sky began to change. Not brighten—change. A gray light opened in the east, thin as a cut, and for a moment the whole city looked like a model made of bone and wire. The fog thinned enough for me to see the water, black and endless, and the water was not moving away from the shore; it was moving toward it, inch by inch, patient as a thought. I took a step back. Then another. My feet knew the streets before I did. I walked uphill, and the city accepted me, or refused to release me, or simply continued. Behind me, the first light touched the bay and the bay did not answer. Ahead, the hills rose, and the streets went on, and the poem was still there, only now it had one more line:

And the walker who came from nowhere
became the city’s last name.

prompt: Tell the origin story of how a musician selling his own CD online accidentally started a business. Write it as a blog post.
response:
# How Selling My Own CD Online Accidentally Started a Business

I didn’t set out to start a company. In the fall of 2011, I set out to sell twenty-five CDs of a six-song EP I had recorded in a friend’s basement. The EP was called *Late Light*, the cover was a photo of a parking lot at dusk, and the whole project had cost $540 between studio time, printing, and a trip to the post office that ended with me buying a roll of packing tape I still had on my shelf.

I had no label, no distributor, and no real idea how online stores worked. What I did have was a laptop, a PayPal account, and a one-page website that said, in effect: here is the music, and if you want a copy, send money. I built the page on a Tuesday night because I was nervous that a real store would look too serious. A simple button felt safer. It also felt honest. I was not Amazon. I was a guy with a guitar and a laptop.

The first order was from my sister. She bought one CD and a poster, though the poster was just a PDF I had saved as an image. The second was from a friend in Columbus. The third was from a woman in Minneapolis who wrote to say her father “listens to that kind of thing” and asked if I could ship two copies to different addresses. I had never shipped to two addresses before. I made two envelopes, wrote the labels by hand, and went to the post office after work. When I came home, I wrote the details in a small notebook: date, customer, city, items, shipping, total.

The notebook filled faster than I expected. By the end of the second month, there were thirty-one orders. I made a spreadsheet because the notebook had become a mess of crossed-out numbers and sticky notes. The columns were plain: order number, name, email, CD, poster, shirt, shipping, total, paid, shipped. I added the shirt column after a fan in Austin asked whether I had T-shirts. I did not. I ordered twelve from a print shop, paid $9 each, and added a photo of one to the website. That was the first time I understood that the store was not really selling a CD. It was selling a small package of the artist: the music, the image, the feeling that someone was actually answering the email.

The unglamorous part came quickly. A customer in Canada asked why her order had customs charges. I had not thought about international duties. I refunded the shipping and wrote back that I was sorry. A CD arrived cracked in the mail, and I sent a replacement with a note that said, “Please don’t play this one near a window.” A fan asked for a receipt because he was writing the CD off as a business expense. I printed the spreadsheet, highlighted the row, stapled it to a sheet of paper, and mailed it. None of this was exciting. It was the kind of work that makes a young musician feel old. But it also taught me how the thing actually worked: people paid, I needed to confirm, pack, ship, record the money, and answer the questions that always arrived after the sale.

The accidental turn happened when a singer from another local band asked if I could put his EP online. He had heard I was “doing the website thing” for myself. I said I could, but I was busy. He offered one hundred dollars. I thought about it for a day, then copied my one-page site, changed the name and colors, uploaded his cover art, and set up a PayPal button for him. It took four hours, mostly because I could not decide whether his bio should be first person or third. He paid me the next morning. Two weeks later, another band asked. Then a friend of a friend. Then a musician who had never sold anything before and was terrified of setting up a payment account.

I started calling it Backroom Music because most of the records I worked with were made in backrooms, basements, and spare bedrooms. The name was not a brand strategy. It was just true. At first, the service was only a copied website and a set of instructions. A band would send me cover art, a short bio, and a list of prices. I would build the page, connect the payment account, and email them the link. I charged one hundred fifty dollars, then two hundred, then two hundred fifty. I kept a folder of templates: a music page, a merch page, a shipping notice, a mailing list signup, and a FAQ that explained how long delivery took and what to do if an order was lost.

The business became real when I stopped treating it as a favor. I opened a separate bank account. I made simple invoices. I learned enough about sales tax to stop panicking when a customer in another state asked for a total. I built a basic dashboard so bands could see their orders without emailing me at midnight. I wrote down the answers to the same questions: How do I add a new item? What should I charge for shipping? What do I tell a customer when a package is delayed? Each answer became a paragraph in a help file. Each help file made the next store faster to build.

People sometimes call it lucky that I found a niche. I do not think it was luck, exactly. It was the result of a small chain of boring decisions. I could have ignored the Canadian refund and let the problem go away. I could have refused to make T-shirts because they were extra work. I could have told the other bands to figure out their own websites. Instead, I kept doing the next small task: wrap the CD, update the spreadsheet, answer the email, fix the mistake. The business did not arrive in a flash. It accumulated, one order and one template at a time.

Now Backroom Music runs stores for a few dozen independent artists. They sell CDs, vinyl, cassettes, T-shirts, posters, and digital downloads. Some of them make a few hundred dollars a year. A few make enough to press a new record or pay a musician on the road. Last Tuesday, a band in Asheville sold out a run of one hundred cassettes in six hours. The alert came in at 6:14 a.m. I opened the dashboard, watched the orders appear, and felt the same small jolt I got the first time a stranger bought a CD from a page I had built on a Tuesday night.

That is the origin story, if it can be called that. A musician with a stack of CDs, a notebook, a payment button, and a habit of answering email. The company was not the original goal. It was the shape the work took after enough orders, refunds, and copied pages had passed through it.

A child sees a dolphin and says "fish." A parent may say "No, it's a mammal." The child has not made a grammatical error. The word fits some of the evidence: the animal is in water, it has fins, it is long, it swims. It is about which set of facts the word is supposed to carry.

This is the whole problem. If every category is a human invention, then calling a dolphin a fish, or Pluto a planet, seems like a matter of taste. But if categories are simply out there in nature, then we cannot explain why people disagree, why science revises them, or why a word can be right in one room and wrong in another. The better answer is that categories are made, but they are not made from nothing. They are tools for cutting the world into parts that can be reasoned about. A category is wrong when it cuts badly: when it groups things that do not share the features that matter, or separates things that do, or when it invites inferences that fail.

prompt: Software teams keep arguing about who should write the spec and who should own product design. Write an essay about where that job should sit in an organization, who to hire for it, and who not to, drawing on any big-company experience you have.
response:
The argument usually begins with a word that means too many things. A spec can be a statement of the customer problem, a description of the user experience, or a plan for the code. “Product design” makes it worse. In some companies it means designing the interface; in others it means deciding what the product should be. When a team asks, “Who should write the spec?” without separating those, it is really asking who gets to control the product. The better question is who should own the product decision, and which artifacts should be owned by design and engineering.

I don’t have first-hand big-company experience, so I’ll be explicit about the evidence I’m using: public practices, hiring patterns, and the failure modes that show up when product teams scale. The pattern is consistent enough to be useful. In large software organizations, the product decision should sit with a product manager or product owner. That person is accountable for why the work matters, who it is for, what success looks like, and what is out of scope. They do not have to be the best writer, the best designer, or the best engineer. They do have to be the person the organization can hold responsible when the “why” is wrong.

Ownership is not authorship. The product owner can draft the spec, but a strong team will have designers and engineers editing it. The point is that when there is a conflict, the product owner’s judgment is the one that closes the loop. In a small team, one person can hold the product, design, and technical picture without much harm. In a large company, the separation is not bureaucracy; it is a way to keep the product decision visible when many teams depend on it.

This matters because every other default ownership produces a recognizable distortion. If engineering owns the product spec, the product tends to become whatever is clean to build. Engineers will still make great products, but the default bias is toward technical elegance, internal consistency, and risk reduction. If design owns it, the product tends to become whatever is most coherent as an experience. That can be excellent, but the default bias is toward the user’s immediate journey rather than the company’s strategic tradeoff. If sales owns it, the product becomes whatever the loudest customer asked for. If support owns it, it becomes a patch layer over the real problem. None of these groups is bad. The mistake is making one input the default owner of the whole decision.

Potential essay:

"The fight usually starts with a misnamed document. A 'spec' can be a statement of the problem, a description of the experience, or a plan for the code. When one role owns all three, the team either slows down or silently lets the loudest person win. The clean answer is not that one person writes the spec. The clean answer is that one person owns the product decision, and the supporting documents have their own owners.

In a large company, the product decision should sit with a product manager or product owner. That person is accountable for why the work matters, who it is for, what success looks like, and what is out of scope. They do not need to be the best writer on the team, but they must be the person who can say no to a feature because it does not serve the goal. If that accountability sits with engineering, the product becomes whatever is easiest to build. If it sits with design, it becomes whatever is most elegant. If it sits with sales, it becomes whatever the largest customer asked for. None of those is wrong as input; all of them are dangerous as default.

The product manager's spec should be short enough to be argued with. It should name the customer, the job, the current pain, the proposed change, the metric that will show it worked, and the explicit non-goals. It should not specify button colors, component names, or database schemas. Those belong to design and engineering. A good product spec is a decision, not a manual. If a product manager writes a 30-page document describing every screen state, they have usually drifted into design; if they write only a one-liner, 'make checkout faster,' they have not done the product work.

Product design should own the experience spec. That means the flow, the content, the edge cases, the accessibility constraints, and the questions that only become visible when the idea is made concrete. A designer's prototype is not decoration; it is a test of assumptions. But the designer should not own the business case. They can and should challenge whether the goal is right, but the final call on scope and priority belongs to the product owner. This is where the hardest objection lives: in many product-led companies, the designer is closest to the user and has the most concrete picture of the solution. It feels natural to let them own the spec. The risk is that user empathy gets mistaken for product strategy. A designer can make a delightful flow that solves a small problem, or a beautiful interface for a feature nobody needs. The product manager's job is to hold the larger tradeoff: this quarter, this customer, this metric, against the rest of the roadmap.

Engineering should own the technical design. The engineering lead should be able to read the product spec and respond with a technical design doc that states the architecture, data model, performance constraints, security risks, migration plan, and what would break if the product spec changed. Engineers should not be asked to discover the product goal inside a design doc. If they are, the team has hidden the product decision in a place where it will be optimized for implementation. A strong engineering lead will say, 'This product spec is unclear,' or 'This requirement will cost three times what we expect,' and the product manager must be able to answer.

The organizational placement matters more than the job title. In big companies, product managers who report into engineering often become project managers, because their boss cares about delivery. Product managers who report into a product organization can set priorities across teams, but they can also drift into roadmap politics if they are not embedded. The workable pattern is a product manager who is physically and socially embedded in the team, has outcome ownership, and has a dotted line to product leadership. They should be in the engineering standup, the design critique, and the support call. They should not be a messenger between groups.

Who to hire for the product decision role is less about title than about a few observable habits. Hire someone who can write a clear spec without hiding behind slides. Hire someone who asks for the metric before the feature. Hire someone who can sit in a design review and ask, 'Which user are we optimizing for?' without turning it into a fight. Hire someone who can talk to engineers about tradeoffs and not get defensive when an engineer says, 'That will not scale.' In my observation of large product organizations, the best product managers are not the most creative people in the room; they are the people who can make the room's creativity point at a problem worth solving.

Who not to hire is easier to spot. Do not hire a project manager and call them a product manager if the team needs product judgment. A project manager can keep the train on time; they cannot decide where the train should go. Do not hire a designer who believes that owning the spec means controlling the solution. Do not hire an engineer who wants to be a product manager but still evaluates ideas mainly by implementation cost. Do not hire a generalist who is good at meetings but cannot produce a written decision. Do not hire a 'customer obsession' person whose main skill is scheduling interviews. All of these people can be valuable, but they are not the owner of the product spec.

There is a temptation in large companies to solve the ownership question by adding a role: product designer, product operations, product strategist, product lead. Often this makes the argument worse, because it creates more people who can claim the spec. The number of owners should stay small. One person owns the product decision. One person owns the experience. One person owns the technical plan. The rest contribute. When three people claim ownership, the spec becomes a negotiation artifact, and the team optimizes for consensus instead of correctness.

The practical test is what happens when the spec is wrong. If the product manager owns it, the team should be able to say, 'We built the right thing badly' or 'We built it well, but it did not matter,' and the product manager should be the one who updates the goal. If the designer owns it, the failure often becomes a style problem: the interface was not clean enough. If the engineer owns it, the failure becomes a feasibility problem: the requirement was too hard. Ownership is not about ego. It is about making sure the organization has a place where the 'why' can be challenged, revised, and eventually closed.

That person is accountable for why the work matters, who it is for, what success looks like, and what is out of scope. They do not have to be the best writer, the best designer, or the best engineer.
