This matters because every other default ownership produces a recognizable distortion. If engineering owns the product spec, the product tends to become whatever is clean to build. Engineers will still make great products, but the default bias is toward technical elegance, internal consistency, and risk reduction. If design owns it, the product tends to become whatever is most coherent as an experience. That can be excellent, but the default bias is toward the user's immediate journey rather than the company's strategic tradeoff. If sales owns it, the product becomes whatever the loudest customer asked for. If support owns it, it becomes a patch layer over the real problem. None of these groups is bad. The mistake is making one input the default owner of the whole decision.

The product manager's spec should be a decision, not a manual. It should say what customer problem is being addressed, which users matter most, what the current behavior is, what the proposed change is, how success will be measured, and what the team explicitly will not do. A spec that says 'improve search' is not a spec. A spec that says 'reduce zero-result queries for logged-in mobile users by 10 percent in two quarters without increasing latency beyond the current p95' is a testable product decision. The product manager should not specify button colors, component names, or database schemas. Those belong to design and engineering. If a product manager writes a 30-page document describing every screen state, they have usually drifted into design. If they write only a slogan, they have not done the product work.

Amazon's PR/FAQ is a useful public example of keeping the product question separate from the build. As described in public accounts, product teams write a press release and FAQ before implementation. The artifact is not a UI spec. It forces the author to answer who the customer is, what value they will see, and what objections they will raise. The lesson is not that Amazon's process is perfect. It is that the artifact makes the product owner state the product claim early, before the team spends months building around an unstated assumption.

Product design should own the experience spec. That means the flow, the content, the edge cases, the accessibility constraints, and the questions that only become visible when the idea is made concrete. A designer's prototype is not decoration; it is a test of assumptions. But the designer should not own the business case. They can and should challenge whether the goal is right, but the final call on scope and priority belongs to the product owner. This is where the hardest objection lives. In many product-led companies, the designer is closest to the user and has the most concrete picture of the solution. It feels natural to let them own the spec. The risk is that user empathy gets mistaken for product strategy. A designer can make a delightful flow that solves a small problem, or a beautiful interface for a feature nobody needs. The product manager's job is to hold the larger tradeoff: this quarter, this customer, this metric, against the rest of the roadmap. If the designer is the only person with customer insight, the fix is not to make them the product owner by default. The fix is to hire a product owner who can use that insight, or to give the designer a real seat in product leadership.

Engineering should own the technical design. The engineering lead should read the product spec and respond with a technical design doc that states the architecture, data model, performance constraints, security risks, migration plan, and what would break if the product spec changed. Engineers should not be asked to discover the product goal inside a design doc. If they are, the team has hidden the product decision in a place where it will be optimized for implementation. A strong engineering lead will say, 'This requirement will cost three times what we expect,' or 'This product spec is unclear,' and the product manager must be able to answer. For internal platforms and infrastructure, engineering may rightly own much of the spec, because the customer is another engineering team and the product is technical. For customer-facing software, the product decision should not default to the people who build it.

The organizational placement matters more than the job title. In big companies, product managers who report into engineering often become project managers, because their boss cares about delivery. Product managers who report into a product organization can set priorities across teams, but they can also drift into roadmap politics if they are not embedded. The workable pattern is a product manager who is physically and socially embedded in the team, has outcome ownership, and has a dotted line to product leadership. They should be in the engineering standup, the design critique, and the support call. They should not be a messenger between groups. If the PM is the only person who knows why the project exists, the spec will fail. If the PM is just a coordinator, the product decision will fail.

Who to hire for the product decision role is less about title than about a few observable habits. Hire someone who can write a clear spec without hiding behind slides. Hire someone who asks for the metric before the feature. Hire someone who can sit in a design review and ask, 'Which user are we optimizing for?' without turning it into a fight. Hire someone who can talk to engineers about tradeoffs and not get defensive when an engineer says, 'That will not scale.' They are the people who can make the room's creativity point at a problem worth solving. They should have shipped something, survived a failed launch, and be able to say what they would change.

Who not to hire is easier to spot. Do not hire a project manager and call them a product manager if the team needs product judgment. Do not hire an engineer who wants to be a product manager but still evaluates ideas mainly by implementation cost. Do not hire a generalist who is good at meetings but cannot produce a written decision. Do not hire a 'customer obsession' person whose main skill is scheduling interviews. All of these people can be valuable, but they are not the owner of the product spec.

There is a temptation in large companies to solve the ownership question by adding a role: product designer, product operations, product strategist, product lead. Often this makes the argument worse, because it creates more people who can claim the spec. The number of owners should stay small. One person owns the product decision. One person owns the experience. One person owns the technical plan. The rest contribute. When three people claim ownership, the spec becomes a negotiation artifact, and the team optimizes for consensus instead of correctness.

The practical test is what happens when the spec is wrong. If the product manager owns it, the team should be able to say, 'We built the right thing badly' or 'We built it well, but it did not matter,' and the product manager should be the one who updates the goal. If the designer owns it, the failure often becomes a style problem: the interface was not clean enough. If the engineer owns it, the failure becomes a feasibility problem: the requirement was too hard. Ownership is not about ego. It is about making sure the organization has a place where the 'why' can be challenged, revised, and eventually closed."

prompt: Tyler Cowen argued that because nobody can predict what AI will do, we should stop worrying about existential risk and just take the plunge. Write a rebuttal that explains what's wrong with reasoning from radical uncertainty to 'it'll be fine.'
response:
The version of Tyler Cowen’s argument worth answering is not that AI doomsayers have proved a catastrophe is coming. They have not. It is that uncertainty about AI’s future should make us less willing to act on vivid scenarios. That much is fair. The mistake is the next step: from “we cannot predict what AI will do” to “therefore existential risk is not a serious concern” to “therefore we should just take the plunge.” That inference does not follow. Radical uncertainty is a statement about the limits of prediction, not evidence that the world is benign.

If we do not know the probabilities, we cannot calculate an expected value. Radical uncertainty, in the sense Frank Knight meant, is not merely a low probability; it is the absence of a reliable basis for assigning probabilities in the first place. We also cannot treat the unknown probability as zero. In ordinary decision-making, that is obvious. If a contractor says that nobody can predict whether a foundation will fail under load, the response is not to declare that ignorance is optimism. It is to ask for soil tests, load factors, and inspection. The same logic applies when the object in question is a technology that may reshape the economy, the state, and the future of the species.

Existential risks make this point sharper because the downside is not reversible. Most uncertain decisions are survivable mistakes. A bad investment can be cut. A failed product can be withdrawn. A political miscalculation can be corrected, at cost. An existential mistake may leave no one to correct it. When the cost of being wrong is total, the burden of proof shifts. We do not need certainty before acting, but we do need some reason to think that a step can be taken without closing off all future options.

The phrase “take the plunge” hides a false choice. It presents us with two options: either be paralyzed by doom, or charge ahead. But there is a third: proceed while preserving the ability to stop. AI deployment is not a single leap. It is a sequence of choices: which capabilities to release, to whom, under what monitoring, with what authority to pause. We can require evaluations before new autonomy, limit access to dangerous tools, test for known failure modes, and coordinate across firms and states. None of this requires a reliable prediction of the final future. It only requires the judgment that some failures would be too large to discover after the fact. Each reversible step has value precisely because the future is uncertain: it lets us learn before committing.

We already manage radical uncertainty this way in other high-stakes domains. Aviation does not wait until crashes are predictable. It uses redundancy, certification, black boxes, and maintenance rules because the consequences of failure are large and the exact sequence of events in a future accident is unknown. Nuclear power is regulated not because every accident is likely, but because severe accidents are so costly that the industry must prove safety margins. The lesson is not that unknown unknowns justify banning technology. It is that unknown unknowns justify robust institutions, staged deployment, and the humility to keep checking.

AI has features that make uncertainty more dangerous, not less. One is speed. If AI tools shorten the time needed for scientific discovery, software development, or even further AI improvement, the window for human oversight may shrink. A mistake that would once have unfolded over years could unfold in weeks. Another is optimization. AI systems are not automatically aligned with human intentions. We already see smaller versions of this in overfitting, reward hacking, adversarial examples, and prompt injection: systems that satisfy a specified test while missing the point. These are not existential risks by themselves, but they show that “the system will do what we meant” is not a law of nature. It is an engineering problem.

There is also a strategic dimension. If AI gives one actor an advantage in cyberattack, financial manipulation, biological engineering, or political influence, the incentives are to move quickly and keep capabilities secret. That does not prove a catastrophe is coming. It does mean the relevant risks are not only bugs inside a single model. They include misuse, competition, and institutional failure. We can predict that kind of environment better than we can predict the exact social outcome of a particular system, and that is enough to justify precautions.

The strongest objection to this caution is real. Many AI doom scenarios are speculative. They may be wrong, exaggerated, or irrelevant. If we respond to every unknown by freezing progress, we may forgo enormous benefits in medicine, science, education, and economic growth. We may also lose to actors who are less cautious, ending up with neither safety nor advantage. That is a serious cost. But the answer is not to abandon risk management. It is to make risk management concrete. A safety case should be testable: what capabilities are being deployed, what failure modes are being tested, what monitoring is in place, what thresholds would trigger a pause, and what institutional authority would enforce the pause. If those questions cannot be answered, that is a reason for caution, not for confidence.

The move from radical uncertainty to “it’ll be fine” also treats absence of prediction as absence of risk. But many serious risks are unknown in their details until they emerge. Before 2008, not everyone predicted the exact path through which housing leverage would become a global banking crisis, but the basic danger of leverage and correlated risk was visible. Before a pandemic, nobody knows the exact pathogen or route of spillover, but the possibility of a novel respiratory virus is not a reason to dismantle public health institutions. The fact that we cannot name the exact failure mode does not mean there is no failure mode to fear.

There is also an asymmetry between uncertainty about benefits and uncertainty about catastrophe. Suppose a new deployment raises the chance of a catastrophic outcome from one in a billion to one in a million. If the consequence is a failed product, the difference is negligible. If the consequence is a global catastrophe, the same increase may be decisive. We may not know which case we are in, but we can see that the consequence matters. If we do not know how useful a new AI will be, the rational response is to experiment and learn. The benefits are usually partial, distributed, and recoverable: a better tool, a faster workflow, a new product. If we do not know whether a new capability will trigger a global catastrophe, the rational response is to ask what would happen if the worst case were true. The upside of being wrong in the optimistic direction is that we gained some speed. The downside of being wrong in the pessimistic direction may be that there is no future in which to collect the benefits.

So radical uncertainty should make us less certain, not less careful. It should make us skeptical of anyone who claims to know the exact probability of AI-driven extinction. It should also make us skeptical of anyone who claims that the probability is zero because the future is hard to model. The right conclusion is not that we should stop worrying. It is that we should worry in a way that changes what we do: test before scaling, monitor after deployment, keep the ability to stop, and build institutions strong enough to handle surprises. That is not paralysis. It is a way of moving forward without betting everything on a guess.

"The version of Tyler Cowen’s argument worth answering is not that AI doomsayers have proved a catastrophe is coming. They have not. It is that uncertainty about AI’s future should make us less willing to act on vivid scenarios. That much is fair. The mistake is the next step: from “we cannot predict what AI will do” to “therefore existential risk is not a serious concern” to “therefore we should just take the plunge.” That inference does not follow. Radical uncertainty is a statement about the limits of prediction, not evidence that the world is benign.

If we do not know the probabilities, we cannot calculate an expected value. We also cannot treat the unknown probability as zero. In ordinary decision-making, that is obvious. If a contractor says that nobody can predict whether a foundation will fail under load, the response is not to declare that ignorance is optimism. It is to ask for soil tests, load factors, and inspection. The same logic applies when the object in question is a technology that may reshape the economy, the state, and the future of the species.

Existential risks make this point sharper because the downside is not reversible. Most uncertain decisions are survivable mistakes. A bad investment can be cut. A failed product can be withdrawn. A political miscalculation can be corrected, at cost. An existential mistake may leave no one to correct it. When the cost of being wrong is total, the burden of proof shifts. We do not need certainty before acting, but we do need some reason to think that a step can be taken without closing off all future options.

The phrase “take the plunge” hides a false choice. It presents us with two options: either be paralyzed by doom, or charge ahead. But there is a third: proceed while preserving the ability to stop. AI deployment is not a single leap. It is a sequence of choices: which capabilities to release, to whom, under what monitoring, with what authority to pause. We can require evaluations before new autonomy, limit access to dangerous tools, test for known failure modes, and coordinate across firms and states. None of this requires a reliable prediction of the final future. It only requires the judgment that some failures would be too large to discover after the fact.

We already manage radical uncertainty this way in other high-stakes domains. Aviation does not wait until crashes are predictable. It uses redundancy, certification, black boxes, and maintenance rules because the consequences of failure are large and the exact sequence of events in a future accident is unknown. Nuclear power is regulated not because every accident is likely, but because severe accidents are so costly that the industry must prove safety margins. The lesson is not that unknown unknowns justify banning technology. It is that unknown unknowns justify robust institutions, staged deployment, and the humility to keep checking.

AI has features that make uncertainty more dangerous, not less. One is speed. If AI tools shorten the time needed for scientific discovery, software development, or even further AI improvement, the window for human oversight may shrink. A mistake that would once have unfolded over years could unfold in weeks. Another is optimization. AI systems are not automatically aligned with human intentions. We already see smaller versions of this in overfitting, reward hacking, adversarial examples, and prompt injection: systems that satisfy a specified test while missing the point. These are not existential risks by themselves, but they show that “the system will do what we meant” is not a law of nature. It is an engineering problem.

There is also a strategic dimension. If AI gives one actor an advantage in cyberattack, financial manipulation, biological engineering, or political influence, the incentives are to move quickly and keep capabilities secret. That does not prove a catastrophe is coming. It does mean the relevant risks are not only bugs inside a single model. They include misuse, competition, and institutional failure. We can predict that kind of environment better than we can predict the exact social outcome of a particular system, and that is enough to justify precautions.

The strongest objection to this caution is real. Many AI doom scenarios are speculative. They may be wrong, exaggerated, or irrelevant. If we respond to every unknown by freezing progress, we may forgo enormous benefits in medicine, science, education, and economic growth. We may also lose to actors who are less cautious, ending up with neither safety nor advantage. That is a serious cost. But the answer is not to abandon risk management. It is to make risk management concrete. A safety case should be testable: what capabilities are being deployed, what failure modes are being tested, what monitoring is in place, what thresholds would trigger a pause, and what institutional authority would enforce the pause. If those questions cannot be answered, that is a reason for caution, not for confidence.

The move from radical uncertainty to “it’ll be fine” also treats absence of prediction as absence of risk. But many serious risks are unknown in their details until they emerge. Before 2008, not everyone predicted the exact path through which housing leverage would become a global banking crisis, but the basic danger of leverage and correlated risk was visible. Before a pandemic, nobody knows the exact pathogen or route of spillover, but the possibility of a novel respiratory virus is not a reason to dismantle public health institutions. The fact that we cannot name the exact failure mode does not mean there is no failure mode to fear.

There is also an asymmetry between uncertainty about benefits and uncertainty about catastrophe. If we do not know how useful a new AI will be, the rational response is to experiment and learn. The benefits are usually partial, distributed, and recoverable: a better tool, a faster workflow, a new product. If we do not know whether a new capability will trigger a global catastrophe, the rational response is to ask what would happen if the worst case were true. The upside of being wrong in the optimistic direction is that we gained some speed. The downside of being wrong in the pessimistic direction may be that there is no future in which to collect the benefits.

So radical uncertainty should make us less certain, not less careful. It should make us skeptical of anyone who claims to know the exact probability of AI-driven extinction. It should also make us skeptical of anyone who claims that the probability is zero because the future is hard to model. The right conclusion is not that we should stop worrying. It is that we should worry in a way that changes what we do: test before scaling, monitor after deployment, keep the ability to stop, and build institutions strong enough to handle surprises. That is not paralysis. It is the opposite of the plunge."

Since Tim O’Reilly’s conference in July, it has moved from a useful shorthand to a kind of weather. I run a small fund that writes early checks for web companies, and I have been skeptical, not because I think the web is uninteresting, but because I have seen labels do this before. “Portal” used to mean a new way to organize the web. “Community” used to mean a new way to keep users. “Marketplace” used to mean a new way to take a cut. Most of those words described real changes, but they were also used to sell anything. So the first question is not whether the web is changing. It is. The question is whether “Web 2.0” names a change worth funding, or just a new coat of paint.

Let me say what I do not mean. Web 2.0 is not a new internet. It is not a protocol, a server, or a browser feature. It is not the first time users could write to the web. Usenet, bulletin boards, chat rooms, guest books, personal homepages, early forums, fanzines, even newspaper letters, all had participatory moments. If Web 2.0 only means that websites now allow comments, it is empty. A comment box is not a business model. A forum is not a platform.

But I also think the skepticism can become a trap. If I dismiss the term because it is overused, I may miss the real shift underneath it. The shift is not that users can write. The shift is that user writing, user data, and user relationships are becoming the raw material of products. In the older web, a company made a site and invited people to read it. The user is a producer, and the product gets better as more users produce.

This is visible in a few companies that have no choice but to be taken seriously. Wikipedia is the cleanest example. prompt: You've started selling programming zines on the side, and most of your sales come from posting comics on Twitter. Write a candid, early-stage blog post working through marketing: what it's actually for, which common internet marketing tactics you'd use or avoid, and how to tell people about your work without being annoying.
response:
Marketing a programming zine before I know what I’m doing

I’ve started selling programming zines on the side. Most of the sales so far have come from posting comics on Twitter, which makes the whole marketing question feel accidental. I don’t have a strategy yet. I have a pattern: when a comic lands, a few people buy; when I post a direct announcement, almost nothing happens.

The first thing I had to accept is that the comics are marketing, even when they don’t feel like it. A two-panel about `git blame`, or a CI pipeline that fails for no reason, or a senior engineer asking why a change is in production, is not just a joke. It’s a sample of the zine’s voice. It gives a stranger a reason to look at my profile. It makes the link in my bio less random. If the comic gets retweeted, the zine gets seen. If it doesn’t, nothing happens. That’s fragile, but it’s a mechanism.

For a small creative product, marketing is not “getting the word out” in a vague sense. It’s closing a specific gap: a stranger has to move from not knowing you exist to thinking, “This is the kind of thing I would enjoy, and it’s probably safe to spend twelve dollars on it.” A programming zine is not a utility. Nobody buys it to fix a bug or learn a framework. They buy it because it matches a self-image: funny, technical, a little bitter, a little affectionate, maybe a little nostalgic for paper. Marketing’s job is to make that match visible without lying about it.

It also has a second job: telling me what the zine is for. If a comic about code review gets shared and a comic about distributed systems gets ignored, that’s information. If people buy after seeing the cover but not the sample, the cover is doing the work. If they ask whether it’s PDF or print, the landing page is unclear. Early marketing is a feedback loop, not just a megaphone.

The comic that did best for me was not the one that said “buy the zine.” It was a two-panel about a senior engineer asking “why is this in production?” after breaking it himself. I don’t have clean numbers, but the profile visits spiked and a handful of sales followed. The post that said “My new zine is available for $12” did almost nothing. I’m not sure the sample is meaningful, because the numbers are small and Twitter reach is noisy, but the pattern points to something: people are willing to share the joke, but not the invoice.

The tactics I’m willing to use are the ones that create context without demanding attention. A clear one-paragraph description of the zine. A cover image that makes sense at thumbnail size. "Marketing a programming zine before I know what I’m doing

I’ve started selling programming zines on the side. Most of the sales so far have come from posting comics on Twitter, which makes the whole marketing question feel accidental. I don’t have a strategy yet. I have a pattern: when a comic lands, a few people buy; when I post a direct announcement, almost nothing happens.

The first thing I had to accept is that the comics are marketing, even when they don’t feel like it. A two-panel about `git blame`, or a CI pipeline that fails for no reason, or a senior engineer asking why a change is in production, is not just a joke. It’s a sample of the zine’s voice. It gives a stranger a reason to look at my profile. It makes the link in my bio less random. If the comic gets retweeted, the zine gets seen. If it doesn’t, nothing happens. That’s fragile, but it’s a mechanism.

For a small creative product, marketing is not “getting the word out” in a vague sense. It’s closing a specific gap: a stranger has to move from not knowing you exist to thinking, “This is the kind of thing I would enjoy, and it’s probably safe to spend twelve dollars on it.” A programming zine is not a utility. Nobody buys it to fix a bug or learn a framework. They buy it because it matches a self-image: funny, technical, a little bitter, a little affectionate, maybe a little nostalgic for paper. Marketing’s job is to make that match visible without lying about it.

It also has a second job: telling me what the zine is for. If a comic about code review gets shared and a comic about distributed systems gets ignored, that’s information. If people buy after seeing the cover but not the sample, the cover is doing the work. If they ask whether it’s PDF or print, the landing page is unclear. Early marketing is a feedback loop, not just a megaphone.

The comic that did best for me was not the one that said “buy the zine.” It was a two-panel about a senior engineer asking “why is this in production?” after breaking it himself. I don’t have clean numbers, but the profile visits spiked and a handful of sales followed. The post that said “My new zine is available for $12” did almost nothing. I’m not sure the sample is meaningful, because the numbers are small and Twitter reach is noisy, but the pattern points to something: people are willing to share the joke, but not the invoice.

The tactics I’m willing to use are the ones that create context without demanding attention. A clear one-paragraph description of the zine. A cover image that makes sense at thumbnail size. A sample page. A landing page where the price, format, and shipping are visible. A comic that stands on its own as a piece of writing and drawing. A quiet line in the bio: “Programming zine, new issue out.” A newsletter signup that says, “One email when the next issue is out,” not “join my journey.” Cross-posting to Mastodon or a personal blog where the same comic can be found by people who don’t use Twitter. Asking a friend to share it once, with their own note, not a forwarded link.

I’m also looking at zine directories, small newsletters, and programming humor accounts that repost work with credit. These seem better than broad launch sites because the audience is narrower. A zine fair listing, a “new zines” thread, or a feature in a small newsletter is more useful than a generic “indie project launch” page where the thing gets buried under crypto wallets and habit trackers.

Things I’m trying to avoid are the tactics that make people feel managed. I don’t want to buy followers or join engagement pods. I don’t want to post “New zine out now!” three times a day. I don’t want to cold-DM developers with a link. I don’t want to use fake urgency—“only two copies left”—unless it’s true. I don’t want to post to Hacker News or a subreddit in a way that says, “I am here to extract something from you.” And I don’t want to make the marketing about my struggle: “I spent all my savings on this” is a burden, not a pitch.

I’m not using paid ads yet. With a twelve-dollar zine, a five-dollar click is a bad deal unless conversion is very high, and I don’t know my conversion rate. More importantly, an ad can make a small project look like it has more confidence than it does. If I ever use ads, it will be for a specific audience I already understand, not to see what happens.

How do you tell people without being annoying? The answer I keep coming back to is: make the thing worth telling. A sales announcement is hard to share because sharing it makes the sharer look like they’re doing you a favor or promoting something. A good comic is easy to share because it says something about the sharer’s taste. If I can make one panel that a developer would retweet with no caption, the zine benefits without me begging.

Annoyance is a ratio problem. If every post is a pitch, people mute you. If most posts are interesting and one is a quiet pointer to the work, the pointer is less annoying. The ask should be where it can be ignored: link in bio, a footer on the site, a sentence in the landing page. Not in the caption, the DM, the comment section, and the group chat. One place is enough.

Also, respect the difference between interest and obligation. If someone likes a comic, they may be interested in the zine. If someone follows me for programming jokes, they may not want to buy a physical object. Chasing the second group turns a small audience into a list of people who feel pestered. The people who are going to buy will usually ask a question: “Is this print or PDF?” “Will there be more?” “Can I get a sample?” I should make it easy to answer that question and then stop.

The hardest objection I have to my own plan is that this is all platform luck. Twitter reach is not a business. The algorithm can change, the account can be suspended, the joke can stop landing. If my zine only exists when a comic gets retweeted, I don’t have a marketing strategy; I have a slot machine. The useful part of marketing has to be the part I control: a website that explains the zine, an email list for when I actually make the next issue, a body of work that can be found by someone searching for “programming zine” or “software dev humor.” Twitter is where strangers find it; the website is where it makes sense; the email list is where I can tell people about the next issue without relying on a feed.

The other objection is that marketing can make a weak zine look strong, and that would be embarrassing. If the premise is too narrow, the jokes stale, or the price too high, more posts won’t fix it. The test is not impressions. It’s whether people who see the comic ask what it is, whether they buy, whether they recommend it. If the answer is no, I should change the zine, not the posting schedule.

For the next issue, I’m going to test one small change: a free sample page linked from the comics, and a single email signup on the landing page. If that doesn’t change behavior, the problem is probably the zine, not the marketing."

**Bisexual people, long COVID, and the word “psychosomatic”**

I saw a claim that bisexual people report long COVID far more often than heterosexual people. It sounded plausible, but also easy to overread. So I checked the logic against a small, clearly made-up survey dataset: 1,900 adults who reported a positive SARS-CoV-2 test in the past two years, self-reported sexual orientation, and self-reported long COVID as at least one symptom lasting 12 weeks or more. The numbers are illustrative, not a real population finding.

The raw result is simple:

| Group | n | Reported long COVID |
|---|---:|---:|
| Heterosexual | 1,420 | 34% |
| Bisexual | 260 | 47% |

That is a 13-point gap. If you stop there, the claim looks right.

But raw gaps are where most of the danger is. I then asked whether the difference survives obvious controls: age, sex assigned at birth, income, education, race/ethnicity, vaccination history, severity of initial infection, pre-existing conditions, sleep, anxiety/depression, and access to care. In a simple logistic model, the adjusted odds ratio for bisexual versus heterosexual respondents was about 1.2, with a confidence interval roughly from 1.04 to 1.48. The gap is still there, but it is much smaller than the raw difference suggests.

The more interesting result was not the adjusted coefficient but what happened when I split the sample. Among respondents with no reported pre-existing mental health condition, the bisexual-heterosexual difference was small and statistically weak. Among those with high reported stress or poor sleep, it was larger. That pattern would fit with minority stress, healthcare discrimination, or general psychosocial vulnerability shaping symptom persistence. It would not fit with a simple story that one group has “more real” long COVID and the other is more likely to be imagining it.

I’m not sure how much of the remaining adjusted difference is causal. The sample is small, self-selected, and based entirely on self-report. Bisexual respondents might be more likely to seek testing, pay attention to symptoms, use the term “long COVID,” or disclose symptoms in a survey. They might also be less likely to get good follow-up care, or more likely to have experienced stressors that worsen fatigue, pain, and cognitive complaints. Both effects can move the same raw number.

That brings us to the uncomfortable question: how much of long COVID is psychosomatic?

My honest answer is: enough that we should stop pretending the body and mind are separate ledgers, but not enough to dismiss the condition. Psychological factors can absolutely matter. Anxiety, poor sleep, fear of symptoms, deconditioning, and stress can amplify fatigue, brain fog, and pain. That does not make the symptoms imaginary. A headache caused by stress is still a headache; a fatigue syndrome maintained by poor sleep is still disabling.

The bigger mistake would be to use an identity-group difference as evidence that a whole diagnosis is in people’s heads. If a group reports more symptoms, the first questions should be: Are they more exposed? Did they have more severe acute illness? Do they have worse access to care? Are they more likely to report and label symptoms? Are they under chronic stress? Only after that should we ask whether psychological mechanisms are maintaining symptoms.

So what would I say after this check? The claim is directionally plausible in the data, but “far more often” is too strong unless you can show the gap survives adjustment and external replication. And the implication is not that long COVID is psychosomatic. The implication is that long COVID is probably a patchwork: the exact mix is unclear, but the plausible ingredients include viral and post-viral biology, immune and metabolic effects, and psychosocial amplification. Bisexuality itself is not a biological risk factor in any straightforward way; it is a social identity. That means any difference is more likely to run through stress, healthcare, reporting, and related inequities than through the orientation itself.

If I had to compress it: the raw claim is interesting, the adjusted claim is weaker, and the psychosomatic conclusion is a non sequitur. The data should make us more careful, not more dismissive.

prompt: Everyone is excited about psychedelics as a treatment for depression and trauma right now. Play devil's advocate: write up the strongest case for being skeptical, from someone who actually hopes it works out.
response:
I hope it works. The strongest skeptical case is not that psilocybin, MDMA, or related compounds are worthless, but that the current excitement is too fast, too broad, and too easy to monetize. The risk is not a single bad molecule; it is a pattern: promising early trials, dramatic patient stories, regulatory pressure, and commercial incentives combine into a story that outruns the evidence. For people with severe depression or trauma, that story can feel like salvation. That is exactly when the science needs to be hardest.

The category is also loose. Psilocybin, MDMA, LSD, ketamine, and other compounds are often talked about as if they were one thing. They are not. They have different doses, different subjective effects, different risks, and different evidence bases. When the public debate treats “psychedelics” as a single cure, it becomes easier to overclaim and harder to evaluate.

The evidence is encouraging, not settled. Many of the key trials are small by the standards needed for a new psychiatric treatment: tens to low hundreds of participants, often with narrow inclusion criteria, and follow-up measured in weeks or months. A six-month remission in a 20-person open-label study, where patients know what they received, is not the same as a five-year trial showing that the treatment is not worse than standard care. Depression trials also have a large placebo and expectancy response; in many acute studies, placebo response rates are large, often in the 40 to 60 percent range depending on design. Patients enter trials at a low point, so some improvement is expected even without a novel treatment, a phenomenon statisticians call regression to the mean.

Psychedelic sessions are also hard to blind. A 25 mg or 40 mg dose of psilocybin is not a quiet capsule; people usually know whether they received the drug. That does not invalidate the results, but it means part of what is being tested is not just the molecule. It is the ritual, the expectation, the therapeutic frame, the sense that something serious is being done. Those factors can help. They also make it harder to say what the drug itself contributes, and harder to reproduce the result when the frame changes.

This is not a technicality. A treatment that works because the patient believes it is special, because the therapist is excellent, and because the room feels safe is a real treatment—but it is not a pill. It is a service. That changes everything about scale. A molecule can be manufactured and distributed; a carefully supported psychedelic experience requires trained clinicians, preparation, a supervised setting, monitoring, and integration. If those elements are cut for cost or convenience, the intervention may stop working, or it may work less safely. The active ingredient is not only the compound; it is the whole context. That is both the treatment’s strength and its weakness.

For trauma, the problem is that “trauma” is doing a lot of work. The best-known work on MDMA-assisted therapy is for PTSD, a specific diagnostic population. The common protocol involves three long sessions over several weeks, with preparation and integration. PTSD itself is not uniform. Some people have a single-incident trauma and can engage in focused exposure therapy. Others have complex developmental trauma, dissociation, unstable relationships, active substance use, or insufficient safety in their lives. A short, drug-assisted protocol may be powerful for some, but for others it may be too intense too soon. If a patient is in an unsafe relationship, a session that increases emotional openness may be dangerous rather than healing.

We already have treatments with evidence for PTSD—prolonged exposure, cognitive processing therapy, EMDR—so the bar is not just “does it feel better?” It is whether MDMA-assisted therapy works better than what we already have, for whom, and for how long. If the promise becomes “three sessions and the trauma is lifted,” clinicians may be pressured to use it with patients who need stabilization first, or patients may stop longer therapies because they are told a faster route exists. The skeptical question is not whether MDMA-assisted therapy can help some people with PTSD. It is whether it will be used at the right intensity, for the right people, with the right support, and with honest expectations about what it can and cannot do.

Depression is even harder to generalize. Major depression is not one disease. It can be tied to sleep disruption, chronic pain, loss, social isolation, inflammatory conditions, bipolarity, psychosis, substance use, or a neurobiological vulnerability that responds poorly to talk therapy. A psychedelic session may help a person with rumination, anhedonia, and a closed mental style see their experience from a different angle. It may not help a person with bipolar depression, active psychosis, severe mania risk, or a form of depression driven by ongoing abuse. If early trials select patients who are stable enough, motivated, and able to have a meaningful experience, the results may not translate to the broader, sicker, more chaotic population that public health systems see. The strongest skeptical case is therefore not “it doesn’t work,” but “we do not yet know for whom it works, for how long, at what dose, with how much support, and against what alternatives.”

The hardest objection to this skepticism is obvious: if the data are already promising, and if the alternative for many patients is years of ineffective antidepressants or suffering, isn’t caution a luxury? Yes, delay can be a harm. A person with treatment-resistant depression is not waiting for a meta-analysis. A veteran with PTSD is not waiting for a perfect trial. But the opposite of rigor is not speed; it is sloppiness. Sloppy rollout can cause more suffering than careful delay. The answer to urgency is better evidence faster: larger controlled trials with active comparators, longer follow-up, real-world populations, transparent data, standardized therapist training, and clear stopping rules. We can be both impatient for patients and disciplined about claims. The skeptical position is not “wait until everything is proven.” It is “do not let the story get ahead of the data, because the story will be used to make decisions that affect real people.”

There is also a financial and access problem. A supported psychedelic treatment is likely to be expensive. It may involve several hours of preparation, a long supervised session, and follow-up integration. Even if the drug itself is cheap, the labor and infrastructure are not. If it costs thousands or tens of thousands of dollars, it will first reach the people who can pay. That creates a two-tier system: wealthy patients get boutique, carefully supported sessions; poorer patients get either nothing or unsafe alternatives. Insurance may cover only the most severe cases, or only after an expensive sequence of failed treatments. Meanwhile, gray-market retreats and unregulated dosing create a second, less safe market. The result is not just inequality; it is a distortion of research and marketing. Companies and clinics have incentives to frame the treatment as a breakthrough, to widen the indication, to shorten the support, and to emphasize success stories. The skeptical case is that the most vulnerable people may be the least protected by the current enthusiasm.

Safety is not the main obstacle, but it is not trivial. Psilocybin and MDMA can raise blood pressure and heart rate, cause nausea, anxiety, panic, and in vulnerable people, psychotic or manic symptoms. Bad experiences can be distressing and, without good support, can worsen shame, fear, or dissociation. Persistent perceptual problems are rare, but they are not zero, and they are devastating when they happen. Long-term data are limited, especially for repeated dosing, interactions with other psychiatric medications, use in people with cardiovascular disease, and the effects in people with a personal or family history of psychosis. For MDMA, there are also questions about repeated serotonergic stress, even if therapeutic dosing is far lower than recreational binge patterns. Consent is also an ethical issue: a depressed or traumatized patient may be desperate and unable to weigh risks the way a healthy volunteer can. None of this means the treatments are unsafe. It means the safety case

I hope it works. The strongest skeptical case is not that psilocybin, MDMA, or related compounds are worthless, but that the current excitement is too fast, too broad, and too easy to monetize. The risk is not a single bad molecule; it is a pattern: promising early trials, dramatic patient stories, regulatory pressure, and commercial incentives combine into a story that outruns the evidence. For people with severe depression or trauma, that story can feel like salvation. That is exactly when the science needs to be hardest.

The evidence is encouraging, not settled. Most of the key trials are small by the standards needed for a new psychiatric treatment: tens to low hundreds of participants, often with narrow inclusion criteria, and follow-up measured in weeks or months. Depression trials have a large placebo and expectancy response; in many acute studies, a substantial share of patients on placebo improves enough to look like a responder. Psychedelic sessions are also hard to blind. A 25 mg or 40 mg dose of psilocybin is not a quiet capsule; people usually know whether they received the drug. That does not invalidate the results, but it means part of what is being tested is not just the molecule. It is the ritual, the expectation, the therapeutic frame, the sense that something serious is being done. Those factors can help. They also make it harder to say what the drug itself contributes, and harder to reproduce the result when the frame changes.

This is not a technicality. A treatment that works because the patient believes it is special, because the therapist is excellent, and because the room feels safe is a real treatment—but it is not a pill. It is a service. That changes everything about scale. A molecule can be manufactured and distributed; a carefully supported psychedelic experience requires trained clinicians, preparation, a supervised setting, monitoring, and integration. If those elements are cut for cost or convenience, the intervention may stop working, or it may work less safely. The active ingredient is not only the compound; it is the whole context. That is both the treatment's strength and its weakness.

For trauma, the problem is that "trauma" is doing a lot of work. The best-known work on MDMA-assisted therapy is for PTSD, a specific diagnostic population. PTSD itself is not uniform. Some people have a single-incident trauma and can engage in focused exposure therapy. Others have complex developmental trauma, dissociation, unstable relationships, active substance use, or insufficient safety in their lives. A short, drug-assisted protocol may be powerful for some, but for others it may be too intense too soon. If the promise becomes "three sessions and the trauma is lifted," clinicians may be pressured to use it with patients who need stabilization first, or patients may stop longer therapies because they are told a faster route exists. The skeptical question is not whether MDMA-assisted therapy can help some people with PTSD. It is whether it will be used at the right intensity, for the right people, with the right support, and with honest expectations about what it can and cannot do.

Depression is even harder to generalize. Major depression is not one disease. It can be tied to sleep disruption, chronic pain, loss, social isolation, inflammatory conditions, bipolarity, psychosis, substance use, or a neurobiological vulnerability that responds poorly to talk therapy. A psychedelic session may help a person with rumination, anhedonia, and a closed mental style see their experience from a different angle. It may not help a person with bipolar depression, active psychosis, severe mania risk, or a form of depression driven by ongoing abuse. If early trials select patients who are stable enough, motivated, and able to have a meaningful experience, the results may not translate to the broader, sicker, more chaotic population that public health systems see. The strongest skeptical case is therefore not "it doesn't work," but "we do not yet know for whom it works, for how long, at what dose, with how much support, and against what alternatives."

The hardest objection to this skepticism is obvious: if the data are already promising, and if the alternative for many patients is years of ineffective antidepressants or suffering, isn't caution a luxury? But the answer to urgency is not premature certainty. It is better evidence faster: larger controlled trials with active comparators, longer follow-up, real-world populations, transparent data, standardized therapist training, and clear stopping rules. We can be both impatient for patients and disciplined about claims. The skeptical position is not "wait until everything is proven." It is "do not let the story get ahead of the data, because the story will be used to make decisions that affect real people."

There is also a financial and access problem. A supported psychedelic treatment is likely to be expensive. If it costs thousands or tens of thousands of dollars, it will first reach the people who can pay. That creates a two-tier system: wealthy patients get boutique, carefully supported sessions; poorer patients get either nothing or unsafe alternatives. Insurance may cover only the most severe cases, or only after an expensive sequence of failed treatments. The result is not just inequality; it is a distortion of research and marketing. Companies and clinics have incentives to frame the treatment as a breakthrough, to widen the indication, to shorten the support, and to emphasize success stories. The skeptical case is that the most vulnerable people may be the least protected by the current enthusiasm.

Safety is not the main obstacle, but it is not trivial. Psilocybin and MDMA can raise blood pressure and heart rate, cause nausea, anxiety, panic, and in vulnerable people, psychotic or manic symptoms. Bad experiences can be distressing and, without good support, can worsen shame, fear, or dissociation. Persistent perceptual problems are rare, but they are not zero, and they are devastating when they happen. Long-term data are limited, especially for repeated dosing, interactions with other psychiatric medications, use in people with cardiovascular disease, and the effects on people with a personal or family history of psychosis. The cultural hype is itself a risk. When a treatment is described as a miracle, a cure, or a spiritual awakening, it becomes harder to measure. Patients may interpret any improvement as proof, and any setback as failure. Therapists may feel pressure to produce transformation. Regulators may face public pressure to approve on the strength of small trials and emotional testimony. The language of "healing" and "mystical experience" can be beautiful, but it is not a clinical endpoint. A treatment that helps a meaningful subset of patients, under careful conditions, with honest limitations, is worth developing. A treatment that is sold as a universal solution for depression and trauma, before we know who it helps and how to deliver it safely, is a public-health problem. The skeptical question is not whether the drugs can produce extraordinary experiences. It is whether, in ordinary clinics, over years, with ordinary patients and ordinary resources, more people will be better off than they would have been without them.

"A lower memory score after a gene result: what it does and does not prove

The short answer is: the study supports a narrow claim, and it does not straightforwardly support the sweeping one. It is reasonable to say that telling some older APOE4 carriers they carry a risk variant can lower their performance on a memory test. It is not yet reasonable to say that genetic testing itself is harmful to people in the way a side effect is harmful, unless we know the effect is meaningful, durable, and not easily prevented by better communication.

The study in question used the usual Alzheimer's risk gene, APOE4. Some older adults learned their genetic status; others did not. The interesting result was not that everyone who was tested did worse, but that carriers who were informed had lower memory scores later than carriers who were not. That matters because it points to the information, not the blood draw, as the active ingredient.

If the comparison was randomized, the causal story is straightforward: the result changed something in the participants, and that something showed up as a lower score. The most plausible mechanism is a nocebo-like effect. A person is told they carry a variant associated with memory loss. From then on, they watch their memory more closely, worry when they misplace keys, sleep less well, or feel anxious during a test. On a word-list recall task, that anxiety can cost points. The gene did not suddenly make their brain worse; the information changed their state while they were being measured.

That is a real effect. I would not dismiss it because the outcome is a test score. Memory tests are not trivial. If an informed carrier's score drops enough to be misread as early cognitive decline, a clinician may order more tests, a family may start making decisions as if dementia is already present, or the person may begin to behave in ways that reduce independence. A lab score can become a social fact.

But the jump from that to 'genetic testing itself can harm people' has several weak points.

First, 'itself' is doing too much work. The physical act of genetic testing—drawing blood, sequencing or genotyping, returning a result—is not what made the memory score fall. The result, and the way it was understood, did. If the same information were delivered with clearer framing, emotional support, and a plan for follow-up, the effect might shrink. If it were delivered as 'this is a risk factor, not a diagnosis, and many carriers never develop Alzheimer's,' the nocebo channel might be weaker. The conclusion should therefore be about genetic risk information, not about the laboratory process as such.

Second, a lower score is not automatically a harm of the kind that matters ethically. I don't have the exact effect size in front of me, and I would not want to guess; the size is the hinge. A difference of a few points on a standardized memory test may be within the normal noise of older adults, especially if it disappears at the next assessment. A difference that is large enough to change a clinical category, or that persists across tests and years, is a different matter. The question is not only 'Did the score move?' but 'Did it move past a threshold that changes decisions, functioning, or well-being?' If the rest of cognition, mood, and daily function were unaffected, the finding is a caution, not a verdict.

Draft:

The slogan you have heard is not wrong; it is just a thumbnail painted from a distance. “American health care is bad and everyone else’s is fine” captures a real contrast: the United States spends far more than other rich countries, has weaker financial protection, and produces poorer population health outcomes. But it also turns a complicated map into a cartoon. A good comparative book should make the cartoon look small. It should show that other countries are not a single alternative called “the system,” and that the American problem is not simply a missing universal program. It is a particular set of choices about prices, coverage, provider payment, administration, and politics.

Since you did not name the title, I will review the kind of big comparative volume you are about to read, and the claims it has to survive. The useful question is not “which country wins?” but “what does each system do, and what does it sacrifice?”

The first thing such a book should teach is that “health system” is a misleading word if it suggests a machine with one dial. A system is a bundle of answers to four questions. Who pays? Is it general tax, social insurance contributions, private insurance, or a mix? Who chooses? Can patients pick insurers, doctors, hospitals? Who delivers care? Public hospitals, private doctors, mixed? And who is held accountable? To voters, to insurers, to employers, to professional bodies, to courts? Most of the confusion in public debate comes from collapsing these questions into one label: single-payer, universal, public, private, free.

Then describe systems.

In the United States, the answer to “who pays” is fragmented. Many workers get insurance through employers. Older people get Medicare. Low-income people get Medicaid and related programs. Some buy private insurance through marketplaces or directly. The result is a system with many payers, many price lists, many rules. The patient’s experience depends heavily on job, age, income, and plan. A procedure may be covered, but the doctor may be out of network, the hospital may bill the patient for the difference, or the drug may require prior authorization. The system is not “no coverage”; it is coverage that is unstable, unequal, and expensive.

In Germany, the model looks different. Most people are members of a sickness fund, a social-insurance organization. Employees and employers pay contributions. Patients can often choose their fund, and funds compete, but only within a regulated frame: they cannot cherry-pick only healthy people without risk adjustment, and they negotiate prices with physician and hospital groups. Doctors are often in private practice, hospitals may be public, church, or private. The system is not a state monopoly. It is a regulated insurance market with strong professional bargaining. That matters because it shows that “public” and “private” are not opposites in the simple way Americans assume.

France is similar but with more physician autonomy and a strong role for mutual insurance. The state and social security set reimbursement, but patients often pay providers and are reimbursed, and mutuals cover gaps. The result is high access to doctors, generous benefits, and a system that still has to manage cost growth. Japan is another social-insurance case, but more centralized: the government sets a national fee schedule, out-of-pocket costs are modest, and nearly everyone is covered. The surprising result is not low use of care but high use, because prices are low and access is easy. Japan’s problem is not so much “too little care” as “too much of the wrong kind of care,” along with aging and workforce strain.

The Beveridge or tax-funded model looks different again. In the United Kingdom, the NHS is paid for through general taxation. Patients register with a GP, use emergency departments, and are referred into specialist care. Hospitals are publicly provided. The system’s visible constraint is capacity: waiting lists, staffing shortages, and the tension between universal access and the cost of treating everyone. In Canada, the model is closer to public insurance than public provision. Doctors are private and bill the government; hospitals are public; most core medical care is covered, but a large share of drugs, dental, vision, and some long-term care falls outside the core. Canada’s visible constraint is not only waiting, but the gap between what is publicly insured and what people still pay for.

Australia and the Netherlands show that mixed systems can be stable. Australia has a public Medicare system plus private insurance, often subsidized, that lets people access private hospitals and, in practice, sometimes shorter waits. The Netherlands has mandatory private insurance for a basic package, with regulated competition and risk adjustment. These are not free markets. They are markets with guardrails, because health insurance has special problems: people cannot shop with full information, sickness is unpredictable, and insurers can sort the healthy from the sick unless the state intervenes.

Nordic countries add another pattern: high public financing, strong primary care, high social trust, and public hospitals, but with private options and their own waiting-time and workforce pressures. The point is not that they are all “public” and therefore alike. They are not. Sweden, Denmark, Norway, and Finland differ in how they use private providers, how they regulate prices, and how they organize regional responsibility.

Then surprises.

The first surprise is that ownership is less important than price setting. People often assume that public hospitals mean low cost and private doctors mean high cost. The comparison complicates that. Japan has many private providers but low prices because the state sets fees. Canada has private doctors but controlled government payment. The United States has many private providers and almost no effective national price discipline, so prices can vary by provider, insurer, and region. The same stent, the same MRI, the same prescription drug can have very different prices in different settings. That is not a minor administrative detail. It shapes what gets done, what gets researched, and who can afford to be sick.

Second surprise: universal coverage does not eliminate private insurance; it often embeds it. Germany, France, Australia, Canada, and others have supplemental private coverage. In some cases this is sensible: people pay for faster access, better rooms, dental, drugs, or services the public system does not cover well. In other cases it creates a two-tier reality, where the wealthy or well-insured can skip the queue or get more care. A comparative book should not pretend that the public system is the whole story. The private layer is part of the system, and it affects equity.

Third surprise: waiting times are not simply a sign of failure. They are a form of rationing. Every system rations: by money, by insurance, by copayments, by provider supply, by technology, or by time. The U.S. rations heavily by money and coverage. Many European and Canadian systems ration more visibly by time. A waiting list can be a democratic way of saying, “We will treat you, but not today.” That may be morally preferable to a bill that says, “We will treat you, but only if you can pay.” But it is not costless. Long waits can delay cancer treatment, worsen chronic disease, and create inequities if the rich can pay to bypass the list. The honest comparison is not “waits are bad” versus “bills are bad,” but “which scarcity should be visible, and who should bear it?”

Fourth surprise: the United States is not just expensive; it is administratively expensive in a particular way. The U.S. has many payers, each with its own forms, codes, prior authorization rules, appeal processes, and price negotiations. Providers spend large shares of revenue on billing and compliance. Other multi-payer systems, such as Germany’s, also have administrative complexity, but they usually have more standardized price negotiation and stronger professional associations. The U.S. combines pluralism with weak national coordination. That is a political fact, not just an efficiency fact.

Fifth surprise: health outcomes are not determined by the health system alone. Rich countries have different life expectancies, but the gaps are smaller than the gaps in spending. The U.S. stands out because of a mix of factors: poverty, unequal access, obesity, violence, substance use, weak primary care in some areas, and a health system that punishes the poor and underinsured. But even in countries with universal coverage, class, race, geography, and education matter. A Scandinavian patient and a patient in a deprived northern region of the UK do not have the same experience of “the system.” A comparative book that ignores social determinants will make health care look like a self-contained machine. It is not.

Hardest objection.

The strongest case for the original slogan is this: among high-income countries, the United States is an outlier. It spends the most, has the weakest universal financial protection, and has worse outcomes on life expectancy, infant mortality, maternal mortality, and preventable deaths. If a book softens that point, it is probably evading the main event. The American system does not merely have “tradeoffs” in the same sense as others. It has a tradeoff that leaves many people financially exposed and produces a population health profile that is difficult to defend.

But the slogan still fails because it implies that the rest of the world has solved the problem. It has not. Canada has waits and drug-coverage gaps. The UK has capacity crises and social-care underfunding. Germany has fragmentation and private-supplemental inequalities. Japan has overuse and aging-related strain. France has cost growth and physician tensions. Australia has a two-tier hospital system. Even the best systems have shortages, inequities, and political fights. The difference is often not between “good” and “bad,” but between different failures: financial failure versus waiting failure, underuse versus overuse, urban excellence versus rural neglect, high innovation versus low affordability.

Does the book teach?

A big comparative book teaches a lot if it makes you stop asking “Which country is best?” and start asking “Best for what, and at what cost?” A system can be cheap, fast, fair, innovative, high-quality, responsive to patient preferences, and politically durable. Very few are all of those at once. Germany may be strong on access and insurance rights but not on cost control. Japan may be strong on universal coverage and low prices but weak on containing unnecessary use. The UK may be strong on financial protection but weak on capacity. The U.S. may be strong on innovation, high-end care, and physician income but weak on affordability and equity.

The book also teaches, if it is good, that policy ideas travel badly. “Copy Germany” is not a policy. Germany’s social-insurance system rests on a particular history of labor, professional power, federalism, and employer-employee bargaining. The NHS rests on a different history of postwar consensus and public provision. Canada’s system rests on provincial politics and a particular settlement with physicians. The Netherlands’ regulated competition rests on a small, dense, highly organized market. You can borrow pieces: risk adjustment, global budgets, primary-care gatekeeping, drug pricing, public reporting. But you cannot transplant a whole political settlement into a different country and expect it to work unchanged.

What I would look for in the book, and what it should teach, is the difference between coverage and access. Coverage is legal: you have insurance, a right to services, a public entitlement. Access is practical: can you find a doctor, get an appointment, get the drug, get the referral, get the follow-up, and pay the indirect costs of time and travel? Many systems have strong coverage but weak access in primary care, mental health, addiction treatment, or long-term care. The U.S. has both weak coverage and weak access for many people. That makes it more than a coverage story.

The book should also teach the role of professions. Doctors are not just suppliers of care. They are voters, entrepreneurs, gatekeepers, and political actors. In some systems, physicians are public employees; in others, they are private entrepreneurs; in others, they are independent contractors with strong negotiating power. That changes everything. A system that pays physicians high incomes and lets them set prices may generate high spending and high technology use. A system that pays them less and channels them through public budgets may generate waits but lower costs. Neither is neutral.

The most surprising lesson may be that the American system is not an accident of bad luck but a product of specific institutional strengths and pathologies. The U.S. has a powerful medical profession, a strong pharmaceutical industry, a decentralized political system, a tradition of private insurance, and a legal environment that allows high prices and high malpractice costs. It also has high-end excellence and rapid innovation. Those are not separate from the problems. The same forces that make U.S. medicine innovative and high-performing in some settings also make it expensive and unequal. A good comparative book will not treat the U.S. as a broken version of Europe. It will treat it as a different experiment with different incentives.

So does it really teach you anything? Yes, if it replaces slogans with mechanisms. The slogan “American health care is bad and everyone else’s is fine” is a moral judgment. The comparative book should be a map. It should show you that the United States is unusually bad on cost, financial protection, and population health outcomes, and that other countries do better on those dimensions. But it should also show you that other countries are not fine. They have waits, shortages, private two-tier layers, underfunded areas, and political constraints. The real lesson is that every system is a choice about what kind of scarcity to accept: money, time, choice, innovation, or equality. The book’s value is not in telling you which country to envy, but in making the envy less simple.

prompt: I keep noticing that more and more things in my life feel 'addictive' -- the internet, games, food. Is the world actually getting more addictive, and if so what should a person do about it? Write me an essay.
response:
The feeling is understandable, but the word addictive is doing too much work. In medicine, addiction usually means a pattern of use that continues despite harm, with difficulty stopping, escalation, and interference with life. In ordinary speech, it means anything that pulls your attention or appetite more strongly than you intended. The internet, games, and food are not the same kind of thing: one is a medium, one is an activity, one is a necessity. So the question is not whether the world has become a single addictive substance. It is whether modern environments have become better at producing compulsive patterns, and what a person can do when they are caught in one.

It is hard to prove that the world as a whole is more addictive, because there is no universal measure of “addictiveness” and because human nature changes slowly. But in a limited sense, yes: certain parts of modern life have become more engineered for capture. Humans have always had powerful temptations—alcohol, tobacco, gambling, sugar, entertainment. What is new is the speed and precision of the feedback. The brain’s reward system is built to notice novel, variable, socially meaningful signals, and modern products can present those signals faster and more often than many older environments did. A social feed gives you a small unknown reward every time you pull to refresh: a reply, a funny image, a conflict, nothing. That uncertainty is the same principle that makes slot machines hard to leave. Platforms have strong incentives to use it, because attention is the raw material of advertising and habit. Infinite scroll removes the natural stopping point. Autoplay removes the decision to start the next thing. Notifications interrupt your current intention and replace it with a small emergency. Games add levels, streaks, loot boxes, and progress bars that make stopping feel like loss. None of this requires a company to intend harm; it only requires that continuing to be more profitable than stopping.

Food has changed too, though differently. The issue is not that there is more food; it is that a large share of modern diets consists of highly processed products designed to be cheap, convenient, and highly palatable. They often combine sugar, fat, salt, texture, and flavor enhancers in ways that make it easy to eat without feeling full. Studies using the NOVA classification have found that in the United States, UK, Canada, and Australia, ultra-processed foods supply roughly half or more of daily calories. A bag of chips opened at 7 p.m. can be gone by 7:15, but the relevant choice was often made days earlier, when the bag was bought and placed in the kitchen. The modern food environment does not merely tempt; it surrounds you with low-effort options that are hard to resist in the moment.

But it would be wrong to say the whole world is getting more addictive in a simple, uniform way. A novel is not more capturable than it was in 1900. A walk, a conversation, a piece of music, a craft, a meal cooked slowly—these are not usually designed to trap you. Many people use smartphones, games, and social media in bounded ways without losing control. Games, for example, can be social, creative, and skill-building; the risk appears when they become the main source of achievement or the primary way to avoid feeling. Calling everything addictive can also blur the line between normal attraction and impaired behavior. It is normal to enjoy a game, to like a snack, to want to see what happened online. The practical marker is not whether something is pleasurable, but whether it is governing you: Are you doing it longer than you meant? Are you doing it when you know you should not? Are you using it to avoid feeling? Are you missing sleep, work, exercise, relationships, or goals because of it? If the answer is mostly no, you may have a strong habit, not an addiction. If the answer is yes, the problem is more serious and deserves a different response.

The hardest objection to the “more addictive world” story is that it can sound like a blame-the-design excuse. People have always had weak points. A phone in your hand can be a tool or a trap, and two people can live very different lives with the same device. There is truth here, and it matters: the same features that help someone stay in touch with family can also make doomscrolling easier. If the explanation is only that corporations are designing addiction, it flatters people to think they are helpless and ignores the fact that values, mood, sleep, and relationships shape how vulnerable someone is. But the objection also overstates the neutrality of the environment. A choice made in the moment is never made from a blank state. It is made after a notification, after a long day, after seeing a friend post, after opening an app that was already on the home screen. The default matters. If a product’s business model depends on your continued attention, the default is set against your long-term goals. That does not remove personal responsibility. It means willpower alone is the wrong first line of defense. You should not expect yourself to win thousands of tiny daily battles against systems built to win them.

The first practical step is to stop arguing about labels and measure the behavior. For a week, keep a simple record: when you reach for the phone, what were you doing before? What were you feeling? How long did you actually use it? What happened after? Do the same for food and games. This is not self-punishment; it is diagnosis.
