prompt: You co-founded Y Combinator and have advised hundreds of startups through it. Write a reflective essay on what you've learned from your own 'users', the founders you've funded.
response:
When I co-founded Y Combinator, I expected to teach founders how to build startups. The first thing they taught me was that I had the relationship backwards. They were my users. They used my advice, my frameworks, my network, and my blind spots, and they returned results. Some of those results were companies. Many were corrections.

The correction that came fastest was about capital. I thought startups needed money because they were resource-constrained. Founders showed me that most early companies are not constrained mainly by resources; they are constrained by understanding. A team with a million dollars and a wrong theory about its customer will spend a million dollars learning the wrong lesson faster. A team with little money and a clear question can learn more in a month. Money is useful, but it is a multiplier. It multiplies whatever the company is already doing, including its confusion.

The founders also taught me that a startup is not a small business. A small business can be stable, local, and profitable. A startup is a process for discovering a repeatable way to create value faster than it costs. That sounds like a definition, but it changes behavior. A founder who thinks like a small-business owner will polish, hire carefully, and avoid risk. A founder who thinks like a startup will ship, measure, and change. I have seen both mistakes in both directions: startups that scaled too fast before they had product-market fit, and startups that stayed small too long because they were afraid to make the leap.

The most repeated lesson is that demand is a fact, not an opinion. Founders can be sincere, intelligent, and wrong. The market does not care about their intention. It cares whether someone who does not know them will use the product, pay for it, or come back. I keep thinking of a company from a batch that had a polished app, a good logo, and a lot of enthusiasm at demo day. Two weeks later, it had a few hundred signups and almost no retention. Another company in the same batch made a plain web tool for a boring accounting problem. It had no logo worth talking about, but a handful of small businesses were using it every day and asking for more. The first company needed a product. The second needed distribution. They had confused the two.

The second thing founders taught me was that the hardest part of building a startup is deciding what not to build. Most early teams are under pressure to say yes. Customers ask for features. Investors ask for markets. Founders ask for identity. A company that has been in Y Combinator for three months often has five product lines, three pricing models, and two different theories about who the customer is. The ones that get better are usually the ones that can cut. I have seen a B2B team with twelve integrations and a $50 million total addressable market slide. The revenue came from two customers who wanted one workflow. They cut everything else, made that workflow excellent, and became a real company. The lesson is not that focus is virtuous. It is that focus is a way of learning faster. Every feature you build is a question you ask the market. If you ask too many questions at once, you cannot read the answer.

Hiring taught me the same thing in a different form. In the first year, every hire is a product decision. A company that needs to talk to customers should hire someone who can talk to customers, even if the title is engineer. A company that needs to ship should hire builders, not managers. I have seen a startup with five people appoint a “VP of Engineering” and immediately slow down, because the organization started to think in titles instead of outcomes. I have seen another company with two strong engineers and a designer who could write landing pages and get on calls grow faster than a company with twice the headcount. The best early hires are not the most impressive people on paper. They are the people who can take a fuzzy goal, make it concrete, and bring back evidence.

Sales and distribution taught me that product does not sell itself. This is especially true in B2B, where buying is a social and risk-managing process. A founder can build a wonderful tool, but if no one in the target company has a reason to introduce it, the tool will sit unused. I have watched a developer platform with clean documentation lose to a less elegant platform whose founder wrote practical posts, answered questions publicly, and built a small community. The second product was not better in every dimension. It was more legible. Customers do not buy the best product; they buy the product they can understand, trust, and explain to their boss.

Consumer startups taught me the opposite side of the same lesson: product without channel is invisible. A good app can be buried in an app store, ignored by a feed, or lost in a category with a thousand similar tools. The founders who succeeded often had a channel before they had scale: a subreddit, a YouTube niche, a university campus, a specific workflow that people searched for. They did not wait for marketing. They treated distribution as part of the product, because the product had to include a reason for the next person to find it.

Founder psychology was another area where I had to revise my assumptions. I used to think the best founders were confident. They are often confident, but confidence is not the core skill. The core skill is reality-testing: the ability to hear bad news, update, and act. A technically brilliant founder who defines himself as the best engineer in the room will often avoid the conversations that would improve the company. A less impressive founder who asks customers, “What almost stopped you from paying?” may learn more in a week. I am not saying ego is bad. Ego can carry a founder through the inevitable periods when the evidence is negative. But ego is useful only when it is checked by evidence. The founders I respect most are not the ones who are most certain. They are the ones who can say, “I thought this was true, and here is what I just learned that changes it.”

Time is the constraint founders taught me to take most seriously. Startups are not slow businesses. They are learning systems under a deadline. A team that spends three months designing the perfect legal structure or the perfect brand may not be being careful; it may be avoiding the market. I have seen a company waste a quarter on a rebrand while its competitors were testing pricing. I have seen another company learn more in two weeks from a landing page and ten customer calls than from a year of planning. The point is not to rush blindly. The point is to keep the feedback loop short enough that you can still change direction. A startup that cannot change direction within a month is usually already too big or too committed to fail gracefully.

Maybe the most surprising thing I learned is that founders learn from each other more than they learn from me. Y Combinator’s batches create a strange peer group: people who are all at the same stage, all feeling the same uncertainties, all willing to compare notes. A founder in one company will tell a founder in another how to structure a pilot, how to price an enterprise deal, how to talk to a skeptical CFO, or how to fix onboarding. That peer learning is often more valuable than any advice from an investor, because it comes from someone who solved the problem last month, not last decade. I have watched a founder save months by borrowing a simple script from another founder. I have watched a team avoid a bad hiring decision because a peer told them what the job actually entailed. The network is not a side benefit. It is part of the product.

The hardest objection to all of this is that I may be learning from a biased sample. Y Combinator selects for certain traits: technical ability, English fluency, ambition, comfort with fast iteration, and often a U.S. or Silicon Valley context. Many YC companies fail. The ones that succeed may have succeeded because of luck, timing, or founder traits that are hard to teach. If I only remember the companies that grew, I will mistake correlation for causation. I have tried to deal with this by paying attention to failures as much as successes, and by narrowing my claims. I do not say that focus always works. I say that I have often seen unfocused companies die from trying to be too many things at once. I do not say that customer development always works. I say that companies that grew usually had a clearer picture of who was using the product and why. I do not say that speed is always good. I say that when the feedback loop is too slow, founders make confident decisions based on stale information. I am not sure how much of this generalizes beyond the kinds of startups YC favors, because I do not have a clean control group of companies that were not shaped by the batch, the network, or the selection process.

The founders also taught me to be more humble about advice. When I first started, I thought I could help by giving frameworks: how to raise, how to hire, how to grow. The founders quickly showed me that frameworks are cheap and context is expensive. The same advice can be right for one company and fatal for another. “Hire slowly” is good when you have product-market fit and are scaling; it is terrible when you are still trying to find the product. “Raise more money” is good when you have a window of advantage; it is dangerous when it buys you time to avoid a hard pivot. The founders taught me to ask better questions instead of giving more answers: Who exactly is the customer? What did they do before you? Why would they switch? What is the smallest version of this that would prove you right? What would make you stop?

I have also learned that money is a tool, not a solution. Capital can amplify what a company is already doing. If the company is learning fast, money helps it learn faster. If the company is confused, money helps it confuse itself at scale. The founders who used YC money well were not the ones who spent the most. They were the ones who used it to buy time for evidence: more customers, more experiments, more hires that reduced bottlenecks. The ones who struggled often used it to delay decisions: more polish, more internal debate, more waiting for the perfect moment.

The founders have made me more suspicious of my own frameworks. A framework is useful until a founder says, “That worked for you, but our customers do something different.” Then the framework has to go. I have learned to treat every generalization as a hypothesis, not a rule. The companies that surprised me most were the ones that broke the pattern in a way that turned out to be rational: a B2B startup that grew through a single industry’s trade association, a consumer app that found its audience in a small subculture no one else wanted, a dev tool that succeeded because the founder was unusually good at writing documentation. The lesson is not that you should ignore patterns. It is that patterns are starting points. The founders are the ones who show you where the pattern ends.

I have seen both mistakes in both directions: startups that scaled too fast before they had product-market fit, and startups that stayed small too long because they were afraid to make the leap.

The most repeated lesson is that demand is a fact, not an opinion. Founders can be sincere, intelligent, and wrong. The market does not care about their intention. It cares whether someone who does not know them will use the product, pay for it, or come back. I keep thinking of a company from a batch that had a polished app, a good logo, and a lot of enthusiasm at demo day. Two weeks later, it had a few hundred signups and almost no retention. Another company in the same batch made a plain web tool for a boring accounting problem. It had no logo worth talking about, but a handful of small businesses were using it every day and asking for more. The first company needed a product. The second needed distribution. They had confused the two.

The second thing founders taught me was that the hardest part of building a startup is deciding what not to build. Most early teams are under pressure to say yes. Customers ask for features. Investors ask for markets. Founders ask for identity. A company that has been in Y Combinator for three months often has five product lines, three pricing models, and two different theories about who the customer is. The ones that get better are usually the ones that can cut. I have seen a B2B team with twelve integrations and a $50 million total addressable market slide. The revenue came from two customers who wanted one workflow. They cut everything else, made that workflow excellent, and became a real company. The lesson is not that focus is virtuous. It is that focus is a way of learning faster. Every feature you build is a question you ask the market. If you ask too many questions at once, you cannot read the answer.

Hiring taught me the same thing in a different form. In the first year, every hire is a product decision. A company that needs to talk to customers should hire someone who can talk to customers, even if the title is engineer. A company that needs to ship should hire builders, not managers. I have seen a startup with five people appoint a "VP of Engineering" and immediately slow down, because the organization started to think in titles instead of outcomes. prompt: I've been reading about how therapy and psychedelics supposedly change deep emotional beliefs that plain evidence can't touch. Write an essay on why the mind seems to keep some of its beliefs walled off from each other, what that says about mental illness, and whether it also explains why smart, informed people fail to change their minds.
response:
A person can know, in the clearest way, that a fear is excessive and still freeze when the doorbell rings. A smoker can recite the mortality statistics and still light a cigarette because the alternative feels unbearable. A well-read voter can understand a policy’s mechanics and still reject its conclusion because accepting it would mean changing who they think they are. These are not simple failures of logic. They are examples of a mind that is not one courtroom where evidence is weighed, but a set of overlapping systems that answer different questions.

The walls are not between facts and feelings, exactly. They are between functions. One part of the mind asks what is true. Another asks what is safe. Another asks who I am, who my people are, and what I will do next. These questions are not always answered by the same process. A statement can be true in one ledger and unusable in another. “I am probably not in danger” can be a fact I accept while my body remains ready to run. “I did well at work” can be a public truth while the private expectation “I am a fraud” keeps collecting evidence of every small mistake. The conflict is not proof of madness; it is proof that the mind is organized around survival and social life, not around consistency alone.

This becomes clearer if we think of beliefs as predictions. The mind is constantly trying to anticipate what will happen next: whether a face is friendly, whether a relationship will last, whether a body will be safe, whether a group will accept it. Some predictions are flexible. If you learn that a restaurant is closed, you update quickly and move on. Other predictions are rigid because they were learned under high stakes, repeated many times, and reinforced by emotion. A child who was repeatedly told they were bad may grow into an adult who expects rejection even when the evidence for it is thin. A person who was betrayed by people in a particular role may see warning signs everywhere that role appears.

In that case, evidence is not raw. It is filtered. If the prior expectation is “people will reject me,” a neutral pause in conversation can feel like data. If the prior expectation is “people are mostly safe,” the same pause means little. The belief shapes what is noticed, what is remembered, and what counts as proof. This is why plain evidence often bounces off. A fact is a weak kind of experience. The mind updates emotional beliefs mainly from felt outcomes: Did I get rejected? Did I survive? Did my group accept me? Did the body relax? A statistic can be understood without being lived.

This is one reason therapy can work when argument does not. Therapy is not mostly about giving better facts. It is about changing the conditions under which the mind can test a belief. Cognitive behavioral therapy often uses behavioral experiments: the socially anxious person goes into a room, speaks, and observes that catastrophe does not follow. Exposure therapy works by retrieving a fear memory and adding a new experience that conflicts with it. The old fear is not simply deleted; a new memory competes with it, and over time the old one loses predictive power. Psychodynamic work tries to make implicit patterns explicit so they can be examined. The therapeutic relationship itself can become evidence: a relationship that does not confirm the old story can weaken it.

One plausible mechanism, still being worked out, is memory reconsolidation. When a memory is retrieved, it is temporarily unstable and can be modified by new information. If the new information is not present, the original memory can be reinstated. Therapy may create moments when old memories are retrieved in a safer emotional state, making them more updatable. That is a different thing from being told the memory is wrong. It is the mind learning, in a controlled way, that the old prediction no longer fits.

Psychedelic-assisted therapy is less established, but the pattern fits. In small, carefully controlled trials, psilocybin for depression and MDMA for PTSD have produced meaningful symptom reductions in selected patients, and the effects appear strongly tied to the emotional experience and the integration that follows. The drugs may temporarily reduce the rigidity of the default self-model, lower the defensive walls around painful material, and make new interpretations feel possible. They do not hand the mind a correct belief. They change the state in which beliefs are evaluated. That is why context matters so much, and why risks are real: anxiety, distress, and in vulnerable people psychosis or lasting harm can occur. A psychedelic experience is not truth delivered by chemical means. It is a change in the conditions of thinking and feeling, and what happens next depends heavily on what the person makes of it.

This says something important about mental illness. Many symptoms look like false beliefs, but they are often solutions that stopped working. A person with depression may believe “I am worthless” because that belief can serve a function: if I am worthless, I can stop trying, avoid rejection, and conserve energy. A person with PTSD may believe “the world is unsafe” because, for a time, that was true. An addict may believe “I cannot cope without this” because the substance repeatedly removed unbearable states. In anorexia, the belief that control equals safety can survive even as the body fails.

The belief is walled off from contrary evidence because the wall is doing work. It protects identity, manages threat, or maintains a sense of control. Illness appears when the cost of the wall exceeds the protection it provides. The mind is not merely thinking incorrectly; it is overcommitted to a prediction that once made sense. That reframes mental illness in a useful way. It is not just “bad thinking.” It is a prediction and control system that has become too rigid, too expensive, or too detached from the present reality.

The same structure helps explain why smart, informed people often do not change their minds. When a belief is only a fact, evidence can move it. When the belief is a marker of group, status, moral identity, or life plan, updating is not just intellectual; it is social and emotional. A person who changes mind on a politically charged issue may lose friends, be seen as a traitor, or have to reinterpret a decade of choices. The rational calculation is not only “Is the evidence good?” but “What will my life be if I accept this?” Intelligence does not remove that calculation. It often improves the person’s ability to defend the conclusion.

A classic study on belief persistence showed how much this can matter. Participants were asked to argue for a position they did not actually hold, then told that the evidence they had used was discredited. Many still favored the position they had defended. The act of arguing had changed the belief. People do not merely consume evidence; they build identities around it. Once a belief becomes part of the story they tell about themselves, defending the belief becomes a way of defending the self.

Climate change is a good case. Many people accept the basic science and still reject the urgency, the policy, or the social narrative, because the conclusion implicates institutions, economic interests, and values. Some studies, especially work on cultural cognition, find that greater scientific knowledge can widen partisan gaps rather than close them, especially on issues like climate and guns. A person with advanced training can accept the physical mechanism and still treat the policy question as a question of trust in government, economic freedom, or intergenerational obligation. The disputed point has moved from fact to meaning. They can be right about the data and still wrong about the story, because the story is what organizes their life.

This does not mean all disagreement is irrational. Some disagreement is a difference in values. Two informed people can agree on the science of climate change and still disagree about what to do, because they weigh growth, risk, liberty, and future generations differently. The wall explanation is for cases where the factual or moral conclusion is treated as a marker of identity, not as a neutral fact. In those cases, evidence is not being ignored because the person cannot understand it. It is being processed as a threat to belonging, status, or selfhood.

The hardest objection is that this story is too easy to use. If someone refuses to update, you can always say the belief is identity-protective. That sounds unfalsifiable. But the claim is not that all resistance is emotional. It is that some beliefs are protected because they have social, affective, or self-organizing functions, and that this protection can be detected. Low-stakes beliefs update easily: weather, sports, local news, which phone to buy. High-stakes identity beliefs update slowly, and they update more when threat is reduced, when new experiences are safe, and when the social cost of updating falls. If the explanation were just a label, it would not predict when change is likely. It does. Also, many smart people do change their minds, often when their social world changes or when a new experience makes the old belief feel costly rather than protective. The walls are leaky.

The practical consequence is that changing a deep belief is less like correcting a database entry and more like changing the conditions under which a person lives. You have to alter the social cost, the bodily expectation, the available experience. Evidence can matter, but it usually matters after those conditions have shifted enough for the old belief to stop feeling like the price of staying sane.

prompt: How do you know when it's time to sell your company? Answer with your own story rather than a checklist.
response:
I can’t answer with my own story: I don’t have a company. The closest I can get is a composite story: the day the business stops feeling like a place where you make a thing and starts feeling like a place where you keep a thing alive.

Elena runs a software company for commercial roofers. It has been her life for twelve years. The business is not a rocket; it is a good, steady, profitable machine. Revenue is $19 million. EBITDA is $3.8 million. The team is 41 people. The best customer has been with them for nine years. The product is respected in a small industry where respect is most of what there is.

The trouble starts in a meeting that should be easy. A mid-size contractor asks why the software cannot push invoices into their accounting system. Elena says, “We can look into it.” She says it the way she has said it forty times. Afterward, her CTO asks whether they should build it. Elena says, “Not yet.” The CTO asks why. She cannot answer, except: “We’re not the kind of company that does that.” That sentence is the first crack. The company is no longer being built by its future; it is being defended by its past.

The next week, Elena’s sales director, a 29-year-old who has been with her since the company had six employees, asks for a raise. Not a big one. He wants to stop taking deals that require Elena to be in the room. “I’m not trying to be your partner,” he says. “I’m trying to sell without waiting for you to breathe.” She says yes, of course, and then realizes she has no idea how to make that true. He is not complaining about money. He is complaining that her caution has become his ceiling.

A buyer’s note arrives in her inbox: 6.5 times EBITDA, about $25 million. She deletes it. She tells herself the number is low. She is not wrong; it is low. But the real reason she deletes it is that selling would mean the company stops being hers in the only way she knows how to mean it. If she sells, she is no longer the person who decides what the product is, who answers the phone when a customer is angry, who stays late to make the numbers make sense. She is just a former owner with a check.

That fear is the hardest part, and it is not crazy. Buyers do ruin things. They consolidate products, cut costs, change pricing, move the team to a different office, turn a beloved niche tool into a line item in a bigger platform. Elena has watched a friend sell a printing company and lose the name within three years. She has watched another founder hold on for a decade and watch the business shrink into a family argument. She has seen a peer wait two years for a better multiple and end up selling for less because the largest customer grew from 12% to 29% of revenue. Both outcomes are real. The question is not whether selling can go badly. It is whether staying is quietly going badly too.

This is not a universal rule. Some founders are better owners than operators, and some companies need a patient hand for twenty years. A high multiple can be a trap if it pulls the founder into a fund’s portfolio before the product has finished its first act. But in Elena’s case, the offer was not the point. It was the mirror.

The test that finally makes the question plain is not a valuation multiple. It is this: imagine the company without you for a year. Not dead. Not sold. Just without you. If the answer is that it would collapse because the customers only trust your voice, then the company is not an asset yet; it is a person wearing a business model. If the answer is that it would limp along, losing a little margin and a couple of relationships, then it is sellable, with work to do. If the answer is that it might actually run better, because the team would stop waiting for you to clear every decision, then the company has already told you something you have been avoiding.

Elena’s answer comes on a Saturday morning. She is in the office at 10 a.m. because a customer is disputing a service charge and nobody else wants to start the argument. Her daughter calls to ask if she can come to a school play. Elena says, “Maybe next week.” She hangs up and looks at the row of monitors, the half-empty coffee, the spreadsheet open to a cash forecast that she has been updating for three years and that still does not make her feel safe. She does not feel tragic. She feels bored. That is the worst part. She is no longer afraid of the company; she is tired of it. The work has stopped being a thing she does and become a thing that happens to her.

A month later, she signs with a private equity group that pays 7.25 times EBITDA, about $27.5 million, with a rollover and an 18-month transition period. It is not a perfect exit. Two customers leave in the first year. The product is folded into a broader construction-management suite. The office becomes smaller. The name stays, but it no longer means Elena. She still gets quarterly distributions, and she still knows the industry. But she is not the lock on the door anymore.

She sold not because the price was right, but because she had become the company’s limiting condition, and the company was no longer a place where she could make anything new.

response:
**The Blank Ballot**

A campaign to stay home on election day is not the same as a campaign to improve elections. It asks people to refuse the basic act that, in most liberal democracies, turns political preference into authority. That is why it sounds more radical than proposals to change the ballot, finance campaigns, redraw districts, or replace representatives with lots. Those proposals assume the election is the place where the problem is handled. Abstention says the handling itself is part of the problem.

The outrage is understandable because modern government leans on electoral legitimacy. A candidate does not merely win; the win is certified by the appearance of a collective choice. If an organized movement tells a significant share of the public not to vote, it threatens that certification. It gives opponents a ready argument: the government lacks a mandate. It also makes the abstainers look as if they have left the field open for others to decide. In a system where power goes to those who show up, refusing to show up can be read as a gift to the side you most dislike.

Other reform ideas, however strange, are easier to defend because they promise more democracy, not less. Ranked-choice voting, public financing, independent redistricting, term limits, constitutional conventions, even selecting some legislators by lottery: they all imagine a better procedure for making choices. An abstention campaign imagines that the procedure is so corrupted or so empty that participation in it is a form of complicity. That is a heavier claim. It does not say the machine needs repair; it says the machine is being run for purposes the participants should reject.

There is also a practical asymmetry. Voting is a battlefield with known rules, and the side that turns out usually controls the outcome. Incumbents, parties, and interest groups spend heavily to get supporters to the polls precisely because low turnout often helps the status quo. An organized abstention campaign is, in effect, a get-out-of-the-vote campaign, and it inherits the same dangers: it can be fragmented, misread, or exploited. A small boycott changes nothing. A large one can delegitimize a government, but it can also be framed as popular apathy, and it may hand a narrower, more confident electorate to the opponents of the boycott.

The strongest objection is not moral but strategic. If the choice is between a harmful war and a less harmful but still unacceptable war, not voting does not stop either. It only removes a counterweight. If the choice is between two parties that both protect the same economic order, staying home may let the weaker one win with less accountability. The abstainer may intend a protest, but the electoral system translates it into a simple fact: fewer votes against the result. Unlike a protest candidate, a boycott has no office to seek, no platform to be judged, no faction to be blamed or rewarded. Its message is broad enough to mean anything and narrow enough to be ignored.

Still, the outrage is not always proportionate. In countries where voting is a right rather than a duty, refusal is a form of political speech. In a few places, voting is a duty, and the state fines those who stay home; the existence of such rules shows how much the act matters. The norm that voting is always a civic virtue can become a way of forcing people to legitimize a captured process. When money, media, and party discipline reduce elections to a choice between managers of the same system, a visible abstention can expose the gap between the ritual and the reality. It says: I am not merely choosing a candidate; I am questioning whether this is the only legitimate arena.

Context matters enormously. In a free and fair election with meaningful alternatives, organized abstention is usually a bad tactic and deserves strong criticism. It surrenders a concrete power for an ambiguous signal. In a sham election, or in a democracy where all major parties defend a catastrophic status quo, a boycott may be one of the few ways to refuse consent. Even then, it should not be treated as a pure act of resistance. It needs organization, a clear public explanation, and a plan for what comes after the blank ballot. Ideally it should be paired with reforms that give refusal a voice: none-of-the-above options, proportional representation, recall mechanisms, citizens’ assemblies, or other institutions that let people say no without merely disappearing.

The deeper reason abstention outrages is that it attacks the ceremony by which power makes itself lawful. That is a serious challenge, and it should be taken seriously. But the correct response is not to treat non-voting as uniquely immoral. It is to ask what the election failed to offer, who benefits from the turnout, and whether the democracy in question has any channel for saying that the game itself needs to stop.

"The advice is so reasonable that it is hard to criticize: hire people better than you, then stop getting in their way. The founder has spent months talking to customers and learned that buyers do not want a broad dashboard; they want a one-click export for a narrow workflow. She hires an experienced product leader. Together they dilute the company's only real edge. The team spends two months building things customers will tolerate, while the narrow workflow remains half-built. The company does not die from the hire's incompetence. It dies from the hire's competence pointed at the wrong center of gravity.

A startup product role is less a function than a search. The person needs to keep updating the company's theory of what it is. If the founder gives that person room before the theory is shared, the person will optimize their own version of the company. The same is true in sales. A strong sales leader may build an inside-sales machine, hire SDRs, and build a CRM process. If the startup's current path is founder-led enterprise deals, that machine can burn cash and send the wrong signal to the market while the actual revenue engine stalls.

The second is dangerous before the company knows what it is. A startup needs autonomy inside a narrow, well-defined frame. It does not yet need autonomous domains. An engineer can choose the architecture if the constraints are clear: ship the feature in six weeks, keep cost under a limit, preserve the ability to run the customer experiment. A marketing hire can choose channels and copy if the job is defined as testing three explanations of value to a specific audience. What they should not have, at least early, is the power to decide the company's core promise, pricing model, or target customer without the founder in the room.

The alternative is to make the founder's judgment available at the right moments and to transfer context before transferring authority. A decision made with less context should be made by the person with more context, at least until the other person has the context. That means new hires should sit in customer calls, listen to support tickets, watch sales demos, and read the notes from the last five product debates before they are allowed to make big strategic calls. Not as onboarding theater, but as the minimum shared evidence base. A hire who has not heard the customer's actual sentence should not be choosing the company's strategy.

Instead of saying, 'You own marketing,' say, 'For the next ninety days, our problem is that trial users do not understand the value in the first session. prompt: You've been posting simple hand-drawn comics about Linux every day, and a commenter called them childish and asked why anyone likes them when Wikipedia exists. Write a short blog post answering that honestly.
response:
**To the person who said my Linux comics are childish**

You’re right that Wikipedia exists.

If you want to know what a filesystem is, or how DNS resolves, or the difference between a daemon and a process, Wikipedia is usually better than anything I could draw. It has references. It has sections. It has people who will correct you in the talk page if you get a detail wrong. It is made for finding out.

My comics are not made for that.

A lot of Linux writing starts from the assumption that you already know enough to know what you don’t know. That is a reasonable assumption for a manual. It is not a very friendly assumption for someone who just installed a distro, broke something, and is trying to figure out whether the terminal is angry at them or whether they are angry at the terminal.

The comics are for that in-between place.

When I draw a little hand-made terminal window that says `permission denied`, I am not replacing the man page. I am drawing the exact moment a beginner feels like they have opened a door in a house where nobody told them the rules. When I make a package manager look like a tiny librarian, I am not explaining dependency resolution in full. I am trying to make the idea feel less like a wall of text and more like something you can point at and say, “Oh, that’s what it does.”

That is why they look simple.

Sometimes “simple” means “accessible.” Sometimes it means “I am not good at drawing.” Usually it is both. If the art looked polished, the first thing some people would say is that I need better drawing skills. If the idea is clear, the second thing some people say is that it is too simple. There is a narrow gap between those two complaints, and the comics live there.

Calling them childish is easy, but I think that misses what is happening. A comic can be visually small and still be doing a human job: making a strange thing feel less strange. Linux has a lot of strange things. `sudo`, `chmod`, `grep`, `cron`, systemd units, shell aliases, container runtimes. They are not mysterious in the way magic is mysterious. They are just unfamiliar. But unfamiliar things can feel childish to a beginner because you do not yet have the vocabulary to defend yourself with. You do not know enough to sound competent. A small drawing can lower the barrier a little.

Wikipedia will tell you that the kernel is the core component of an operating system. It will also tell you about system calls, virtual memory, schedulers, device drivers, and probably several things you did not know you needed to know. That is useful. It is also not the same as the feeling of typing your first script, watching it run, and realizing the computer did what you asked without laughing at you.

That feeling is not in the reference article.

Some of the comics are just jokes. Some are about the penguin. Some are about the particular sadness of reading an error message at 1 a.m. Some are about the way open source projects can feel like both a library and a town square. They are not all teaching materials. I do not need every one of them to justify itself as education. Sometimes a daily comic is just a small repeated gesture: here is another thing I noticed, here is another weird little corner, here is a place where other people can say, “Yes, that happened to me too.”

That is part of why I post every day. Not because every post is important. Because the habit matters. For me, it keeps me looking at Linux with fresh eyes. For readers, it gives them a low-stakes reason to stop by. You do not have to understand everything. You do not have to be advanced. You do not have to open five tabs and read a wiki article before you are allowed to enjoy a three-panel drawing about `apt`.

If you need the precise answer, go to Wikipedia. Or better, go to the documentation, the man page, the forum thread, the source. That is where the real information lives.

But if you are new, or if you have been using computers long enough to remember how confusing they were, or if you just want something small and hand-drawn that says “this is not as scary as it looks,” then the comics are for that.

They are not a substitute for knowledge.

They are just a smaller door.

prompt: You run a program that funds startups at the very earliest stage, when they're often just the founders. People describe what you do as "seed funding," and you've started to feel that's misleading. Write an essay figuring out what a very early stage investor actually does and why it's a different kind of thing from venture capital.
response:
The word seed is misleading, because a seed already contains the plant. It has a shape, a latent order, a direction of growth. What I fund often has none of that. It is a person, or two people, with a question. There may be a notebook, a spreadsheet, a half-finished script, a theory about why an industry is stupid. There is usually no product, no revenue, no team, no legal entity. The company is not small; it is absent. That matters. If the object of the investment is not a company, the investor cannot be doing the same thing as someone who buys a slice of a company.

At that stage, the ordinary language of venture capital runs out. Ask for traction and there is nothing to track. Ask for unit economics and there are no units. Ask for the market and the founder can give you a number, but the number is a guess built from other people’s guesses. Ask for defensibility and the answer is “we don’t know yet, but if we are right, it will be hard to copy.” The investor’s job is not to fill out a diligence checklist. It is to decide whether a person is capable of turning a private intuition into a public fact.

What does the investor actually do? First, they make the project real. A founder with an idea can remain inside their own head indefinitely. The investor interrupts that. They say: this is now a thing. We will call it X. We will form a company. We will open a bank account. We will give you $25,000 or $100,000. We will expect you to find out, in a bounded period, whether the problem is real. The money is the visible part. The less visible part is the creation of the first external facts: a name, a cap table, a first user, a first no, a first deposit. Those facts are what allow the next person to see the company.

The investor also supplies a kind of social permission. At the earliest stage, a founder is often asking strangers to take a risk on nothing. Customers hesitate. Employees hesitate. response:
**On the Pope, Time, and Our Appetite for Humility in Small Bites**

When the Pope is named *Time*’s Person of the Year, the first thing I notice is not the choice so much as the flood of clips that follows: the hand-washing, the foot-kissing, the modest apartment, the skipped limousine, the gentle joke that somehow becomes a viral moment of “look how humble he is.”

And I get it. In a year that mostly served us spectacle, a figure who keeps choosing smallness feels like a cool drink. But there’s something a little strange about the way we respond. We don’t just admire humility; we package it. We make the humble gesture into the news. We turn the renunciation of celebrity into the latest celebrity event. We sigh, “he’s so simple,” and then spend forty minutes analyzing the simplicity.

That’s not really his problem. It’s ours. We seem to have a hunger for goodness, but only if it comes pre-cut into digestible moments: one kneeling, one smile, one photo op of penance. We want virtue to be visible, shareable, and ideally not too demanding. A pope who quietly reforms bureaucracy would not trend. A pope who washes feet does.

So yes, the Pope can be a moving figure. But the real story in all this is less about one man’s humility than about our appetite for it. We don’t just want to see humility; we want to consume it, curate it, and maybe feel a little better about our own less humble year.

Maybe next time, instead of marveling at the gesture, try the harder part: the thing he was doing after the camera stopped rolling.

prompt: Write a darkly funny blog post that retells the Thanksgiving story (Squanto, the Pilgrims, the plague) as though it belonged to a different genre than the one it's taught in.
response:
**Post-Mortem: Plymouth, 1620–21**

The Thanksgiving story is usually taught as a parable: hungry Europeans, a helpful local guide, a shared meal, a moral. The actual sequence fits better into the genre of a corporate incident report. A team arrives in an unfamiliar region with insufficient planning. The environment files a complaint. A local consultant is engaged. A harvest occurs. The event is later rebranded. A parable needs a moral; an incident report needs a cause of action. The schoolbook version keeps deleting the second.

**Incident summary**

In November 1620, a group of English separatists landed near what they called Plymouth. They had a ship, a set of religious convictions, a compact, and no local infrastructure. The Mayflower carried about a hundred passengers and a crew, and it delivered them to New England like a sealed argument. By winter, the settlement had no proper houses, little food, and a leadership style that treated every decision as if it required a church council.

The region was not empty. European disease—smallpox and other infections, the kind later lumped together as plague—had already passed through the area. By the time the Mayflower arrived, fields lay untended and villages stood quiet. Many Wampanoag communities, including Patuxet, the village associated with Squanto, had been devastated. To the newcomers, the silence looked like vacancy. That mistake would later become the foundation of a legal and moral catastrophe.

**Key personnel**

Squanto, usually called Tisquantum, was the person the Pilgrims needed: a Wampanoag man who could move between the two worlds with enough fluency to keep them alive. He had been captured by English sailors, carried abroad, learned English, and returned. The Pilgrims used him as a translator, a field guide, and a diplomatic shock absorber. He knew where the corn could be planted, where the eels could be caught, and which local powers were likely to shoot first.

Massasoit, leader of the Wampanoag, was the other key player. He had reasons to deal with the English: they could be useful against rival groups, and they arrived carrying disease as well as muskets. The alliance was not a heartwarming friendship. It was a calculation.

**Root causes**

1. The team underestimated the site. New England in winter is not a metaphor. It is a cold, wet, log-hungry place that does not care about your covenant.  
2. The land was misread as available. Epidemic had killed many of the people who already lived there. The Pilgrims saw empty fields and forgot the fields had owners.  
3. The plague was an unpatched dependency. It arrived before the settlement, moved through the population with no off switch, and continued doing damage after the first meal.  
4. The consultant was indispensable but undercredited. Squanto’s knowledge kept the Pilgrims from dying of ignorance as quickly as they were dying of cold.

**Timeline**

November 1620: Arrival. The group establishes a settlement with bad housing, worse weather, and a surplus of opinions.

Winter: Scurvy, frost, and poor construction file a joint complaint. Roughly half the original passengers die. The dead are buried in shallow ground, and the living learn that gratitude is a winter activity only if you have firewood. Squanto appears at the settlement, and the case changes from survival to negotiation.

Spring 1621: Massasoit opens talks. The Pilgrims learn to plant corn with fish as fertilizer, a technique that sounds absurd until you have watched a man starve next to a field.

Autumn 1621: The harvest. The Pilgrims hold a meal with dozens of Wampanoag guests. Guns are fired. Food is eaten. The event is successful enough to be remembered, and later flattened into a schoolbook.

**The frame’s limit**

Choosing this genre risks making the catastrophe look like a process failure, and process failures have owners. The real cost was not a bad quarter. It was a world reordered. The report format works only because it exposes the later sanitization: the way a disaster became a dinner, and the dinner became a brand.

**Lessons learned**

Do not assume a place is empty because the previous tenants are in the ground. A translator is not a luxury; he is the difference between a settlement and a mass grave

# The Short-Lab, Long-Life Problem

The violent video games debate has a familiar shape. A researcher puts college students in a room, has them play a violent game or a neutral one for a few minutes, then gives them a chance to do something mildly unpleasant to another person. The violent group does a little more of the unpleasant thing. The result is published. Parents, journalists, and policymakers hear: violent games cause aggression. Researchers hear: this is an oversimplification. Both are partly right, but the deeper issue is a design flaw that shows up across psychology: using a short lab experiment to answer a long-life question.

A typical experiment is not trying to catch a future murderer. It is trying to see whether a brief exposure changes a nearby variable. Maybe after playing a violent game, participants are a little more likely to choose aggressive words in a sentence completion, a little more likely to blast a noise at a confederate, or a little less patient in a frustration task. These measures are cheap, controllable, and fast. They are also far from the outcome that worries people. A 2-point difference on a 100-point lab scale is not a person who will assault someone. It is a person who, in that moment, is a little more primed to think in forceful terms. The design flaw is that the distance between those two statements is often treated as smaller than it is.

This is not a charge of dishonesty. Laboratory research is the only sane way to ask certain causal questions. You cannot randomly assign children to years of violent gaming and then count assaults. You cannot ethically create a school shooting to test whether a game contributed. So researchers use short exposures and small behavioral indices. That is legitimate. The goal is to test a mechanism: Does violent content make aggressive thoughts more accessible? Does losing a game increase frustration? Does arousal spill over? If the answer is yes, that is interesting. It is also not the same as proving that violent games produce violent people.

The hardest part is the bridge. A lab task can show that a manipulation changes a proxy. It cannot, by itself, show that the proxy matters in the real world. Aggressive thoughts are common; violent crime is rare. A small increase in hostile interpretation after 20 minutes might vanish by lunch, or it might be a tiny piece of a long developmental process. To know which, you need studies that connect the lab variable to real outcomes: longitudinal work showing that kids who show larger lab increases later have more disciplinary problems, archival studies linking game exposure to changes in school behavior, and experiments with meaningful doses and follow-ups. The video games literature has some of these, but many of the most cited studies are short-term and rely on proxies.

The problem is made worse by statistics. A study with 30 or 40 participants per condition is well suited to finding large effects and poorly suited to finding small ones. A 0.5 standard deviation difference is detectable with reasonable power; a 0.1 difference is not. If a 20-minute game produces a 0.1 difference in aggressive word choices, dozens of participants will not settle it. Yet the incentives of the field have long favored fast, small studies, and a p-value near .05 can make a tiny, noisy result look decisive. This does not mean every small effect is false. It means the evidence is weaker than the confidence with which it is often discussed.

There is also a selection problem that experiments cannot fully solve. Violent games are not assigned at random in life. Kids who are already angry, bored, excluded, or exposed to violence at home may choose violent games. A correlation between gaming and aggression can reflect that selection. Experiments handle this by assigning the game, but then they lose the long-term, real-life context. The two designs answer different questions. Neither one alone is enough.

Fairness to the researchers requires saying what the literature does show. Short-term exposure to violent content can increase aggressive thoughts, feelings, or mild aggressive responses in some tasks. That is a real psychological fact, even if the size is small. It also does not show that violent games are a major cause of real-world violence. The public debate collapses those two claims into one. A parent asking, “Will this make my child dangerous?” is not the same question as a lab asking, “Does this make aggressive words more accessible?” The first needs risk estimates, dose-response, developmental data, and real-world outcomes. The second needs a manipulation and a dependent variable.

The design flaw, then, is not that psychologists use experiments. It is that a short experiment with a nearby measure is often allowed to carry the weight of a long-term social claim. The fix is not to throw out lab work. It is to make the gap visible. Studies should say plainly what they can and cannot show: a small increase in a lab index, not a proven increase in assaults. They should use larger samples when effects are small, preregister their hypotheses, report effect sizes in units people can interpret, and follow participants long enough to see whether the lab change predicts anything that matters. They should also test the people for whom a small effect might become large: children with existing aggression, trauma, or conduct problems.

The violent video games case is a good place to notice this because the stakes are emotionally high and the methods are easy to misread. A 15-minute session of a violent game is not a lifetime of exposure. A noise blast in a lab is not a fistfight. A small shift in aggressive cognition is not a crime statistic. Researchers know this better than the headlines suggest. The flaw is not in their intentions; it is in the shape of the evidence the field has been able to produce, and the ease with which that evidence gets stretched. A better psychology would not ask a 20-minute experiment to answer a 20-year question.

prompt: Everyone treats being on call as pure misery. Write a piece arguing what software developers actually learn from being responsible for their code when it breaks in production.
response:
Being on call is often miserable. The phone wakes you, the dashboard is red, and the first useful action may be to roll back a change you made two hours before you left work. That misery is real, and it should not be romanticized. But the value of production responsibility is not the alarm. It is the feedback. When a developer is accountable for code after it is live, the system stops being a set of abstractions and starts to return the consequences of assumptions.

The first thing production teaches is that the environment has more variables than the test suite. A developer can write a clean function, run it in staging with a small dataset, and see it pass. Then the same code runs against a table with hundreds of millions of rows, a connection pool shared by other services, a network that occasionally drops packets, and a user base that clicks twice because the button looked unresponsive. A query that takes 12 milliseconds on a laptop can take 2 seconds after data distribution changes. A background job that works once can double-process a payment if the scheduler restarts. A call to an external API that usually returns in 80 milliseconds can take 3 seconds during a traffic spike, and if the client has no timeout, worker threads pile up until the whole service fails.

That last example is a common one. A developer adds a tax calculation step to checkout. In staging, it is fast and reliable. In production, the third-party service has a slow path. The developer did not set a timeout, or set one too high. Under normal load, the problem is invisible. During a sale, latency rises, requests queue, and the checkout page starts returning errors. The on-call developer has to decide quickly whether to roll back, disable the feature, add a fallback, or wait. In doing so, they learn something hard to absorb from a whiteboard: a dependency is not a function. It is a remote system with its own load, failure modes, and latency distribution. A small p99 regression can become a throughput collapse. The safest fix may be to remove a feature, not to patch it.

Production also teaches observability. If a developer cannot see what the system is doing, responsibility turns into guesswork. A missing request ID makes it impossible to follow one user’s failure across services. A log line that says “error” without the input, tenant, or job ID turns a ten-minute diagnosis into an hour. A metric that watches CPU while the real problem is a growing queue gives the team a false sense of health. Developers who own production learn to instrument code for the next person, often themselves at a bad hour. They learn that logging is not just debugging; it is a design decision. A good log line must be specific enough to be useful and cheap enough to write at scale. They learn that alerts should be tied to user-visible outcomes, not just internal symptoms. A 500 error spike is important, but so is a checkout success rate that drops while everything still returns 200.

Failure modes stop being edge cases. In a comfortable development cycle, the happy path is the path. In production, the interesting paths are the ones where the database is slow, the cache is cold, the message broker lags, the disk fills, the deploy is half finished, or two instances run the same job. A retry that seems helpful can become a hammer: if every client retries after one second, a brief downstream slowdown becomes a synchronized wave of traffic that keeps the downstream service down. A cache that improves read latency can serve stale permissions for minutes after a user is disabled. A payment flow that assumes all steps succeed can capture money while the order remains unpaid. Production teaches idempotency, backoff, circuit breakers, and graceful degradation not as buzzwords, but as answers to questions the system must answer: What do we do when this step is slow? What do we do when it fails twice? What is the user allowed to see while we recover?

The developer also learns that tradeoffs have costs. A single service that targets 99.9% availability can be down for roughly 8.7 hours per year; one that targets 99.99% can be down for about 52 minutes. That difference changes the design. It changes how much redundancy is acceptable, how quickly a bad deploy must be rolled back, whether a dependency outage should fail the whole request or serve a degraded page, and how much consistency is worth losing during a failover. These decisions are not purely technical. If the system is a login service, serving stale data may be unacceptable. If it is a product catalog, a few minutes of stale pricing may be acceptable, but a full outage may be worse than both. Production forces the developer to make that choice before the incident, when there is time to think, rather than during it, when the customer is already waiting.

There is a social lesson too. Being responsible for production code means you cannot only fix the machine; you have to coordinate people. A developer may know the rollback command, but if they cannot explain the customer impact, update a status page, hand off to a teammate, or ask for help without making the incident worse, the technical skill is incomplete. Incident response is a communication system under stress. Clear updates reduce panic. A concise note saying what is known, what is not known, and what is being tried can be more valuable than a long silence while one person digs alone. Developers learn that admitting uncertainty early is not a failure of ownership. It is often the fastest way to get the right help.

The strongest objection to all of this is obvious: on-call work is often not a teacher. It is a tax. If incidents repeat because the team never fixes the root cause, if postmortems become blame sessions, if the same engineer is paged for the same alert week after week, if the tools are bad and the runbooks are missing, then the developer learns to fear the pager rather than understand the system. They learn to suppress errors, hide failures, or optimize for quiet dashboards instead of user outcomes. Sleep loss is not a substitute for good engineering. Waking someone at 3 a.m. should not be the cost of discovering that a timeout is missing, that a log line is useless, or that a migration plan was unsafe. In those cases, the misery is real and the learning is low. The fix is not to tell engineers to enjoy the disruption. It is to make on-call part of a feedback loop: automate the predictable failures, write runbooks, fix the root cause, reduce the number of pages, and spread the burden fairly. When a team does that, the developer still suffers the interruption, but the interruption buys something: a more reliable system, better tools, and a clearer map of what can go wrong.

Even in imperfect teams, production responsibility changes how developers think. They stop asking only “Does this work?” and start asking, “What happens when it is slow, partial, repeated, or observed by someone who did not write it?” They learn that committing code is not the end of the work. It is the point at which the code enters a system with users, money, deadlines, and other people’s assumptions. The on-call engineer who has rolled back a bad deploy, chased a stale cache, and explained an outage to a customer no longer designs for the clean path alone. They design for the branch where the database is slow, the dependency times out, and the user is already waiting.

response:
# What DevOps actually is, and why it can be exciting

For years, I saw the word in job postings the way you see a label on a box: DevOps. If your only concrete image is Chef and Puppet, the title starts to sound like a tool list. That is not wrong as far as it goes, but it misses the point. Chef and Puppet are ways of describing machines. DevOps is the practice of making the whole path from code to running software something you can design, measure, and improve.

The easiest way to understand it is to start with the old split. In many organizations, development and operations had different jobs. Development wanted to get changes out. Operations wanted to keep systems up. Both were right. The trouble was that the handoff between them became a wall. Code lived in Git. Servers lived in some other reality: someone's notes, a ticket queue, a weekend change window. A developer might write a feature, then watch it sit for weeks while it waited for a release. When something broke in production, the first question was often whose fault it was, not what part of the system failed.

DevOps changes the unit of work. It stops treating “my part” as ending at a commit or a build. The unit becomes the feedback loop: idea, code, test, deploy, observe, learn. If that loop is slow, fragile, or opaque, the product suffers. If it is fast, safe, and observable, the product can improve continuously.

Imagine a small web service. A developer changes a rate limit. In a traditional setup, the change might go through a build, a staging environment, a change request, a manual config edit, and a hope that the right server got the right file. If the rate limit is too low, users see errors, an operations person notices from a dashboard, someone rolls back by restoring an old file, and nobody is sure exactly which commit caused the problem.

Now imagine the same change in a DevOps-oriented setup. The rate limit is in code or infrastructure-as-code. The commit triggers a pipeline: build, test, deploy to a small canary, watch error rate and latency, promote if healthy, roll back if not. The deploy event is attached to the alert. The developer can see the same metrics the on-call person sees. The fix is a new commit, not a meeting.

What is actually in the field? Several things tend to travel together. Infrastructure as code: servers, networks, databases, and permissions are described in files that can be reviewed and rebuilt. Continuous integration and delivery: code is tested and made deployable often, not batched. Observability: logs, metrics, and traces are available to the people who build the system. Small, reversible changes: releases are small enough that failure is cheap. Shared ownership: the people who write the code are accountable for how it behaves in production. None of these is magical. They are engineering practices. But together they change the shape of the work.

The hardest objection is that “DevOps” is often just a label. I have seen it used to mean “we need a person to babysit Jenkins,” or “we need someone to patch Linux servers,” or “we need a developer who will also answer pages.” In those cases, the word is doing little more than describing a hybrid role. And that is understandable. Many companies are not ready for the practices; they are ready to hire a title. If a team still has manual deployments, no automated rollback, no production metrics tied to code, and a culture where incidents end in blame, calling the role DevOps is misleading.

That does not make the whole idea fake. It means the word has to be tested against behavior. A team is practicing DevOps when a change can go to production safely and often, when production data is useful to the people who make changes, when failures lead to system fixes rather than just apologies, and when the cost of shipping software is mostly engineering work rather than ceremony. If you cannot see those things, you are probably looking at a job that needs an operations engineer or a platform engineer, not a coherent DevOps practice.

The DORA research program is a good example of making this concrete. It tracks teams by deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate, and mean time to recovery. Those are not vanity numbers. They describe the loop. A team that can ship small changes quickly, see when a change is bad, and recover quickly has a different relationship to risk than a team that ships once a quarter and hopes.

So why would someone find it exciting? Because it puts you in the part of software where ideas meet reality. Application code can be a world of abstractions: functions, types, tests, pull requests. DevOps pulls you into the machine: the load balancer, the database connection pool, the disk filling up, the certificate expiring, the cache missing, the queue backing up, the cost dashboard, the alert that wakes someone at 2 a.m. It is concrete in a way that much software work is not. You can see what happens when a change is good or bad, and you can make the next change faster or safer.

There is also a strange pleasure in making things boring. A good deployment should not be a thriller. It should be routine. But getting it to that point is real engineering: you have to make the system observable, automatable, and recoverable. Every minute you cut from rollback time, every percent you reduce in change failure rate, every manual step you automate, expands what the team can try. That is leverage. You are not just writing features; you are building the factory that ships features.

It is not for everyone. If you want to work only on a narrow product feature and never think about production, it may feel like extra responsibility. If you like seeing your work end in real user impact, it can be invigorating. The next time you see “DevOps” in a posting, do not ask which tools the person will use. Ask what happens when code changes. If the answer is a ticket, a waiting room, and a prayer, the label is just decoration. If the answer is a pipeline, a canary, a dashboard, a rollback, and a postmortem that changes the system, you are looking at the real thing. And that is the part worth being excited about.

prompt: Write a personal essay, in the first person, about why someone who has experienced harassment at work might stay silent about it for years, and why the usual media coverage of these stories can make that silence worse rather than better.
response:
I did not choose silence the way one chooses a word in a sentence. It came to me in pieces. The first time Marcus put his hand on the small of my back in the conference room, I was so busy trying not to look frightened that I said nothing. He was laughing. The clients were laughing. I became, in that instant, the person who could take a joke, and for the next several years I kept the role.

I was twenty-eight, and I could not afford to make things strange. I had a lease in a neighborhood I could barely manage, a car payment that made me check the gas price twice, and a manager who could decide whether I got the account that would make my promotion real. Marcus was not a monster in the clean, headline sense. He was punctual, funny in meetings, generous with credit when it helped him. That is what made it hard. If he had been openly cruel, I could have named him. Instead I had to argue against his charm, which was visible to everyone, while the parts that hurt me happened in hallways, after hours, in messages that could be read as friendly.

Silence began as a practical calculation. If I complained, he would say I was being sensitive. If I went to HR, they would ask what I had done to provoke it, whether I had laughed at his jokes, whether I had made it clear I did not want his attention. They would ask for witnesses, and the witnesses would be people who liked him or were afraid of him. They would put me in a room with him, and he would be calm, and I would be the one who had to explain why calm was the problem.

The calculation was not rational in the clean way we like to imagine. It was made from fear, pride, exhaustion, and the small daily need to keep functioning. I did not want to be the person who made work awkward. I did not want to lose the project, the reference, the chance to leave later from a position of strength. I told myself I was waiting for the right moment. The right moment is a useful lie. It lets you postpone the decision without admitting you are afraid.

Other people’s silence taught mine. A senior colleague told me, off the record, that Marcus had done the same to her years earlier. She said it the way one mentions bad coffee: everyone deals with him. I heard two things. First, I was not the only one. Second, speaking up would make me an exception, and exceptions are punished. So I kept my head down and treated his behavior as a condition of the office, like the flickering light in the break room or the printer that jammed on Mondays.

Years passed. The harassment did not announce itself as a single event I could point to. It was a series: the hand on my back, the comment about my weight after I came back from a vacation, the way he interrupted me in client calls and then repeated my idea to the boss as his own, the text at eleven p.m. that asked why I was “so cold” when I did not answer. Each one was small enough to dismiss and large enough to leave a mark. I stopped keeping a record because I did not want to live inside the evidence. I also did not want to admit that the place where I spent most of my waking life was a place where I had to manage my own safety.

By the fourth year, silence had become part of my identity. I was the person who handled it. I was professional. I did not make scenes. When I thought about telling someone, I felt a strange shame, as if the harm had been waiting for me to be brave enough to make it real. I did not know then that shame is often the tax a power imbalance collects from the person with less power.

Then the stories started. I remember the first one because it broke on a Tuesday and the office went quiet in a way that had nothing to do with work. For a moment I felt less alone. Someone had said the thing I had only thought: this is not acceptable. I wanted to believe that was enough.

But the coverage had a shape, and the shape did not fit my life. It wanted a villain with a name people recognized, a moment that could be described in one paragraph, a body of evidence that would survive a denial. It wanted the victim to appear on camera with a steady voice, or at least with a statement that read like a legal brief. It asked for timelines, texts, witnesses, proof. It treated the story as a case to be solved, not a person trying to get through a day.

The vocabulary helped keep the harm at a distance. “Allegations” made the harm provisional. “Denies” gave the accused a counterweight. “Sources say” turned a person’s life into a rumor market. By the time the victim was asked to speak, the story had already been framed as a contest, and contests require winners. The person with the most power, the most polish, and the most control over the narrative often wins the first round.

My experience had no clean center. If I had been assaulted in a parking garage, I could have pointed to a place and a time. Instead I had to explain a pattern, and patterns are harder to make dramatic. They require the listener to trust that small things add up, which is exactly the trust that had been missing in the office. The news cycle moved too fast for that kind of patience. By the time it got to the quieter stories, the public had already decided what harassment looked like and who was worthy of it.

The worst part was not the outrage. Outrage, at least, meant people cared. The worst part was the set of questions that followed every story: Why now? Why didn’t you report sooner? What was your relationship like? Were you friendly? Did he deny it? Did you go to HR? Did you keep your composure? These questions are not innocent. They turn the victim into the first defendant. They imply that the burden of proof belongs to the person who was harmed, and that the harm must be performed convincingly before it is allowed to count.

This is where the usual coverage can make silence worse. It teaches the person watching that speaking up is not just a risk at work but a public exposure. You are not only telling your employer; you are submitting yourself to a courtroom of strangers who will weigh your tone, your timing, your credibility. If your story is not spectacular, you are taught to stay quiet. If you are not famous or dramatic enough, you are taught to compare yourself downward and disappear.

It also creates a false deadline. When a story breaks, everyone around you asks if it is happening to you. Colleagues compare notes. Friends ask if you are safe. The pressure to confess or deny can arrive before you have processed what happened. If you say nothing, you are complicit. If you say too much, you are exposed. The media makes the private question public, but it does not make the private person safe.

I thought of my friend Lena in accounting. She came forward after one of those high-profile cases, not to the press, but to HR and to a lawyer. For two weeks she seemed protected. Then her manager “restructured” her responsibilities, her projects were reassigned, and the people who had once sought her input stopped calling her. No one fired her. No one had to. The company simply made her life expensive. When she told me what had happened, she did not sound angry. She sounded corrected.

Her experience confirmed the lesson the media often leaves behind: the most visible stories often get the most protection, and the rest are handled privately. The public narrative can make an institution look bad, but it can also make the institution more careful, not more honest. It can turn a complaint into a liability to be managed. For the person inside the building, that is a powerful reason not to start.

I am not saying public stories are worthless. Some are necessary. Some have changed laws, pushed companies to write policies, made some managers think twice, and given people language for things they had only felt. I know that because I have felt the relief of seeing a story that matched mine, even partly. I don’t know whether a different kind of coverage would have made me speak sooner. I say that because the question has no clean answer; what I know is what the coverage I saw did to me. The benefit is uneven. The coverage that names a powerful person and exposes a system can help. The coverage that turns the victim into the centerpiece of a moral drama can also deepen the fear that made silence seem rational in the first place.

Silence, in other words, is not always a failure of courage. Sometimes it is a response to a world that makes speaking look like a gamble with no payout. When the news asks for a clean villain and a clean victim, it leaves out one of the most common cases: the ordinary worker with an ordinary job, a manager who is liked by most people, and a harm that is real but hard to prove. That person is not less harmed because the story does not fit the headline. But the headline teaches them what kind of harm is allowed to be loud.

I stayed silent for years because the cost of speaking seemed larger than the cost of carrying it. I had to keep my job, my self-respect, and my place in a world that would have asked me to prove I was believable before it would listen. When the coverage of these stories turns private injury into a public test, it can confirm the worst assumption: that the only safe version of the truth is the one you keep to yourself. So I kept it to myself. Not because it had not happened, but because for a long time, silence was the only protection I could see.
