prompt: A lot of people tell me they'd like to start a technical blog but don't know what to write about that anyone would find useful. Write an essay on one good answer to that: using the things you've personally struggled with as the source of posts.
response:
The most reliable source of technical posts is not a list of hot topics, but the pile of problems you have already survived. When you struggle with something long enough, you accumulate material that is hard to invent: the wrong guesses, the versions, the error messages, the moment the explanation clicked. A post built from that struggle can be useful even if the final answer is a single line of code, because the reader gains not only the fix but the path that leads to it.

Many people wait for a topic that feels big enough. They think a useful post must introduce a new architecture, benchmark a framework, or explain a language feature from first principles. That standard makes blogging feel inaccessible because it asks you to be ahead of the problems you are currently solving. A personal struggle inverts the standard. You do not need to be the first person to encounter the problem; you need to have encountered it closely enough to describe it. The value is in the reduction of uncertainty for a reader who is standing in the same fog.

A debugging story is useful because it preserves the sequence of evidence. If a post says, “The problem was a missing timezone setting,” the reader may copy the setting without understanding why. If the post says, “The job ran at 02:00 UTC, the dashboard showed 04:00, and I first suspected cron because the log timestamp changed after a server reboot,” the reader learns how to separate clock, locale, and scheduler. The second version is longer, but it transfers. The reader may face a different stack with the same shape: a local assumption colliding with a remote default.

This is where specificity matters. A struggle is useful when it includes the details that make the problem reproducible in the reader’s mind: the OS, the library version, the exact error, the code path, the environment variable, the timing. “My build failed after a dependency update” is too vague to help many people. “After upgrading from Node 16 to 18, the webpack dev server exited with ERR_OSSL_EVP_UNSUPPORTED during the first hot reload” gives a reader enough to recognize their own incident. Specific details also make the post easier to find, because people search with the words they saw in their terminal, not with the abstract name of the concept.

There is a common fear that a personal struggle will be too basic. If it is basic, that may be a reason to publish, not a reason to hide it, provided the mistake is common and hard to diagnose. A missing semicolon is not a post. A promise that is created but not awaited, a cache key that omits a user ID, a permission denied that only appears in production because of file ownership, a test that passes alone but fails in the suite because of shared state—these are small in hindsight and expensive in the moment. They are useful because they occupy the gap between “I know the language” and “I know how this system behaves under my constraints.”

The harder objection is that a personal struggle may be too local. Your bug might depend on a weird internal tool, a one-off data migration, or a configuration mistake that no one else will make. That is true. Not every struggle should become a post. The test is not whether the problem was impressive, but whether the mechanism is recognizable. If the lesson is only “our legacy service has a typo in its hostname,” the post will not help many readers. If the lesson is “when a service intermittently returns a 502, check whether the load balancer is using a stale upstream list after a failed rollout,” then the local incident becomes a case study. You can keep the concrete example and abstract the pattern: here is what I saw, here is what was actually happening, here is how I confirmed it, here is what to check when you see the same symptoms.

This is why the best struggle-based posts are not confessions; they are case studies. The personal part is the evidence that the problem was real and that the writer paid attention. The useful part is the explanation. You do not need to publish every false start, but you should include the ones that teach. A reader who is stuck often needs to know not only what to do, but what not to waste time on. If you spent two hours changing a Dockerfile before realizing the image was cached, that information can save someone else an evening. If you tried five configuration flags before finding the one that mattered, naming the dead ends gives the reader a map of the territory.

Struggles also help you write at the right level. When you explain a problem you have actually solved, you know which details are load-bearing. You know that the reader cannot skip the paragraph about how the service discovers the database, because that is where the bug hid. You know that the reader does not need a tutorial on the framework, because the issue is not the framework. This is harder to do from a planned topic, where you may spend ten paragraphs setting up a problem that no one in your audience is having. A personal struggle gives you a built-in audience: the version of you from three days ago, and the other engineers who will meet the same version of the system.

There is a practical constraint, though. A struggle is raw material, not a finished argument. Before writing, ask whether the post has a transferable claim. “I fixed my app” is not enough. “The app failed because the retry logic amplified a temporary network error into a queue backlog” is a claim. You can test it by trying to state the lesson in one sentence without naming your project. If you cannot, the post may be too local. If you can, the project details become examples supporting the lesson. This editing step keeps the blog useful rather than merely personal.

It also helps to write while the struggle is still fresh. The details that make a post useful are easy to forget: the exact flag, the line number, the odd behavior under load, the environment variable that looked harmless. A short note taken during the incident—what you expected, what happened, what you tried, what versions were involved—can become a post later. You do not need to write immediately, but you do need to preserve the evidence. A post written a month later from memory often becomes generic because the strange particulars have faded.

One more objection is that writing about your struggles may make you look inexperienced. In technical writing, the opposite is usually true. A careful account of a hard problem shows judgment: you can distinguish symptom from cause, you can reproduce the issue, you can explain the system to someone else. The risk is not that the struggle is too hard to discuss; it is that you stop at the fix and leave out the reasoning. A post that says “this was tricky, but here is the solution” gives the reader a result without the method. A post that says “I first assumed X, then saw Y, then tested Z” gives the reader a way to think.

prompt: I finally got around to reading The Black Swan, years after everyone else. Write me a book review that engages with the ideas rather than summarizing them, including where you think Taleb is right and where his advice might be dangerous. Some humor welcome, since reviewing him seems like a risky business.
response:
**The Black Swan, or How to Be Right About the Unpredictable Without Becoming Useless**

Reviewing Nassim Nicholas Taleb is a little like walking into a room where someone has just thrown a chair at the whiteboard. There is a certain masochism in it: he has already written the review of everyone who reviews him, and it is unkind. *The Black Swan* came out in 2007, so by now it has acquired the sheen of prophecy: the book that saw 2008 coming, that warns about pandemics, that mocks the experts who still do not learn. Reading it years after everyone else means you can skip the excitement of being surprised and go straight to the more uncomfortable question: what do we do with a warning that is hard to test and easier to brand?

Taleb writes with the energy of a man who has personally been harmed by Gaussian distributions. There are jabs, anecdotes, and a certain theatrical contempt for the academic, the consultant, and the official statistician. It is funny in the way that a good emergency drill is funny: you laugh because the scenario is absurd, and then you realize the scenario may be your office. The useful part of the book is not the bird but the bruise it leaves on our confidence.

His strongest point is that we are bad at the tails. In many areas, average outcomes are predictable and extreme ones are not. A hospital can estimate the average number of patients per day and still be caught flat-footed by a virus. A city can model traffic and still be paralyzed by a storm. A financial system can price individual loans and still miss the moment when all the loans become bad at once. In 2008, the problem was not that banks had never seen a bad loan; it was that the correlations exploded. The model had priced risk as if the world were a collection of separate dice, when it was more like a house of cards with one wobbly card in the middle.

Taleb is right that expertise can become a performance. We remember the forecaster who called the crash and forget the hundred who called a soft landing. We study the startup founder who bet everything and became rich, not the twenty who bet everything and became cautionary tales. Survivorship bias is real, and it is one of the book’s best public-service contributions. It reminds us that the visible world is a sample, not a census, and that the sample is often skewed by the fact that the dead do not write memoirs.

But the same bias can be turned into a blanket distrust of all evidence. If every expert forecast is suspect because the past is unreliable, then the next step is not humility; it is paralysis. The turkey in Taleb’s famous example is fed every day and concludes life is safe until the day it is not. That is a great warning against overfitting to normal times. It is also a recipe for a turkey that never eats, because every meal might be the last. Risk is not only the hidden knife; it is also starvation. A person who treats every stable institution as a future slaughterhouse may avoid one bad outcome by missing every good one.

Another of Taleb’s themes is our love of story. We turn accidents into plots: the genius who saw the future, the market that corrected, the crisis that was inevitable. Stories make the world manageable. They also make it false. Here, again, he is often right. Post-hoc narratives can hide the role of luck, timing, and power. But if we reject all narrative, we lose the thing that allows us to act. Epidemiology is a story about transmission. Engineering is a story about load and failure. Public health is a story about cause and effect. The goal is not to believe the story blindly, but to keep the story honest with numbers, tests, and humility. A model that says “the storm will arrive Thursday” is not a prophecy; it is a tool for moving the boat.

The dangerous part begins when the book’s skepticism about experts is applied without domain limits. Taleb is most convincing in systems that are reflexive, political, and fragile: markets, media, bureaucracies, fashion. In those systems, the act of prediction changes the world, and the people in charge have incentives to flatter the present. He is less convincing, or at least more selective, when the domain has stable laws and feedback. Weather forecasting has improved dramatically. Vaccines work because of causal mechanisms, not because experts are confident. Bridges stand because engineers test materials and build redundancy. To say “experts are overconfident” is useful. To say “therefore the nurse, the meteorologist, and the structural engineer are all performing” is not wisdom; it is a mood.

Taleb’s practical advice often takes the form of a barbell: keep most of what you have in very safe places, and put a small slice into high-risk, high-upside bets. The logic is attractive. You avoid the middle, where you are exposed to hidden fragility but not rewarded enough for the risk. In personal finance, this can make sense: a person with $100,000 might keep $90,000 in boring, low-risk assets and use $10,000 for speculative investments, understanding that the $10,000 can vanish. The key is that the safe part is large enough to matter, and the risky part is small enough to survive.

But the advice has a class structure. For someone with $100,000, a 10 percent speculative sleeve is a real option. For someone with $10,000, it is $1,000, which may not be enough to change their life and may be too much to lose. “Build optionality” sounds neutral, but optionality is often a product of existing wealth, networks, and slack. A person working two jobs does not have the luxury of experimenting with high-risk bets. If the lesson of the Black Swan is that rare events can ruin you, then the first protection is not a clever portfolio; it is not being one bad month from catastrophe. Taleb’s advice is best when it is read as a warning against leverage, and worst when it is read as a lifestyle brand for people who can afford to play.

He also favors a negative approach: remove the bad rather than chase the good. Do not overeat, do not overwork, do not over-leverage, do not over-specialize. This is good advice in many areas. Redundancy is underrated. A life with too few irons in the fire is fragile. A company with one customer is fragile. A city with one power source is fragile. But “do less” can become a conservative slogan. Sometimes resilience requires positive action: building hospitals, funding research, maintaining infrastructure, regulating banks, requiring seatbelts, testing software. The opposite of fragility is not minimalism. It is robustness, and robustness often costs money and organization.

The hardest objection to my own reading is that I may be doing exactly what Taleb warns against: taking a strange, disruptive idea and fitting it into a moderate, manageable category. He is not simply saying “experts are wrong.” He is saying that many systems are fragile because they are optimized for the normal case and punished for preparing for the abnormal. If I condemn his advice as dangerous, I might be using a comfortable narrative to avoid the harder lesson: that we should design institutions and lives to survive our mistakes. That is a fair charge. The answer is that the warning and the brand are not the same thing. A fire alarm is valuable even if it sometimes screams over burnt toast. The problem is not that it is loud; it is that people start trusting it only when the house is already on fire.

There is also a methodological problem. Black Swan thinking can become unfalsifiable. If an event is surprising and costly, it is a Black Swan. If experts predicted it, they were probably part of the narrative, lucky, or talking about a different version of the event. If they did not predict it, the framework wins. That makes the concept more a rhetorical shield than a precise theory. I am less sure how much of Taleb’s later public persona belongs to the book and how much is simply the cost of being right online; the two have become hard to separate. But the useful claims underneath—fat tails, model risk, overconfidence, survivorship bias—are testable enough to be worth taking seriously. The danger is when the label becomes an identity: “Taleb was right” replaces the work of asking which institutions, models, and decisions actually failed.

Consider a pandemic. Taleb would be right to say that no one could predict the exact timing, the exact virus, or the exact economic pattern. He would be wrong if the lesson became that pandemics are so unpredictable that we should not fund public health, stockpile supplies, or build hospital capacity. The same event supports both humility and preparation. The correct response is not to pretend we can forecast the future, but to build systems that can absorb a future we did not forecast: testing capacity, vaccination infrastructure, fiscal reserves, redundant supply chains, and the social safety net that keeps people alive when the model breaks. Climate change is not a Black Swan in Taleb’s sense; it is a slow, known risk with uncertain timing and severity. Confusing the two can be dangerous. A Black Swan is a surprise. A gray rhino is a large, obvious risk that people ignore because it is boring. Climate, debt, aging populations, cyberattack: these are not swans. They are rhinos wearing swan costumes. The book’s real value is reminding us that the unknown unknowns exist. Its real danger is making the known unknowns feel equally mysterious.

*The Black Swan* is best read as a warning against fragility, not as a manual for avoiding the world. Taleb is right that the future is not a gentle continuation of the past, that experts often overstate their knowledge, and that rare events do the heavy lifting in history. He is less right—or his advice is more easily misused—when it becomes a license to distrust all expertise, avoid all preparation, or treat life as a portfolio of clever hedges. The person who reads him and then checks the fire extinguisher, funds the emergency account, diversifies sources of income, and still trusts the nurse has learned the useful lesson. The person who reads him and concludes that everything is chaos, all institutions are corrupt, and the only rational response is to hide in cash and contempt has learned the wrong lesson, and may be more exposed to the very swan he is trying to avoid. A Black Swan is hard to see. A person who has read Taleb and stopped thinking is easier to spot, and usually more dangerous.

Reviewing Nassim Nicholas Taleb is a little like walking into a room where someone has just thrown a chair at the whiteboard. The Black Swan came out in 2007, so by now it has acquired the sheen of prophecy: the book that saw 2008 coming, that warns about pandemics, that mocks the experts who still do not learn. Reading it late means you can skip the excitement of being surprised and go straight to the more uncomfortable question: what do we do with a warning that is hard to test and easier to brand?

Taleb writes with the energy of a man who has personally been harmed by Gaussian distributions. There are jabs, anecdotes, and a certain theatrical contempt for the academic, the consultant, and the official statistician. It is funny in the way that a good emergency drill is funny: you laugh because the scenario is absurd, and then you realize the scenario may be your office. The useful part of the book is not the bird but the bruise it leaves on our confidence.

His strongest point is that we are bad at the tails. In many areas, average outcomes are predictable and extreme ones are not. A hospital can estimate the average number of patients per day and still be caught flat-footed by a virus. A city can model traffic and still be paralyzed by a storm. A financial system can price individual loans and still miss the moment when all the loans become bad at once. In 2008, the problem was not that banks had never seen a bad loan; it was that the correlations exploded. The model had priced risk as if the world were a collection of separate dice, when it was more like a house of cards with one wobbly card in the middle.

Taleb is right that expertise can become a performance. We remember the forecaster who called the crash and forget the hundred who called a soft landing. We study the startup founder who bet everything and became rich, not the twenty who bet everything and became cautionary tales. Survivorship bias is real, and it is one of the book's best public-service contributions. It reminds us that the visible world is a sample, not a census, and that the sample is often skewed by the fact that the dead do not write memoirs.

But the same bias can be turned into a blanket distrust of all evidence. If every expert forecast is suspect because the past is unreliable, then the next step is not humility; it is paralysis. The turkey in Taleb's famous example is fed every day and concludes life is safe until the day it is not. That is a great warning against overfitting to normal times. It is also a recipe for a turkey that never eats, because every meal might be the last. Risk is not only the hidden knife; it is also starvation. A person who treats every stable institution as a future slaughterhouse may avoid one bad outcome by missing every good one.

Another of Taleb's themes is our love of story. We turn accidents into plots: the genius who saw the future, the market that corrected, the crisis that was inevitable. Stories make the world manageable. They also make it false. Here, again, he is often right. Post-hoc narratives can hide the role of luck, timing, and power. But if we reject all narrative, we lose the thing that allows us to act. Epidemiology is a story about transmission. Engineering is a story about load and failure. Public health is a story about cause and effect. The goal is not to believe the story blindly, but to keep the story honest with numbers, tests, and humility. A model that says "the storm will arrive Thursday" is not a prophecy; it is a tool for moving the boat.

The dangerous part begins when the book's skepticism about experts is applied without domain limits. Taleb is most convincing in systems that are reflexive, political, and fragile: markets, media, bureaucracies, fashion. In those systems, the act of prediction changes the world, and the people in charge have incentives to flatter the present. He is less convincing, or at least more selective, when the domain has stable laws and feedback. Weather forecasting has improved dramatically. Vaccines work because of causal mechanisms, not because experts are confident. Bridges stand because engineers test materials and build redundancy. To say "experts are overconfident" is useful. To say "therefore the nurse, the meteorologist, and the structural engineer are all performing" is not wisdom; it is a mood.

Taleb's practical advice often takes the form of a barbell: keep most of what you have in very safe places, and put a small slice into high-risk, high-upside bets. The logic is attractive. You avoid the middle, where you are exposed to hidden fragility but not rewarded enough for the risk. In personal finance, this can make sense: a person with $100,000 might keep $90,000 in boring, liquid assets and use $10,000 for speculative investments, understanding that the $10,000 can vanish. The key is that the safe part is large enough to matter, and the risky part is small enough to survive.

But the advice has a class structure. For someone with $100,000, a 10 percent speculative sleeve is a real option. For someone with $10,000, it is $1,000, which may not be enough to change their life and may be too much to lose. "Build optionality" sounds neutral, but optionality is often a product of existing wealth, networks, and slack. A person working two jobs does not have the luxury of experimenting with high-risk bets. If the lesson of the Black Swan is that rare events can ruin you, then the first protection is not a clever portfolio; it is not being one bad month from catastrophe. Taleb's advice is best when it is read as a warning against leverage, and worst when it is read as a lifestyle brand for people who can afford to play.

He also favors a negative approach: remove the bad rather than chase the good. Do not overeat, do not overwork, do not over-leverage, do not over-specialize. This is good advice in many areas. Redundancy is underrated. A life with too few irons in the fire is fragile. A company with one customer is fragile. A city with one power source is fragile. But "do less" can become a conservative slogan. Sometimes resilience requires positive action: building hospitals, funding research, maintaining infrastructure, regulating banks, requiring seatbelts, testing software. The opposite of fragility is not minimalism. It is robustness, and robustness often costs money and organization.

He is not simply saying "experts are wrong." He is saying that many systems are fragile because they are optimized for the normal case and punished for preparing for the abnormal. If I condemn his advice as dangerous, I might be using a comfortable narrative to avoid the harder lesson: that we should design institutions and lives to survive our mistakes. That is a fair charge. The Shape We Are Supposed to Fit

When a talented artist keeps doing what he thinks he is supposed to do, the first thing to notice is not the work but the phrase “supposed to do.” The work may be good. The hours may be serious. The applications may be polished. And still the life can feel stuck, because the person is moving inside a frame that was never tested. He is not choosing between options so much as trying to make his days fit a picture of what an artist’s life is supposed to look like. When the picture and the days do not match, he concludes that something is wrong with him, or with his effort, rather than with the picture.

This is not a rare failure of honesty. Many of us carry a set of assumptions about what a good life or career must look like: it should be coherent, respected, progressive, based on some authentic core, and visible enough to be judged. These assumptions are often useful. They summarize what has worked for other people, what institutions reward, what families fear. A map can help you walk. The trouble begins when the map is mistaken for the only territory, or when the route on it is treated as a moral requirement. Then a life that is actually workable can feel like a disgrace, simply because it does not look like the approved diagram.

For your friend, the limiting assumption may be that a serious artist must be recognized by a certain kind of audience: galleries, curators, critics, peers with the right credentials. If that is the frame, then many ordinary moves stop being options. Teaching a workshop feels like giving up. Taking a design job feels like betrayal. Making small objects for friends feels amateurish. Collaborating with a local business feels like selling out. The options are not gone; they have been disqualified in advance by the rule that only one kind of success counts. A person can be talented and still feel trapped not because the door is locked, but because he has decided that only one door in the building is real.

The frame also tends to turn adjustment into identity. If a good career must be a single narrative—studied, discovered, pursued, mastered—then any patchwork looks like failure. But many working lives are patchwork. A person may spend ten hours a week making, sixteen earning a living, four learning a new skill, and the rest maintaining health and relationships. That is not a lack of commitment; it is a budget. The all-or-nothing frame makes budgets invisible. It says: either you are doing the true thing, or you are compromising. In practice, the true thing is often a ratio, not a pure substance.

This is where assumptions about a good life become especially costly. We are often taught that a good life must be impressive, chosen from a clear authentic self, and stable enough to be shown to others. prompt: You've been running a small software business that sells to teachers for a few years, mostly in spare hours around a brutal Japanese salaryman job, and you're about to quit to go full time. Write a long, practical blog post for programmers who want to run a business on the side with only a few hours a week: what actually lets you pull it off?
response:
# I Ran a Software Business for Teachers From a Salaryman Job. Here’s What Actually Made It Possible

I’m about to quit my day job.

For the past few years, I’ve been running a small software business that sells to teachers. My day job is the kind of brutal Japanese salaryman job that leaves you with a tired brain at 21:30: morning meetings, afternoon client work, a long commute, and the occasional business trip that turns the evening into a hotel room, a laptop, and a half-dead body. I built the side business in 30- to 90-minute pieces. Sometimes I worked on it during lunch. Sometimes I answered one support email before bed. Sometimes I did nothing for a week.

People ask how I pulled it off without burning out.

The honest answer is that I did not pull it off by being heroic. I pulled it off by making the business small enough, boring enough, and automated enough that it could survive my absence.

If you are a programmer and you want to run a software business on the side with only a few hours a week, the first thing to understand is this: a side business is not a startup with fewer hours. It is a different animal. A startup can absorb chaos because it has time, money, and tolerance for mess. A side business has none of those in surplus. It has to be narrow, self-serve, low-support, and reachable in small doses. If it requires more than that, it will become a second job.

What actually lets you pull it off is not willpower. It is design.

Below is what I learned.

---

## 1. Start with the channel, not the code

As programmers, we usually start with the product. We see a problem, we sketch a feature, we build a demo. That is understandable. Code is the part we understand. But for a side business, the first question is not “What can I build?” It is “Can I reach the buyer with the hours I actually have?”

If your customers are teachers, ask: where are they already spending time? What do they already read? Where do they complain? How would one teacher tell another teacher about a tool?

For me, the answer was online teacher communities, a few blogs, social posts, and word of mouth. I could spend 30 minutes a day reading threads, answering questions, sharing examples, and collecting emails. That was enough. If I had needed to cold-call schools, book meetings, or run paid ads from day one, I would have failed.

Do not build the product until you can get in front of potential customers repeatedly without a full-time marketing job.

A practical test: can you talk to 100 potential users in a month using only 30 minutes a day? If not, the customer is probably wrong for a side business.

I spent more time listening to teachers than writing code in the early months. I read what they were frustrated by, what they already tried, what they would pay for, and what they refused to use because it added work. That was more valuable than any feature list.

---

## 2. Choose a problem that is small, recurring, and personal

Teachers are busy. Their problems are often practical and repetitive: making worksheets, organizing class lists, tracking homework, preparing materials, managing seating charts, communicating with parents, planning lessons.

For a side business, you want a problem that is:

- small enough to solve in a narrow product,
- recurring enough that the customer comes back,
- personal enough that an individual teacher can decide to buy it.

The last point matters a lot.

If the buyer is “the school,” stop. School purchases often mean budgets, approvals, procurement, security reviews, invoicing, training, and support. That is a sales job. A side business should not have a sales job.

I focused on tools that a single teacher could buy for their own classroom. The teacher is the user, the buyer, and the support contact. That keeps the loop short.

A good side-business problem often sounds boring. “Make practice worksheets faster” is not exciting. “Build an AI-powered learning platform” is exciting, but also enormous. Teachers do not need exciting. They need time back.

If the problem is too broad, you will end up building a platform. If the problem is too rare, you will not have enough customers. You want something a teacher needs every week or every term.

---

## 3. Make the product do one job

The biggest temptation for a programmer is to make the product do too much.

You build the core feature. Then you add a dashboard. Then you add analytics. Then you add a mobile app. Then you add an API. Then you add integrations. Then you add AI. Then you add a team workspace. Then you add a settings page with 40 options.

Every one of those is a support surface.

For a side business, the product should do one job so well that the user rarely needs you.

My product’s core loop was simple: create a class, enter student names or labels, choose a worksheet or class-management task, and export or use the result. That was it. No fancy dashboard. No deep reporting. No integrations with school systems. No mobile app. No “smart recommendations.”

Each feature you add is not just code. It is documentation, support questions, edge cases, bugs, migration work, and user confusion. A feature that takes two hours to build can create twenty hours of maintenance over a year.

When I was tired, I used a simple rule: if a feature would require explaining itself in a support email, I delayed it.

Programmers often think the bottleneck is the build. It usually is not. The build is the part we enjoy and understand. The business is the set of unglamorous processes around the build: signup, payment, onboarding, support, renewal, cancellation, refund, data deletion, privacy questions, and “why did my PDF come out wrong?”

If you cannot write those processes down on one page, you do not have a side business. You have a demo with ambitions.

---



## 4. Self-serve is not a preference. It is the business model

A side business needs to work when you are asleep, commuting, stuck in a meeting, or on a business trip.

That means the customer must be able to buy and use the product without you.

No phone calls. No onboarding meetings. No “let me show you around.” No custom setup. No “email me your class list and I’ll import it.”

If a teacher has to ask you a question before they can get value, the product is not done.

I aimed for this: a new teacher can sign up, pay, create a class, and produce something useful in under 10 minutes. If it took longer, I treated that as a product bug, not a user problem.

Self-serve means:

- clear signup,
- obvious first step,
- default templates that work,
- simple pricing,
- payment that works,
- documentation that answers the obvious questions,
- cancellation that works without an email request.

This is where a lot of small software businesses die. They are easy to build but hard to use without the builder standing next to the customer.

A teacher should not need to understand your architecture. They should not need to know what a “workspace” is, what a “template instance” is, or why the export button is disabled. They need to solve their problem and leave.

If your product requires a 20-minute video tutorial before first use, it is probably too complex for a side business.

---

## 5. Support is the real product

The product is not the code. The product is the thing that keeps you from answering emails.

Support is the killer of side businesses.

Suppose you have 100 paying teachers. If 10% need one support email per month, that is 10 emails. If each takes 15 minutes, that is 2.5 hours per month. Manageable.

If 50% need one email per month, that is 50 emails. At 15 minutes each, that is 12.5 hours per month. At 30 minutes each, that is 25 hours per month. That is gone. That is your side business hours. That is your sleep.

Support is not just email. It is:

- “I can’t log in.”
- “The PDF is blank.”
- “Can you add this font?”
- “How do I delete a student?”
- “Can you export this for me?”
- “Our school needs a custom invoice.”
- “Can you integrate with our LMS?”
- “Why did my subscription renew?”
- “I want a refund.”
- “Can you do a quick call to show me how this works?”

Each of those is a small time leak. Individually, they seem reasonable. Together, they become a job.

I tried to keep support as low as possible by making the product predictable.

Things that helped:

- default templates that worked without configuration,
- clear error messages instead of silent failures,
- validation so bad input was caught early,
- a FAQ that answered the top five questions,
- a status page for outages,
- self-serve cancellation,
- self-serve data export and deletion,
- simple pricing with no confusing tiers,
- no custom work unless it could be generalized and documented.

I also batched support. I did not answer emails every time my phone buzzed. I checked at set times. That kept the business from bleeding into the whole evening.

A useful metric is support hours per paying customer per month. You do not need a perfect number. You need a warning system. If support is eating more than 10–20% of your business hours, something is wrong. Either the product is too confusing, the customers are too diverse, the price is too low, or you accepted too many edge cases.

When support rises, do not just work harder. Fix the cause.

Sometimes the fix is documentation. Sometimes it is a better default. Sometimes it is removing a feature. Sometimes it is raising the price so you can afford to be more selective. Sometimes it is saying no to a type of customer.

---

## 6. Do not sell to schools

This is one of the hardest lessons.

A school deal can look attractive. One school might mean 20 teachers. That seems better than acquiring 20 individual teachers one by one.

But a school deal often changes the entire shape of the business.

Suddenly you may need:

- a security questionnaire,
- a data processing agreement,
- a formal invoice,
- a purchase order,
- single sign-on,
- admin controls,
- custom data retention rules,
- training for staff,
- a named account manager,
- a longer sales cycle,
- legal review,
- procurement approval,
- renewal negotiation,
- and a different support relationship.

A school deal that pays 10 times an individual customer can easily cost 100 times as much in time.

For a side business, that trade is usually bad.

I sold to individual teachers. If a teacher wanted to buy for their school, I kept it simple. If they had a school card and could handle the purchase themselves, fine. If the school wanted to go through procurement, I said no or pointed them elsewhere.

This limited growth. That was the point.

A side business should not require you to become a vendor. Once you become a vendor, you inherit the customer’s internal processes. You start caring about their compliance calendar, their IT constraints, their renewal politics, and their internal definitions of “done.”

That is a real business. It can be a good business. But it is not a side business for a person working a brutal day job.

If you want to sell to schools, be honest with yourself: you are building a B2B company, not a side project. B2B can be great, but it usually requires more time, more trust, and more operational maturity.

---

## 7. Price like a side business

Pricing is not just a number. It is a filter.

If your price is low enough that an individual teacher can buy it without a meeting, you keep the sales cycle short. If your price is high enough that it requires a budget conversation, you have added a sales process.

For a side business, I would choose a price that is easy for the buyer to approve personally.

The exact amount depends on your market. In some countries, teachers may pay out of pocket. In others, they may use small classroom funds. In Japan, the comfortable price point may be a few hundred yen per month. In the U.S., it may be a few dollars per month. The important thing is not the currency. It is the decision process.

A good side-business price has these properties:

- the buyer can decide quickly,
- the price is easy to explain,
- the annual option reduces friction,
- there is no complicated tiering,
- the price covers your support cost,
- and you can raise it later without breaking trust.

I would avoid a permanent free tier unless it is extremely limited and requires almost no support. Free users are still users. They still get confused. They still write emails. They still expect things to work. But they do not pay.

A free trial can work. A free tier is a different commitment.

If you have 1,000 free users and 100 paying users, the free users can drown you. I have seen small tools become support black holes because the free version was too useful but too under-resourced.

If you want to use a free tool for marketing, make it small, obvious, and low-support. A one-page worksheet generator that exports a PDF can be fine. A free “class management platform” with accounts, imports, and notifications is probably not.

If your product is confusing, raising the price will not fix it. But if your product is stable and you are spending too much time acquiring too many small customers, a higher price can reduce volume and make the business more sustainable.

## 8. Market in 30-minute chunks

You do not need a growth hack. You need repeated, small, useful exposure.

Thirty minutes a day is 175 hours a year. That is not enough to become a category leader. It is enough to become the obvious small tool in a narrow niche if the product is self-serve and the audience is reachable.

For teachers, marketing works best when it looks like one helpful teacher talking to another teacher.

What worked for me:

- sharing a specific worksheet template,
- showing a before-and-after,
- posting a short screen recording,
- answering a common question in a thread,
- sharing a teacher’s result with permission,
- writing a short note about a problem I had seen,
- sending a simple email to my list,
- asking happy users to forward the tool to a colleague.

I did not try to be everywhere. I picked a few channels where teachers already were and showed up consistently.

One of the most important marketing assets is an email list. Not because email is magical, but because it gives you a direct channel that you own. Social platforms change. Algorithms change. Groups close. Schools block sites. Your list remains.

Do not overthink this. The goal is not to build a brand. The goal is to make the next teacher find you with low effort.

"Research taste is mostly calibration. A problem can be excellent and still be wrong for you. A 'good' problem for a second-year is not the most important open problem in the field; it is a problem where your effort can change the answer. That means you need to judge four things at once: importance, tractability, fit, and communicability. Importance asks whether a result would matter to someone outside your lab. Tractability asks whether you can get a first result before morale and funding collapse. Fit asks whether you have the skills, data, compute, theoretical background, and advisor support. Communicability asks whether you can explain the question, the method, and the result in a paragraph, a talk, or a paper.

A problem that fails any one of these can still be worth a small probe, but it is usually not the right main project. A problem that is important but intractable becomes a dissertation-shaped hole. A problem that is tractable but unimportant becomes a busywork paper. A problem that is important and tractable but not yours becomes a project where you are always one dependency away from stopping."

Good.

Section 2: Build raw material.

"You cannot train taste by sitting with a blank page. Taste comes from comparing many problems to their outcomes. Build a case file. For each paper you read, especially ones that influenced your field, write down: What question did the authors choose? Why was it worth asking? What was already known? What was the gap? What made the problem tractable? What would a weak version of the same idea have looked like? What result would have made the paper fail? What did the paper change?

Do this for recent papers and older ones. A paper from five years ago that is still cited often reveals a problem with durable importance. A paper from one year ago that nobody discusses may reveal a fad or a dead end. Read critiques, negative results, retracted or corrected claims, and 'lessons learned' posts when you can find them. They are more instructive than successful papers because they show where the ground gives way.

The point is not to memorize topics. It is to build patterns. You begin to notice that good empirical problems often have a clear comparison, a plausible mechanism, and a dataset that can actually test it. Good theory problems often have a toy case that captures the core difficulty. Good systems problems often have a bottleneck that can be measured. Bad problems often have a cool method attached to a vague application, or a broad goal with no first experiment.

Keep the file simple. One paragraph per paper is enough. After a few dozen entries, you will start to recognize the shape of a problem before you have fully read the abstract. That recognition is the beginning of taste."

Section 3: Filter.

"Use a filter, not a single rule. There is no formula that turns a topic into a good problem, but a set of questions can stop you from wasting months. Write a one-page memo for each candidate. The memo should force you to answer: What exactly is the question? Why now? What is known? What is unknown? What would a good result look like? What would a bad result look like, and would it still be informative? What is the smallest experiment, proof, or analysis that would test it? What resources are needed? What is the main risk? What would make you abandon it?

Then score the problem, but only as a way to make your judgment explicit. Importance: who cares, and what would they do differently? Tractability: can you get a first result in 4-8 weeks? Fit: do you have the skills and access? Timing: is the field ready for this, or is it too early or too late? Audience: who will read it, and what do they already believe? Fallback: if the main result fails, what artifact remains?

A useful test is the citation test. Imagine a future paper citing yours. What would it say? 'We follow X for Y' is weak if Y is trivial. 'X showed that A fails under B, which motivated our approach' is stronger. If you cannot imagine a citation that matters, the problem may be too narrow, too broad, or not connected to a live debate.

Another test is the baseline test. In empirical work, ask what the strongest existing method or explanation would predict. If your result is not clearly better or different from that baseline, it may not mean much. In theory, ask for a simple example where the claim is true and one where it is false. If you cannot construct them, the claim is probably not yet clear.

Do not let the memo become bureaucracy. Its purpose is to reveal what you do not know. If you write 'Why now?' and cannot answer, that is a signal. If you write 'Kill criteria' and feel reluctant, that is also a signal. A good problem should be able to survive being written down."

Section 4: small bets.

"Run small bets before committing. A second-year student has limited bandwidth, so the goal is not to launch a grand project; it is to buy information. Choose two or three two-week probes on your top candidates. Reproduce a key result. Collect a small dataset. Build a baseline. Prove a toy lemma. Run a pilot on a subset. Interview a domain expert. The probe should be cheap, time-boxed, and designed to fail in a way that teaches you something.

Small bets expose hidden costs. A problem that looks clean in a memo may depend on a dataset that is messy, a proof that requires a lemma nobody has written, a hardware setup that takes a month, or an ethics review that is longer than expected. These are not trivial details; they are often the difference between a project and a life sentence. If a probe reveals that the key variable is not measured, or that the baseline already solves the toy case, you have saved months.

Do not dismiss small projects as 'not real research.' Finishing small things is one of the best ways to develop taste. The last mile of research—robustness checks, baselines, writing, reviewer objections—is where many problems die. If you have not done the last mile before, you will overestimate how easy it will be. A two-week project that produces a figure, a table, or a short negative result is valuable even if it never becomes a paper, because it gives you a concrete sense of what the work feels like.

When you run a probe, write down what you expected and what happened. 'I thought the data would be clean; it was not' is a calibration event. 'I thought the proof would take two weeks; the first lemma was already hard' is a calibration event. Over time, these notes become a personal base rate."

Section 5: feedback.

"Get feedback from people who can afford to be honest. Do not ask, 'Is this a good idea?' That invites politeness. Ask specific questions: 'What would it take for this to be a strong paper?' 'What do you think is missing?' 'What baseline would you expect?' 'What result would surprise you?' 'Who else is working on this?' 'What would make you stop?'

Ask people one or two steps ahead of you: senior PhD students, postdocs, junior faculty, or researchers who have published the kind of work you want to do. They know the local standards and the hidden dependencies. Also ask one skeptical outsider, someone outside your immediate subfield, to test whether you can explain the problem plainly. If they cannot say what the question is or why it matters, your problem statement is probably not ready.

Treat feedback as data, not as an attack. If three different people point to the same weakness, update. If they are confused, ask them to say exactly where the chain of reasoning breaks. Keep a list of objections and how you resolved them: you fixed the design, you narrowed the claim, you found prior work, or you abandoned the idea. This list is part of your taste training. It teaches you which objections are real and which are noise.

Do not rely only on your advisor. Your advisor's taste is valuable, especially for scope, audience, and institutional fit, but if you never form your own judgment, you will remain dependent and slow. Bring options, not just questions. 'Here are three problems I am considering, with memos and probes. Here is what I think the risks are. Which one would you fund, and why?' That gives your advisor something concrete to shape and forces you to think like the owner of the project."

"The common failures are less exotic than they sound.

One is choosing a topic instead of a problem. 'Deep learning for healthcare' is not a problem. It is a field. A problem has a question, a unit of analysis, and a test. If your idea is a noun phrase, shrink it until it becomes a sentence.

Two is chasing novelty for its own sake. A brand-new topic can be exciting, but novelty is not the same as value. Sometimes the best contribution is a careful answer to an old question that everyone assumed was settled. Conversely, a slightly old question can be valuable if it is underexplored in a setting where it matters. Ask what would be new in the result, not just in the title.

Three is method-driven problem selection. You have a cool algorithm and you look for an application. This often produces work where the method is the star and the problem is an afterthought. The fix is to ask what the method can reveal that other methods cannot, and whether the application has a real bottleneck that the method addresses.

Four is data-driven problem selection. You have a dataset and you search for a question. Data availability can make a project easier, but it does not make it important. Ask what can be learned from this data that was not known before, and whether the data can actually support the causal or comparative claim you want.

Five is benchmark chasing. If a field is saturated on a metric, squeezing out a small gain may be low-value unless you understand why the gain happens or show that it transfers to a harder setting. A better problem often lives in the failure cases: where the current best methods break, why they break, and whether a fix generalizes.

Six is underestimating dependencies. Many projects die not from intellectual difficulty but from access: data, compute, IRB approval, domain collaborators, maintenance, or a person who must sign off. List the dependencies before you start. Mark which are under your control. If a critical dependency is outside your control and has a long lead time, the problem is riskier than it looks.

Seven is overestimating your own speed and skill. This is normal. You have not done enough finished work to know how long proofs, experiments, or writing take. The correction is not humility for its own sake; it is probes and milestones. If a task looks like three months, ask for a two-week version that would reveal whether the estimate is plausible.

Eight is not defining a strong baseline. In empirical work, a result without a good comparison is often uninterpretable. In theory, a claim without a toy example is often untestable. Before you commit, write down the baseline you would have to beat or explain. If you cannot, you do not yet understand the problem.

Nine is designing a problem where only a positive result matters. If a null result would be useless, the project is brittle. Good problems have informative failure modes: a negative result that clarifies a boundary condition, identifies a missing variable, or rules out a mechanism. If failure teaches nothing, the design is probably wrong.

Ten is ignoring the audience. A problem may be interesting to you but not to the people who will read it. Ask who will care, what they already believe, and what would change their mind. If the answer is 'everyone' or 'no one', the scope is probably off. A good PhD problem usually has a clear readership: a subfield, a community of practice, or a set of adjacent groups that would benefit from the result.

Eleven is not killing fast. Sunk cost is the enemy of taste. If you have written kill criteria and they are met, take them seriously. A quick pivot is not failure; it is the system working. The expensive mistake is spending another six months on a problem because you have already invested three.

Twelve is confusing activity with progress. Reading more papers, writing more code, collecting more data, and attending more seminars can feel like research, but if they do not answer a question or reduce uncertainty, they are maintenance. Progress is a change in what you know, what you can do, or what you are willing to claim.

Thirteen is not checking prior work thoroughly. A problem that seems new may be old, or may have been tried and abandoned for a reason. Search backward and forward through citations, check preprints, look for talks, and ask people who have been in the field for a while. If you find prior work, do not just panic; ask what it did, what it left open, and whether your version is meaningfully different.

Fourteen is letting your taste become only your advisor's taste. Your advisor can save you from bad scope and bad politics, but you still need to learn to make calls. If you cannot explain why a problem is good without saying 'because my advisor said so,' you are not developing judgment. Use your advisor as a coach, not an oracle.

Fifteen is not recording what you learned. Taste is memory. If you do not keep a case file of problems, probes, objections, and outcomes, you will repeat the same miscalibrations. The record does not need to be elaborate. It needs to be honest."

Section 7: practical loop.

"A practical loop for the next three months. This is not a universal schedule, but it is a way to force calibration.

Days 1-15: Build the case file. Read 15-20 papers... write one paragraph each. List 10 open questions you notice.

Days 16-30: Generate candidates. Write 30 one-sentence problem statements. Do not judge yet. Use sources: papers, talks, advisor projects, domain problems, failure cases, anomalies. Then cut to 10.

Days 31-45: Memo and feedback. For top 5, write one-page memos. Ask 3 people for specific objections. Update memos.

Days 46-60: Probes. Pick top 2. Run two-week probes. Write what you expected, what happened, what the hidden costs were.

Days 61-75: Decide. Choose one problem or a pair of linked problems. Define a 3-month plan with milestones: first result, baseline, write-up, next experiment. Define kill criteria.

Days 76-90: Execute first milestone. Do not let the plan drift. At the end, write a short postmortem: what was right, what was wrong, what you would change.

The goal is not to have a perfect problem by day 90. The goal is to have a live problem, evidence that it is tractable, and a record of how you decided. That is how taste compounds."

The letter contains a common trap. If a person says she does not know who she is, she often means she has no stable story: no fixed set of tastes, no clear origin, no answer that would satisfy a form or a friend. From there it is a short step to the conclusion that she has nothing to say. The songwriter’s reply—she did not need to know—sounds like a dismissal of identity, but it is more useful if heard as a correction of timing. You do not need to know yourself in order to begin. You may need to know enough to pay attention, and the rest can be learned in the making.

There are at least two kinds of self-knowledge. One is the answer you can give when someone asks what you are about. It is the narrative self: the story you tell about your values, your past, your commitments. The other is the smaller, less flattering knowledge of your own responses: what you notice first, what you avoid, what you can do with your hands or voice, what makes you stiffen, what you keep returning to. A person can be badly off on the first and richly equipped on the second. A woman in a new city may not know what kind of person she is becoming, but she may know that she cannot bear loud kitchens, that she is drawn to the river at dusk, that she writes in short sentences when she is afraid. That second kind of knowledge is often what art actually uses.

If creative work required the first kind, a great deal of important work would have to wait until people reached some settled middle age or emerged from a crisis with a label. But many makers work precisely because they are unsettled. Bob Dylan did not become an electric rock artist by first resolving who he was; the recordings show a person testing a new voice and letting the voice answer. Picasso moved through cubism, classicism, and caricature without waiting for a fixed identity to approve. The work is not a report from a finished self. It is a way of becoming one.

This is why the songwriter’s reply is tempting. A young maker often feels she must first collect a biography, sort out her wounds, and decide her style before she is allowed to produce a thing. But the making can do the collecting. A writer may begin a scene in which a character is supposed to be angry and discover, mid-page, that the character is actually ashamed. The writer has learned something about her own capacity for shame. A musician may hum a phrase and find that it carries a grief she had not named. A painter may mix two colors and see an emotion she would not have

The letter contains a common trap. There are at least two kinds of self-knowledge. One is the answer you can give when someone asks what you are about. The other is the smaller, less flattering knowledge of your own responses: what you notice first, what you avoid, what you can do with your hands or voice, what makes you stiffen, what you keep returning to. A person can be badly off on the first and richly equipped on the second. A woman in a new city may not know what kind of person she is becoming, but she may know that she cannot bear loud kitchens, that she is drawn to the river at dusk, that she writes in short sentences when she is afraid. That second kind of knowledge is often what art actually uses.

If creative work required the first kind, a great deal of important work would have to wait until people reached some settled middle age or emerged from a crisis with a label. But many makers work precisely because they are unsettled. Picasso moved through cubism, classicism, and caricature without waiting for a fixed identity to approve. The work is not a report from a finished self. It is a way of becoming one.

If a maker cannot tell a genuine impulse from an affectation, a memory from a borrowed image, a need to please from a need to tell the truth, the work may become hollow. A young poet may write beautifully in the voice of every poet she admires and have no center. A photographer may take technically clean pictures that do not matter to him. prompt: Everyone in crypto is proposing new governance models, but they nearly all boil down to some form of voting. Write a post questioning that: what's wrong with voting as a governance mechanism, especially for decentralized communities, and what could replace it?
response:
**The vote is the wrong primitive for most decentralized governance**

A DAO has $10 million in its treasury. A proposal appears: invest $2 million in a new yield strategy. Token holders vote. The result is 63% yes, with 7% of all tokens participating. What just happened? Not a decision in any strong sense. Not a contract. Not an allocation of responsibility. It is a signal from a subset of token holders, with no clear obligation attached to the outcome. Yet the next step in most crypto governance discussions is not to ask whether a vote was the right tool, but to propose a better vote: delegated voting, quadratic voting, liquid democracy, elected councils, on-chain referenda, off-chain forums feeding into on-chain ballots. The form changes. The underlying move does not.

That is the problem.

Voting is seductive because it is simple, familiar, and easy to encode. A yes/no button feels democratic. It turns disagreement into a number. It gives a community a sense of collective agency without requiring anyone to build the harder institutions that make collective action work over time. But a decentralized community is not a town meeting, and most of its governance problems are not problems of preference aggregation. They are problems of coordination, competence, risk allocation, and accountability.

A vote makes sense in a state because a state has a bounded population, compulsory jurisdiction, and a monopoly on enforcement. Citizens cannot easily leave. Taxes are mandatory. Laws bind everyone. Voting provides legitimacy to coercion. A decentralized protocol is different. It is open, global, pseudonymous, and exit is cheap. Users can move their funds. Developers can fork. Liquidity can migrate to a competing protocol. The central question is not “who rules?” but “how do strangers coordinate and allocate risk without a central authority?” A referendum is a poor answer to that question.

What a vote does not do is discover knowledge. A token holder’s preference about a treasury investment is not evidence that the investment will work. The person running the strategy, the counterparty, the auditor, the market maker, and the people who have already tried a similar approach all have different information. A vote collapses all of that into yes or no. It cannot distinguish “I want this because it benefits my position” from “I have spent two years testing this and it survives realistic stress cases.” Governance is not just about who wants what. It is about who knows what, who is accountable for what, and who bears the downside when the answer turns out to be wrong.

Voting also tends to be captured by intensity rather than judgment. Low turnout means the motivated minority decides. In token-weighted systems, the vote becomes a function of portfolio size, leverage, and short-term position rather than long-term stewardship. In one-person-one-vote systems, you get sybil risk unless you solve identity, and solving identity in a permissionless way is hard. Even when participation is high, the vote measures who showed up, not who should decide. A person with a small token balance and a strong ideological position can have the same vote as a person who has built a business on the protocol, if the system is one-person-one-vote. In a token-weighted system, a whale with a short-term trade can outvote a group of long-term builders. Neither version is very good at finding the people best placed to make the decision.

Then there is the responsibility gap. If a vote passes and the treasury loses money, who is liable? The voters? They cast a costless preference. The proposers? Maybe they receive a bounty. The protocol? It absorbs the loss. Voting socializes downside while privatizing initiative. That makes proposals reckless in subtle ways. A person who has no skin in the game beyond their vote can support a risky or ideological change with the same ease as they would reject it. If the decision fails, the loss is diffuse. If it succeeds, the benefit may be concentrated. That is not a stable basis for governance.

Votes are also too coarse. A proposal bundles many decisions into one text: the amount, the counterparty, the terms, the timing, the risk limits, the exit conditions. Voters cannot approve the idea but reject the counterparty, or accept the amount but demand better collateral. The real negotiation happens before the vote, in the proposal itself, usually written by a small group. The vote then becomes ratification, not deliberation. That is why many on-chain votes feel like a performance: the decision has already been made, and the vote is there to make it look legitimate.

This is especially bad for operational and technical decisions. Patching an exploit, adjusting an oracle parameter, pausing a market, or changing a risk limit requires speed, expertise, and accountability. A vote is slow and creates a false sense of collective ownership. A protocol does not need to put integer overflow to a referendum. It needs engineers, auditors, staged rollouts, circuit breakers, and clear escalation paths. When technical decisions are governed by vote, the result is often either delay or a thin layer of democratic legitimacy over a decision that was really made by a small technical team.

Many governance tokens are, in practice, a way to make a token look useful. The vote is a feature for the token, not for the protocol. Proposals are few, turnout is low, and the important decisions are made off-chain by the team, the whales, and the most organized stakeholders. That is not governance. It is legitimacy packaging.

The strongest objection to this view is obvious: if not voting, what stops governance from becoming rule by experts, founders, whales, or foundations? That is a real risk. Any mechanism that gives decision rights to a few people can be captured. But the alternative to voting is not “no rules.” It is a stack of narrower mechanisms, each with its own accountability, and voting reserved for the rare cases where a community truly must choose among incompatible claims.

The first replacement is a constitution made of rules, not ballots. A good constitutional layer is mostly defaults, limits, and triggers. No single investment above 10% of the treasury. No leverage above 2x. No withdrawal above a certain size without a 30-day delay. No parameter change without a sandbox test and a rollback plan. No manager authority without collateral. The point is not to remove all human judgment, but to make most decisions automatic and to push judgment to the places where it is most valuable. A vote should be the exception, not the operating system.

The second replacement is modular autonomy. Instead of one central treasury deciding everything, split the community into units: liquidity, grants, research, risk, development, operations. Each unit has a budget, a mandate, and a boundary. A grants team does not vote on lending parameters. A risk committee does not decide marketing. Teams get operating grants with milestones, public dashboards, and clawbacks. If a module underperforms, its budget shrinks. If it works, it gets more authority. This turns governance into internal markets and accountability rather than a single assembly trying to manage everything.

A concrete version would look like this. A DAO creates a manager marketplace for treasury capital. Any manager can submit a strategy, accept a $500,000 mandate, post 20% collateral, agree to a 10% single-asset limit, and submit to a three-month review. If the strategy underperforms the agreed benchmark by more than 5% after fees, the mandate is reduced. If it survives and performs well, it can be renewed or expanded. The community does not vote on each trade. It sets the arena, enforces the rules, and lets capital flow to the people who demonstrate skill and accept risk.

Markets are not perfect. They can be manipulated, they ignore externalities, and they underprovide public goods like security research and developer tooling. But for many decisions, especially capital allocation, a market is more informative than a vote because it forces participants to put money behind their claims. A vote says “I prefer this.” A market says “I will pay for this, and I lose if I am wrong.”

Prediction markets and forecasting can replace votes in another way: by improving the information available before a decision is made. Before a large parameter change, the community may not know the probability of a run, an exploit, or a liquidity shock. A prediction market or calibrated forecasting process can aggregate that uncertainty. What is the chance this change causes a 20% drop in volume? What is the expected cost of this exploit over six months? What is the probability this oracle will fail under stress? The output is not a decision. It is a better estimate. That is often what governance actually needs.

Bonding and insurance can do the same work from the accountability side. If a proposer wants to change a parameter or allocate funds, require a bond. If the change causes measurable harm, the bond is slashed. If it works, the bond is returned or rewarded. Let third parties insure the risk. Their premiums reveal how dangerous the community should consider the proposal. This makes governance costly in the right way: not costly because of quorums and ceremony, but costly because bad decisions have consequences for the people making them. Tying decision rights to liability has legal complications, but the principle is sound: control should come with risk.

Technical problems need technical governance. Code upgrades, security patches, and protocol invariants should be handled by peer review, audits, staged rollouts, canaries, circuit breakers, and bug bounties. Ethereum is a useful example. Major upgrades are not decided by token votes. They are pushed by core developers, client teams, auditors, and social consensus among node operators. That process is elite and imperfect. It has not prevented all mistakes. But it has handled major upgrades without turning every technical choice into a referendum. A protocol can be decentralized in deployment and still use highly competent, bounded technical authority internally.

Exit and reputation should also be treated as governance mechanisms. In an open ecosystem, users vote with their feet. If a protocol is mismanaged, liquidity leaves, developers stop contributing, and the brand decays. Forks are a form of governance too: they allow a dissatisfied community to preserve the old rules or try a new one. A healthy protocol should expect exit and treat it as information, not betrayal. The question is not how to force everyone to stay and vote, but how to make staying worthwhile.

For disputes, use courts, arbitration, or small adjudicative bodies rather than general voting. When two parties disagree over a shared resource, a court can decide based on rules and evidence. Its legitimacy comes from the rulebook, the appeal process, and the reputation of the judges, not from a majority. A panel of three appointed for one year, with appeal to a larger panel, can resolve disputes over misappropriated funds, contested grants, or unclear intellectual property rights. That is slower than a vote, but it is more legitimate than a 51% token outcome in a low-turnout ballot.

Voting still has a place. When a protocol must change its constitution, distribute newly created rent, or choose among incompatible visions that cannot be resolved by markets, rules, or courts, some form of collective choice is needed. A fee change is a legitimate vote if it is a one-time constitutional choice about who receives protocol revenue. But if the community then votes on every fee parameter, every pool, every treasury spend, and every grant, the vote has become management. Even where voting is appropriate, it should be narrow, rare, and constrained: a cooling-off period, a high bar for binding effect, separate stakeholder classes where interests are structurally different, and a clear fork path if the result is contested. A vote can also be a coordination signal for a fork: if a large enough share rejects a change, the result is not that the minority must obey, but that the ecosystem may split.

The reason crypto keeps proposing new voting models is that voting is easy to explain and easy to code. A button on a website feels democratic. But a decentralized community is not a single polity. It is a network of contracts, markets, reputations, and local experiments. The best governance is the kind that makes fewer decisions collectively: clear rules, bounded authority, skin in the game, and the ability to exit. If a protocol needs to vote on every treasury allocation, every parameter tweak, and every grant, it has not decentralized governance. It has centralized indecision.

prompt: It's the day before the 2016 US election and the race looks close. I'm worried everyone will draw sweeping conclusions about the country from whichever way it falls. Write a short essay on how we should think about what the result will mean.
response:
A close election is the worst kind of evidence for a simple story. It gives each side a winner and a loser, and the margin looks like a verdict. But a presidential election is not a national opinion poll, and a close one is especially hard to read.

The presidency is not decided by the national popular vote. It is decided by state margins, many of them narrow. In 2000, George W. Bush lost the national popular vote to Al Gore by about 540,000 votes, but won the office because of the Electoral College; the final margin in Florida was 537 votes. In 2016, a one- or two-point shift in Pennsylvania, Ohio, Florida, or North Carolina can matter more to the outcome than a million votes cast in a state that is safely blue or safely red. If tomorrow’s result is close, it may mean that the two candidates are nearly tied in a handful of counties, not that the country is evenly split on every issue raised in the campaign.

Voters are also choosing candidates, not answering a questionnaire. Clinton and Trump are not neutral bundles of policy. They carry different records, styles, and symbolic meanings. A voter may be moved by trade, immigration, health care, foreign policy, anger at Washington, fear of social change, or a judgment about character. The same margin can be produced by different mixtures of those motives. A Trump win in Michigan could reflect resentment over manufacturing jobs, opposition to immigration, or rejection of Clinton. A Clinton win in Ohio could reflect fear of instability, support for the existing regulatory state, or higher turnout among Black and urban voters. Until we know which counties moved and who showed up, the number does not by itself tell us which story is true.

A winner will also have real power. The president sets an agenda, uses the veto, makes appointments, directs agencies, and speaks with authority. That is not nothing. But a presidential victory is not a clean referendum, and a close victory is the least clean kind. Presidents share power with Congress, the courts, governors, party organizations, and a bureaucracy that does not always move. In 2008, Barack Obama won by more than seven points in the popular vote and 365 electoral votes to 173. Two years later, Republicans took the House and gained Senate seats, and the political space for his agenda shrank. If a landslide can be checked by midterms, a narrow win should not be mistaken for a national settlement.

The strongest objection to this cautious reading is that it may sound like it is denying voters their choice. If people have picked between two visions, and one vision wins, the winner’s coalition has earned a legitimate claim to lead. In a two-party system, the choice between Clinton and Trump is a substantive choice, not a trivial formality. That is true. But a legitimate mandate is still a limited fact. It means that a coalition large enough to win key states is organized, motivated, and willing to show up. It does not mean that the whole country has adopted the winner’s diagnosis of America’s problems, or that the result settles how deep, how permanent, or how policy-specific the underlying sentiment is.

So the first task after the vote is not to declare a verdict but to separate the map from the message: which counties changed, which groups showed up, whether the winner gained support or the loser’s base stayed home, and which institutions now stand between the winner and the policies he or she wants. Those details are less dramatic than a national diagnosis, but they are where the meaning actually is.
